chapter: Three stories
name: Story one
text:
Tereza picked up her pace because she was getting cold.

Dusk fell on the city, so she tried not to linger anywhere unnecessarily. After a while, however, she stopped to look into the light of a street lamp and watch the falling snow. And it was... gorgeous. She wondered when she had last seen something like this. She remembered. Back then in the mountains, still as a little girl. Right there she saw flakes so big and falling so much that it resembled falling feathers.

The surrounding park was covered in snow and glistened beautifully in the lamplights. Tereza felt the flakes tickle her cheek and let herself drift away in nostalgia for a while longer. Still, when she exhaled and a puff of steam rose from her mouth, she snapped back to reality. To that reality where it freezes in the winter and the tips of the fingers freeze.

She shook the snow from her coat and hair and wanted to set off again, but at that moment she was overcome with anxiety. It was just a moment. As a warning. Something just wasn't right.

Maybe it was the surrounding silence. Silence, as if all life had suddenly passed away. But something told her that she was not alone.

She set off towards home with a quick step.

Girl, don't worry, she was calming down. Once you have enough money with you, you are immediately nervous and see crooks around every corner.

Nevertheless, she accelerated and continued at a very brisk pace. After a while she wasn't even cold anymore. A few more minutes of walking and she would be home...

She heard footsteps.

Or was she just imagining it? She looked back and saw a stocky man trudging off the footpath. He wasn't going straight to her, and there was still quite a distance between them, but if they both continued walking like they had been, their paths would soon cross. The idea suddenly made her extremely uncomfortable. And that creeping feeling.

She added to her stride again. She almost ran. Was she imagining it, or did the stranger also speed up?

Dammit, stop being so dramatic, she thought. You need to calm down.

After all, nothing is happening at all. She stopped and began searching her pockets for cigarettes. The man continued walking, but Teresa did not, so unless something unexpected happened, he would miss her by a considerable distance. She was relieved. At least a little.

She pulled out a box, a cigarette and a lighter, and inhaled her favorite smoke. She was calming down. That was the job of nicotine. Even the fact that the guy went his own way and didn't pay attention to her at all.

Tereza suddenly found the whole situation absurd. What was she crazy about? She has been here almost daily and has never had anything happen to her, nor does she know of anyone else who has experienced anything bad here. She was never afraid here. And today someone should rob her just because she has a bundle of money with her, which no robber has any idea about? She doesn't have it written on her forehead, so what are the chances that...

Someone put a hand on her shoulder. She immediately flinched, turned, and cowered in sheer terror.

There were two thugs standing in front of her. One unusually small and stocky. A massive mustache under his nose, the ends of which flowed loosely into a long black beard. He was wearing a leather biker outfit that looked like he'd been through a lot; as well as its owner, who was certainly no more than thirty years old. His dark eyes measured Tereza with a hard look that did not bode well.

The age of the other would perhaps be impossible to guess for an ignorant observer. He could easily be in his fifties, but he didn't have to be any older than his partner. When someone takes drugs so often and for so long that they sell their soul to them and they become everything to them, you don't even know how old they are. He was tall, thin, and his sunken cheeks were covered by badly shaved stubble. He was apparently missing several teeth. Not to mention his clothes... They looked like they were pulled out of a trash can, although he didn't stink now in winter. His gaze was empty and watery, which frightened Tereza even more than the darkness in his companion's eyes.

"Good evening. Wouldn't you have some spare change, lady?" whined the junkie. His voice was as blank as his gaze; and most likely life.

"Good evening. I don't have any. Sorry. Goodbye," answered Tereza neutrally and was about to leave.

No sooner had she turned than she felt that terrible hand on her shoulder again. She hated being touched by a stranger, and this was especially unpleasant. She tried to shake her hand off, but it gripped her and turned her around – the little biker was obviously a big strong man.

"Leave me!" she hissed. There was defiance in the way she said it, but also a desperation that the bearded man didn't miss. His eyes sparkled, but he withdrew his hand.

"And a cigarette? Wouldn't you have one?" wheezed the tall man, as if nothing had happened. That man, or rather what used to be man, had sunk so low that he no longer cared.

It dawned on Teresa that getting rid of them might not be so easy. By looking for cigarettes, whose location she knows precisely because she has just finished smoking, she can at least buy time to think about what to do next. She immediately appreciated the idea - that's when she thought to find pepper spray in her purse and hide it in the palm of her hand. She regretted not having a revolver with her. Either way, she would try to avoid any conflict; she wouldn't provoke them too much and could play for time—sooner or later someone might walk by even in this little-frequented area.

After a while, she handed over the entire box to the rascal in an attempt to appease them and be left alone. "Keep it, there's a lighter in there too. Take care."

"Kind of generous, isn't she? Why, I guess?" a dwarf joined the conversation. His voice sounded ominous. He wanted to instill fear in her. He wasn't after the loot so much, he was just enjoying it. He wasn't broken like his buddy, but sadistic and evil.

She didn't answer and tried to clear the field when she felt that strong hand on her shoulder again. This time she turned without resistance.

"Leave it!" she said firmly, trying not to show her fear.

"Then behave yourself and don't turn your back when I talk to you," said the little one, almost mockingly.

She didn't know what to answer. She pressed the pepper spray in her hand and prepared to use it.

"I asked you a question, as far as I know..."

"Excuse me, for what?" The trace of hopelessness in her voice that had inadvertently escaped her pleased him.

"Why are you so generous?" he asked in a kindly tone that irritated and frightened her.

"I guess I am," she sneered.

"Then you'll surely find a little spare change too, right?" the junkie rejoined the conversation. His voice sounded condescending and condescending, not at all matching what was going on around him. He perceived the whole situation obscurely, as if the body he inhabited was acting independently of his will. But it didn't matter to him anymore, he just wanted another dose, everything else was secondary to him.

She decided to leave without saying a word. And if he tries to hold her again... She gripped the pepper spray. She felt that intrusive hand on her shoulder again. A wave of anger shot through her.

That's enough! No one will touch me!

She quickly turned around. She raised her hand to counterattack. However, the dwarf was faster. He sensed her intentions. He grabbed her wrist and gripped it so hard that she dropped her weapon. She screamed. He jerked her hand downwards. She lost her balance and was heading for the ground. At the last moment she stopped her fall with her knee. There was a pain in the leg. She tried to fight back with her other hand, but the attacker caught that as well. She was at her wits end. The little robber continued to push her hands to the ground and she had no choice but to kneel down.

"Help!" she called.

"Shut up!"

"Somebody help me!" she did not give up and screamed as hard as she could.

The assailant grabbed both of her wrists with one hand while reaching for the knife with the other.

"Will you shut up now?"

This time, Tereza obeyed the call.

"Please don't hurt me."

"We'll see," smiled the burly man. "Take her things," he said towards the long man.

She knew resistance was futile. She knelt on the cold ground, feeling the wet snow. She tried not to notice the roving hands of the junkie, which were expertly going through her pockets, taking out all the valuables from them and casually throwing them into her purse, which the robbers were about to leave with.

If I don't cause trouble, maybe they'll let me live, she thought. She even hoped no one would walk by and scare the guy with the knife. He might panic and use it.

“Good girl,” the smaller assailant interrupted her thoughts with a mischievous smile on his lips. Meanwhile, the taller one finished the search and held the loot firmly in his hands.

The dwarf suddenly jerked her hands violently, which she didn't expect. She crumpled to the ground.

Luckily, she heard the two men running away. The shadows on the path beside her faded away.

For a long time she lay on the ground exactly as the vagabond had thrown her, recovering and not wanting to move. She would have called someone, but she also lost her phone... And most of all, she lost a wad of money.

She regretted her decision to cut her way through the park; however, she could not change anything with regret. She sat down, then stood up. She wasn't in much pain, the snow cover was soft, although wet and cold. On the one hand, she thought that it could have turned out worse, on the other hand, she was really sorry and upset about losing so much money. She looked around and slowly - still a little in shock - limped her way home.

A crescent moon shone in the sky.

chapter: Three stories
name: Story two
text:
Rosalie smiled at the departing guest, "Take care and come again."

"You too, and thanks," he replied. He always enjoyed coming back and left a decent tip each time.

Rosalie had a rather short-tempered and impatient nature. In her small tavern, however, she was basically nice, attentive and listened to customers. Every morning she promised herself in front of the mirror that today she would be even more professional than yesterday. She just happened to be behind the counter, a completely different world opened up in front of her, and she had it all in the palm of her hand. At that moment, it didn't matter how she felt or what her mood was. There was only one thing - to do her job precisely.

She demanded the same from her employees. "Show your guests only the best of you," she used to say.

She knew she was there for her visitors and they were there for her. Her smile, kind word, friendly environment - all these were the reasons why they came back again and again; well this and good beer to be exact.

Such was the source of her livelihood. And she wanted to earn it.

"Well gentlemen, we're closing," she said cheerfully to the table of regulars and looked around the place; most people were already gone. In addition to the regular guests, there was one more couple and a kind of strange patron at a table in the corner.

"Come on, Rouzí, bring us one more," demanded one of the regular customers.

"Well, what shall I do with you?" she smiled. "One last thing and off to bed, okay?"

"Thanks, you're the best!" a wave of joy rose from the table.

"Every woman is the best when you've been drinking..." she interjected with a smile.

She poured six beautifully dewy beers, took three in each hand and carried them to the table. Then she cashed in on a young couple who also wanted to pay. However, the weirdo in the corner made no move to leave.

She walked up to him with a smile and asked, "We're closing slowly. Can I bring you the bill?"

He fixed her with a thoughtful and unusually penetrating look. He was clean-shaven, balding, but the remnants of his hair were carefully trimmed and combed back. He didn't smile. It occurred to Rosalie that he hadn't smiled once in all that time. In fact, he didn't even speak! He also ordered the beer with a wave of his hand.

So maybe that's why I found him strange, she thought. And he's a bit scary. Did he even understand what I was telling him? Of course he did... Why wouldn't he? I highly doubt this particular guy is out of it. So why didn't he answer? And why is he still watching me?

That moment seemed absurdly long to her. At that he shook his head.

He reached into the pocket of the jacket he was still wearing. He didn't take them off the whole time; even though it was warm here. He took out a leather wallet and a banknote from it, which he placed on the table with a vigorous movement. The owner and waitress in one person started hunting for money back in her purse. The man shook his head, picked up the banknote he had placed there earlier, and handed it to the waiter. His gesture was utterly convincing and confident, which Rosalie liked; and let's be honest, she liked such a generous tip just as much.

"Thank you very much," she said with a slight blush and moved away from the stranger. She didn't know what to think of him.

The table of regulars gradually paid - some in cash, others on a tab. The guests began to rise and gradually disappear into the night. Rosalie said goodbye to each of them individually, she had known them for a long time and over time she grew to like them. But she already saw herself in bed, so she completely forgot about the mysterious stranger while saying goodbye to the noisy group.

As she closed the door, the person reminded her in an ice-cold voice, "So we're left here alone."

She was startled; she nearly jumped out of her skin. "Shit!" she exclaimed.

Then she hesitated a little. "Sorry, you startled me," she said conciliatoryly and even with a hint of a smile.

The stranger said nothing, but remained seated behind the table. It didn't look like he was about to leave.

"Thank you for visiting, but unfortunately I'm closing now."

"Close up. At least we'll have peace and quiet," he replied slowly.

"Quiet for what? Look, sir, I'm working tomorrow, I need to get some sleep, so if you..." she gestured to leave.

"Calm down for a business meeting," he measured every word.

"I don't know what you're offering or what you're looking for, but I'm not interested right now. We can meet tomorrow, okay?"

"Take a seat with me. In your own interest. It won't be long," came the uncompromising voice from the corner table.

She thought for a few seconds.

This guy certainly doesn't act like someone who came to whitewash my cash register. He doesn't look nervous, he drew attention to himself and also wanted me to sit next to him. A thief would use the element of surprise, wouldn't he? But the fear of him is nothing, she thought. What the hell could he want from me? Anyway, probably the fastest way to get rid of him is to talk to him.

"Fine, but only five minutes," she said conciliatoryly as she sat down at the table.

"I don't even need that much time," came the icy voice.

He waited for her to sit down before continuing.

"I have an offer for you from my employer. It offers protection to your business."

"Protection from what?" she was playing for time. She didn't like where their conversation was going.

"To the criminals. He only wants ten percent of your profits for it," he hung on every word.

"So you came here for protection money? Get out of my establishment immediately and don't come back, you scumbag!" she slipped. She herself was immediately frightened. She knew it wasn't wise to make him angry, but the audacity of a man who had come to threaten Rosalia in her own pub really made her angry.

The mobster smiled. He was clearly amused by her reaction. This made her even more upset.

There was a glimmer of something human in his voice for the first time, perhaps the smile was to blame. "Think about it. Mr. Bogdanov is one of the most respected businessmen. It is an honor to work with him."

She folded her arms over her chest and measured him with a hostile look.

"But it's also a big mistake not to do business with him," he said so slowly and coldly that it sent a chill down her spine.

He suddenly stood up and she instinctively pulled away.

He ignored it and said goodbye, "I'll come for an answer tomorrow. I hope you won't refuse. It would be a shame. Goodbye," he said firmly.

When the door closed behind him, Rosalie was still sitting behind the table, visibly upset.

She didn't sleep much that night, she still had to think about the events of the day.

How serious is this goon? What actually happens if I don't pay? Is the Russian mafia really threatening me? Or just a few dogs who bark but don't bite? But the poor guy didn't look twice for that. He had an expensive tailored suit and acted like someone who knew exactly what he was doing... But what if it was just a show? Maybe he's a clever con artist. Anyway, I'm not going to pay someone just because they scare me! It's all absurd! I could call the cops too, but what would I tell them? And what could they do for me? You can't rely on them even in much simpler cases, I've already tried that and got burned badly. Moreover, if it is really a mafia, then they can have the police somehow "solved". Oh well, if that gangster comes again, I'll send him to hell.

With that she concluded her thoughts shortly before falling asleep.

The next day passed quite calmly. Rosalie was mainly troubled by lack of sleep in combination with the usual hustle and bustle in the pub. She put her mobster out of her head for the job itself. After all, she had already decided that night that she would not give him anything. Evening came and he was still nowhere.

He walked through the door just before it closed and headed with a slow step towards the table in the corner. The owner blocked his way.

"You are no longer welcome here," she stated forcefully, trying not to show her fear.

"As you wish, I won't bother," the man replied without any emotion.

He turned to the door. He took a step. Then he stopped, reached into his pocket, and handed Rosalia a small piece of paper. "What if you happen to find out that you do need protection after all..."

She hesitantly accepted it from him. The man walked away without another word.

"This is not good," she said to herself almost inaudibly.

If he threatened, pressured, or tried to convince her, she would probably feel more at ease. A dog that barks does not bite. But he just left ominously.

That means he's probably not done with me; if so, he would probably try something else, she thought.

She opened her palm. There was a business card.

She hesitated. Shouldn't I call him? No! After all, I'm not going to pay anyone who starts unleashing horror. It is my hard earned money; and I won't give you to any fool.

After closing the pub, she went up the stairs to her small apartment, where she headed straight for the covers. As soon as she lay down, she immediately fell asleep. It was no wonder. She desperately needed sleep.

Even today, however, she was not allowed a thorough rest. She couldn't estimate how long she had been asleep when she was awakened by the sound of glass clinking followed by a noise coming from downstairs. From her business!

Firemen's horns rang out on the street. She threw on a robe and quickly ran down the stairs.

Smoke was billowing from the premises...

In the end, the damage was minimal. She learned from the firemen that someone probably started the fire on purpose, but she was lucky in the accident. Someone called for help just in time; given how little had burned, it would seem - if it wasn't nonsense - that the call was recorded on the emergency line perhaps even before the fire broke out.

The police wrote a report. For a moment, Rosalie considered telling the lawmen about her situation and turning to them for help. However, that quickly passed her by when she realized that she was the main suspect and the police consider insurance fraud to be the most likely motive for the arson.

Seriously kiss my ass with that, you idiots, Rosalie thought.

She dialed the goon's number. The person was already expecting the call.

chapter: Three stories
name: Story three
text:
Katina dipped a sponge in soapy water and went to scrub the sign from the window.

Although she didn't have to, she wanted to leave a nice clean up after her. In addition, the inscription symbolized the end of her enterprise:

SALE! 90% OFF!

She needed to get rid of the supplies, she had no further use for them. When the glass was clean, she smiled involuntarily, as she hated dirt and washed things made her happy.

She climbed down from the window, poured out the black water, and began to slowly load the rolls of leftover canvas that were still left in the store into the car. While doing so, she nostalgically looked around the place where she went to work almost every day for the past eight years, because she really liked sewing and selling the fabrics themselves.

Her business has worked for a long time, but now it is necessary to move on. She was a little sad, on the other hand, she knew how to take life as it is. She certainly had no regrets, and even at this moment she was glad she had gone into business then. Those were beautiful years...

She started - like most entrepreneurs - in the red, barely making ends meet and sometimes even sleeping in her small shop so she could open early in the morning. She closed late in the evening and sewed after nights, which was her "extra service" that she tried to differentiate from the competition and stand out.

It worked. Customers were happy with what they bought in her little shop, so word of her opening spread pretty quickly. Katina's business slowly began to flourish. Sometimes she did better, sometimes worse. One time she made a lot of money, the other time she was happy to cover the expenses. Over time, she also accumulated some savings for worse times, which gave her peace of mind.

In the last year, however, it all took a bad turn - customers slightly decreased and they spent less in her store, which turned out to be a rather fatal problem in combination with the rising cost of rent. At first, profits only fell, then the company began to find itself more and more often at a loss. Katina did what she could, but the savings were slowly and inexorably melting away. Like many entrepreneurs who have experienced good times and bad times, she always believed that things would get better again and did not want to close her business.

But one day she reached the point where she simply couldn't pay for everything anymore. So she paid the suppliers, as well as the rent, but did not pay the VAT. The tax office will just have to wait. After all, she had been paying outrageous sums to the state for many years.

When the situation still did not improve, she did what she had been putting off for so long - closed the shop for good. She didn't owe anything to the suppliers or the owner, that would have made her very sorry, but she didn't pay VAT to the state for two quarters - there was nothing to pay it from. She received a call to pay some time ago, but she did not respond to it. If she doesn't have it, she simply doesn't have it, she closed the shop and the tax office is out of luck. In any case, she paid a lot of money to the state in all kinds of levies during that time and she never wanted anything from him, so she herself had no conscience about the unpaid tax.

While these and many other thoughts raced through her mind, she loaded the car with everything that was left of her small business. She walked in and took one last look around the shop. It was completely empty and she thought it looked sad. She remembered a similar sight when she first rented it, but it didn't look sad then; rather full of hope. She smiled slightly.

"Thanks, shop, it was nice. Hopefully my successor will have better luck," she sputtered. At the same time, she shed a tear.

She went outside, closed the shutters, which also served as a grille, and locked them. She got into the car, looked back one more time and waved. She headed towards home.

Over the next few days, she was thinking about what she wanted to do - probably sewing again - so she sent out a few resumes, and also did some paperwork. One afternoon someone rang the bell. Katina quite nonchalantly opened the door, only to be startled by two men.

"Good afternoon, Miroslav Dráb, Financial Office for the Central Bohemian Region, regional office Kladno," the first introduced himself.

"Good day, Vojtěch Sebral, also the tax office," said the other.

"I hereby deliver to you a writ of distraint (seizure order) for the sale of movable property. Please sign it here," Dráb spoke again.

Katina was startled and slammed the door in their faces.

"Come on, madam, be sensible."

"Go away!" she replied desperately.

"We can, but we'll come again. You can't avoid it."

She didn't answer. She was scared and didn't know what to do.

"Well, as you wish," he grumbled. Then she heard them both leave.

She stood outside the door for a moment in utter shock. She looked through the peephole and saw an empty hallway. She unfastened the latch and opened the door. She just wanted to make sure they were really gone. When she was sure, she closed the door and tried to fasten the latch, but her hand was shaking.

She slumped into her chair and tried not to burst into tears. This was her nightmare. Problems with official authority and everything connected with it.

Before, she naively believed that the authorities were there for her, but as she did business, she gradually began to realize that it was all a little different. She does not represent a customer to the officials. If only that! She is not even a sheep to be sheared for them, because many of them do not even realize that they live on her taxes. No, they mostly just treated her like a troublesome insect. This position, combined with having to deal with them, seemed infinitely humiliating to her.

If she had something, she would have paid, but she basically had nothing. And not at all as much as they demanded. Of course, she could try to negotiate with the tax office, but her resistance to that was too strong. As long as her business flourished, she paid the state every crown it demanded. After all... what was left for her if she didn't want to end up exactly the way she ended up. But when she had nothing to give, the tax office sent bailiffs on her.

She knew that what she was doing was not helping herself. It was perfectly clear to her that this couldn't go well. But she simply couldn't overcome the disgust that the tax office's hyenism evoked in her at that moment.

If she did nothing all the time and just lived on support, the state would not only want nothing from her, but would even give her money. For the fact that she ran a business, thanks to which many people could buy the fabrics of their dreams and which supported not only her, but also the state, she now has people on her neck who want to take even the little she has left. She tried to push the whole thing out, it was too stressful.

However, they appeared again in a few days. She pretended not to be home.

Just let it ring, she thought.

"We know you're home. Open!"

She remained silent.

"We have a locksmith with us, he will open the door."

She looked through the peephole—and indeed; the bailiffs stood in the corridor accompanied by another man. It was bad. However, Katina did not want to let them in. She suspected it wasn't wise, but letting strangers invade her privacy and take her things was an absolutely unbearable thought for her.

"As you wish," replied the enforcer.

Immediately she heard the locksmith getting to work.

After a while, the lock loosened, but the door didn't even move, as it was secured from the inside by a massive latch.

"Have a mind and open for us! We'll get there eventually anyway," said the bailiff, less confidently.

She was as quiet as a mouse, and when she heard the three men leave, she felt a certain - if short-lived - relief.

She didn't even know how much time had passed when there was a sharp voice behind her door: "This is the Police of the Czech Republic. In the name of the law, open the door!"

She didn't know what to do, despair was taking over her, but she didn't want to open the door. The state had already taken so much money from her and had such a thorough overview of every item in her accounting that she had had enough. The idea that this rabble would rummage through her personal belongings made her sick!

"Open the door or we'll be forced to kick it out."

She didn't answer. The whole situation was so desperately unpleasant and absurd that the clueless Katina withdrew into herself and shut out what was happening in front of her apartment.

And suddenly a BANG! The door flew open. Policemen and bailiffs burst in. They legitimized her. She didn't protest. She also signed the seizure order in the end. What else did she have left? The police officers commented on the broken door and instructed her that she should have opened it. Enforcement officers from the tax office began to tape things up. Katina just stood quietly, unable to resist, watching everything as if in a dream and wondering what she had actually done so terrible... Yes, she probably could have handled the situation more actively and sensibly, but who did she hurt to deserve this? She went to the window, looked out, sang softly to herself, and let the uninvited guests do what they wanted in her house.

name: Anarcho-capitalism
text:
Three stories. The first about foul robbers who robbed a defenseless woman; the second about mobsters threatening violence, instilling fear and collecting protection money; however, the third is different, as it is about an unsuccessful small business woman who got into trouble through her own fault and subsequent laxity. At least that's how most people perceive these stories. Are you among them? Then this book was written just for you; I would like to offer a different point of view for consideration, which you don't have to agree with, but I will be very happy if you at least think about it - if possible without prejudices and pre-formed conclusions, for which you only look for arguments in retrospect.

I hope everyone will agree when I say that the actions of the robbers and the mafia are reprehensible. But let's ask ourselves the question - why is this so? For what reason do we reject looting and the collection of protection money? Well, we consider it wrong to appropriate someone else's resources by force (or the threat of violence) against the will of their owner, because whoever spends his time and energy to get something deserves to enjoy the fruits of his labor in peace; no one should have the right to take them from him just because he has more power at a given time and place. Of course, it happens sometimes and there will always be similar incidents, but it is important to condemn such behavior and stand against it.

But what are taxes? Unfortunately, the same thing; people have to give their resources to someone (the state) under the threat of violence. It is not so clearly visible at first glance, because the state violence is somewhat hidden; while in the first story the use of force was quite explicit, in the second less so, and in the third the force was actually used only after the victim had been given many chances to solve the situation differently. However, these are technical differences, not moral ones; in all cases, the attacker claims foreign resources and uses force to obtain them if they are not given to him. In general, the stronger a robber is, the more chances he can afford to give his victim: the vagabonds in the park had to turn Teresa around right away, because if they let her go, they would lose the loot; the mob could have given Rosalia some time to think, but when that didn't help, they resorted to intimidation; the state could afford to give Katina many chances, because when she didn't take any of them, he just robbed her in broad daylight without anyone saying anything.

I'm not saying there aren't differences between park pickpockets, the mob, and the state; I am merely pointing out that although there are many differences of a technical nature between robbery, extortion, and taxation, ethically it is still the same thing: The strong threatens the weak and demands that they pay him; if he does not pay, violence will be used against him, which will eventually force him to pay anyway. I fully understand that this sounds absurd in the case of the state, and you may well be tapping your forehead now; however, all of history is full of cases of obvious atrocities that were considered normal or even right at the time. If someone defended the accused during the witch trials by saying that their blasphemy didn't hurt anyone because witchcraft doesn't exist, he might very well end up at the stake himself. And what about the violence of the master against the slave? If any one in a slave society were to declare that it was morally as bad as violence to a free man, he would be laughed at by all; after all, something like this cannot be compared at all! Just like you can't compare robbers, the state and the mafia...

One might argue that the state provides various services to citizens for the money it collects; on the other hand, when the robber buys something with the victim's stolen money (perhaps all of it), his robbery hardly ceases to be a robbery (the Japanese yakuza mafia sometimes helps victims during natural disasters; this does not excuse its crimes, however). It is also true that in a (democratic) state, people voted and enacted taxes; but just because people vote and legalize something, it does not automatically become justified and legitimate (then we would have to admit that everything that has ever happened with the sanctification of a sufficient number of people was in order - for example, although not only, the democratic election of Hitler to power or the subsequent holocaust, which was also in accordance with the law of the time). Someone can also argue that the state clearly declares its intentions to tax and there are rules for this; certainly yes, however, when the mafia declares its intention to collect protection money as clearly as it does, it is difficult to call it legitimate. For a similar reason, the argument that the taxpayer can move out if he doesn't like it doesn't hold up; so can the protection money payer.

Good; but even if we morally reject the state, who will build roads, educate children, care for the poor, heal the sick, protect the environment, catch criminals, adjudicate disputes and guard borders against enemies? Paradoxically, it was the search for answers to these questions and the search for the most effective way to solve the above (and other) problems that led me years ago to reflect on the ethics of the functioning of the state; I strongly resisted it, I didn't like the idea at all, but long discussions, in which my goal was to show the necessity and necessity of the state establishment, finally convinced me that morality and efficiency go hand in hand, but in complete opposition to the state. I became an anarcho-capitalist.

What does that mean, you ask? What is anarcho-capitalism? Although most people associate anarchy with egalitarians, communists and the left in general, there are also anarchist schools based on respect for property rights and the free market, which they believe could replace all functions of the state, as absurd as that sounds; and anarcho-capitalism is one such school. Like all other anarchists, anarcho-capitalists passionately love freedom and heartily hate the state; however, our reasons (and means) are different - the highest value for us is freedom and the responsibility that is inextricably linked to it, while we - unlike most other anarchists - believe that real freedom can be achieved through respect for private property and property rights, because in our eyes, a free person is one who can enjoy the fruits of his own work and make his own decisions about life, without anyone forcing him to do something or taking from him what is his. The state then represents the greatest usurper and aggressor, ordering people how they should and should not live, not to mention forcing them to hand over to it most of what they earn. All of this is done under the threat of violence, because whoever does not obey, does not pay the protection money (loosely called taxes) and defends his property against the aggressor, will end up behind bars at best, or underground at worst.

Anarcho-capitalism is by no means a heartless materialistic ideology reducing people to mere numbers in an accounting without any rights. On the contrary, I personally believe that people should help each other, so I donate part of my income to the poor who, in my opinion, need it. Anarcho-capitalists are certainly not against solidarity (in fact, on the contrary; I would describe most of the ones I know as very compassionate and kind people), they just believe that it should be voluntary and no one should be forced into it under threat of violence (which is exactly what the state does). We are not indifferent to human rights either; the difference from how they are perceived by the state, which restricts the freedom of its citizens in order to enforce them, is that we define them using property rights - for example, we derive the "right to life" from the principle of self-ownership, according to which people are the owners of their bodies, so attacking them is a violation of their property rights.

Anarcho-capitalists are not social engineers, eager to plan people's lives; on the contrary, we are convinced that everyone can make the best decisions about their own lives, because no politician (or anyone else) knows what is best for others. It is not our interest to dictate to anyone how to live, we only consider it right not to force anyone to do anything, as long as the person in question looks after his own and does not attack others in any way; and even if the majority democratically votes to intervene against him, it will not turn a bad thing into a good one.

We just want to live freely in peace and quiet; we want to love, have fun, work, decide for ourselves. We do not want and need someone who will forcefully take most of the fruits of our labor and "for a reward" dictate to us what we can and cannot say publicly, what we can and cannot sell and buy, under what conditions we can and cannot work. We want to make our own decisions and, of course, bear all the consequences. We want to raise our children without our rulers deciding which values we should lead them to more and which ones less or when, in what way and in which institutions they should be educated. Because that's freedom.

"It's a nice fairy tale, but without the state, our society simply wouldn't function," you think? Well, such an objection is perfectly natural, and I should be surprised if no one made it; after all, it was the first thing that came to mind when I first heard about anarcho-capitalism. And it's no wonder, because this is exactly what we've all been presented with since elementary school; after all, it is the state that determines what is taught in schools. On the other hand, a century or two ago slavery was perfectly normal, an institution thousands of years old. Before it was abolished in many countries, the most common arguments for its preservation were something like this: "The abolition of slavery is a nice fairy tale, but without slaves, society simply wouldn't work because there wouldn't be enough people to work." Doesn't that sound familiar? At that time it was also absolutely clear to most people that the abolition of slavery was pure utopia. But today?

History is paved with huge mistakes of humanity, which sometimes take hundreds or thousands of years to correct; and I am not asserting anything here other than that states are just another such error in a series. I know very well how difficult it is to think constructively and dispassionately about theses that question the very foundations of what was instilled in us from a young age, so I ask the reader to be patient and open-minded when reading a book about how a free stateless society might one day function. I do not claim that everything must necessarily look exactly as I describe, because it is realistically impossible to predict exactly where human creativity will take us; perhaps reality far exceeds my expectations. However, when I first read about anarcho-capitalism, I could not imagine how the market could replace all the functions of the state; so in this book I deal with individual areas in which the state operates and try to describe how state laws could be replaced by free market principles.

name: A few words in the introduction
text:
Sixteen chapters will now follow. The first four contain certain general principles. Twelve others describe how individual areas managed by the state today (such as education, healthcare, judiciary, police and many others) could function in a free market. Finally, you can look forward to a few bonus chapters and quick answers to some common objections to a stateless society.

Since the first four chapters mainly contain theory, they may not be very readable for some (although I tried not to be too boring); however, those who want to read straight away about how this or that could work without the state can skip to the fifth chapter (about money). However, it should be taken into account that throughout the book I refer to the first four theoretical chapters in the explanation - especially the second one.

When reading about how individual industries could function in a free market, one must always remember that when I mention an alternative to providing certain services without state intervention, I am certainly not claiming that this is the only possible non-state way. It is absurd to think that none of the millions of businessmen could devise the provision of that service better than I outline it here (or as any handful of the best politicians could); just imagine what this world looked like just a hundred years ago, and how the brilliant ideas and diligence of many people exceeded even the assumptions of the most daring visionaries of the time. The free market simply cannot be predicted; if so, he would go to plan centrally, which is not possible, as we will soon show. These are only possible variants of how such a world could (but might not) look like.

Because state-controlled schools convince us of the necessity of the state and the correctness of democracy from an early age, when our minds and opinions are just beginning to form, I write my texts as an opposition to such claims. But my opponents have one huge advantage; they started much earlier (within the state education system) and have already planted in most people's heads in advance that the ideas I advocate are absurd, unrealistic, undesirable and meaningless. Hand on heart: Who among you, dear readers, is already negative about the idea of a stateless society? And who of you who do have seriously and open-mindedly entertained the idea for some time? I know many will reject this book; however, I would like to ask you not to do so based on "arguments" such as: "Everyone knows that wouldn't work," but after mature - and if possible unbiased - reasoning.

It is possible that you will find chapters in the book that will make sense to you, but also some that you will definitely not be able to identify with; that's perfectly fine. I'm not proclaiming a revolution, there's no need to abolish the state overnight, for now it's more than enough to reduce it. Even if, after reading this book, you come to the conclusion that we need the state, but there is even a single industry that you previously thought should be managed, but you have changed your mind, I consider that a great success. And if that doesn't happen either, I will be very happy if you at least think about the necessity or dispensability of the state.

name: 1. Scarce resources and the price system
text:
Everyone has probably heard of the invisible hand of the market; some refer to it, others ridicule it. However, not everyone knows that this is a relatively old phrase; and even fewer people suspect that this label was first used in the eighteenth century by the British thinker Adam Smith in his work "The Wealth of Nations". However, it is sometimes surprising how little many - and sometimes even people with a diploma certifying their economic education - imagine under this term; very often their awareness ends with the fact that the author probably wanted to metaphorically indicate that the market will somehow arrange everything.

The truth is that Adam Smith probably really meant to say what the market will arrange; however, this is no vague "somehow" - there is a perfectly clear and comprehensive theory of how and why this happens. Two centuries later, this idea of his was further developed and, above all, much better described by the outstanding economist of the Austrian school of economics, Ludwig von Mises (and his student Friedrich August von Hayek, who received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974 for his work, continued this). Its essence, which applies to each of us, can be summarized as follows: If I do something for people that pleases them, they will gladly pay me for it. Therefore, wealth in a free market is a measure of how much a person has done for others according to their own rankings of values. But let's start from the beginning.

When people hold discussions on the topic of what the proper social order should be, how society should be organized, some propose anarchy, others minarchy, others monarchy, some democracy/socialism... But what are they really talking about? What is the difference between these – and other – systems? It is primarily a matter of deciding how to use what we only have a limited amount of - i.e. labor force, natural resources, means of production, material. Collectively, we call such goods "scarce resources" and by this we mean (simplistically) anything that is limited in quantity, so that people must share it (when one person uses something, no one else can use it at the same time).

Rare resources are for example: meat, computer, cow, operating surgeon's work, iron ore mine, miner's work, mine cart, steel ingot. On the contrary, rare resources in normal conditions are not: air (by breathing, you do not limit anyone else's breathing - so, for example, in a submerged submarine or a space shuttle in orbit, air is a rare commodity) or sunlight. Using the example of air, we can see beautifully that the rarity of resources can change over time and space.

The utility of scarce resources is subjective. For me, for example, a juicy steak is of more use than a head of cabbage; for a vegetarian it will probably be the opposite. And it is the subjectivity of utility that is the basis for voluntary exchange. If I have cabbage and a veggie steak, we can exchange it, increasing the utility of what we own for both of us (it's also worth noting that this transaction makes people better off without anything being produced; voluntary exchanges generally increase the utility of all participants in this way). Now let's imagine that there will be someone else standing next to him who is willing to give the vegetarian two heads for that piece of meat. Presumably, the vegetarian's utility from two heads of cabbage exceeds his utility from a single head, so he will prefer this exchange to the exchange with me.

Therefore, if a vegetarian knows someone with whom meat can be exchanged for cabbage, meat begins to have value for him as well. The value is also subjective and corresponds to either the direct benefit from the given good or the benefit of what can be exchanged for this good. In the second case, we still have to calculate that the exchange costs some time, always carries with it certain risks, and we are never completely sure that it will take place. These are all factors that reduce value - we'll get to the implications of that later. For now, it is important to realize that the value of goods is assigned by individual people (so it is subjective), either according to the direct benefit they bring to them, or what they can exchange them for.

A small complication occurs when I have cabbage to exchange, I want a steak, but my vegetarian friend (who owns meat) doesn't feel like a head at the moment, but he would rather have bread. In that case, I have to look for someone to trade bread for cabbage. If the transactions are more complicated in this way, another problem arises: If the vegetarian trades meat only for heads, it is immediately clear to him which store will end up with the most heads; however, if he exchanges indirectly through other people through completely different goods, comparing the advantages of individual trades is difficult or impossible. This led to people choosing some suitable commodity (typically precious metals) to use as a universal medium of exchange (called money); then it was not necessary to determine ratios between countless different goods, the ratio of each good to money was always sufficient, with the help of which the exchange ratio between any goods could be easily determined.

We call the exchange rate of some good and money the price. One basic observation can be made about price: In a group of people who trade with each other (we can call such a group a market), the price of a single good in different exchanges usually does not vary much; of course it changes over time, but it is usually almost the same for different sellers in the same period within the same market. Why? Every buyer tries to buy as cheaply as possible, every seller wants to sell as expensive as possible; while each buyer has a maximum (and each seller a minimum), above which (or below which) the price will no longer go, because their subjective benefit would not increase with such a deal, but would decrease. Buyers then tend to buy from sellers with the lowest prices; sellers want to be bought from them, so they lower the price (compete), but not so much that they lose. In this way, the price stabilizes at a level acceptable to everyone who participates in the exchanges - and we can call such a stable price the market price.

All the findings stated so far are quite trivial and each of us probably understands them (at least on a subconscious basis) - but we stated and described them precisely so that we could draw further consequences from them. First of all, it is necessary to realize what circumstances affect the prices of goods. When consumers are a little more interested, or when something starts to run out on the seller's side, it becomes rarer, so sellers can raise prices without losing customers (if they kept the original price, the item would simply sell out immediately). On the other hand, when the demand for something falls, or if there is a way to get/produce much more of it for the same effort, the price will fall, because sellers can afford to lower the price (to attract as many customers as possible).

What will happen if a natural resource starts to run out, or if its further acquisition becomes expensive? From the above it follows that its price will increase; as well as the price of products made from it. And the consequences of this price increase? First, consumers begin to buy less of it (because it is expensive, they begin to look for alternatives to do without it), thus saving something that is itself scarce. And secondly (probably most importantly) the increased price will attract other entrepreneurs to enter the industry and look for better solutions (use of other raw materials, more efficient mining, more economical production, production of substitutes, and so on). Prices serve as a great carrier of information about the world: We don't even need to know what happened where, why something is in short supply, we just need to try to maximize our utility (which we do anyway) and it's likely that we won't waste; we don't have to invent any solutions to remote problems at all, we don't have to have a cure for everything, we just have to wait and the natural desire of entrepreneurs for profit will solve those problems: The greater the lack of something, the more it is missing, the more people are motivated to deal with it, because they can get rich from it.

Conversely, when a resource becomes more available (and again it doesn't matter for what reason; most people may not know about it at all - it will still affect their behavior, this information will be transmitted to them through prices), producers can lower prices to lure customers away from competitors. They will proceed in this way as long as possible, so that they can make a profit from it, for which it is still worthwhile for them to do it. If the product becomes cheaper, people will tend to buy more of it and possibly replace it with other more expensive substitutes (thus, what is abundant is used a lot, but what is scarce is not wasted). A similar situation occurs if consumers simply begin to demand less of the given goods. Some sellers will go down in price (if they can), others will change their supply, and others will go bankrupt, which is correct (there is a surplus of the good, so it must be stopped, which is exactly what happens if some producers change their supply and those who don't go bankrupt).

The following also follows from the last two paragraphs: Those who make the best use of scarce resources, i.e. transform them into something that is even more beneficial to society, become rich. On the contrary, those who waste precious resources, i.e. transform them into something that has less value for society than the resources they use for it, become poor and subsequently go bankrupt. To solve all problems like "how/if to provide a service" or "how/if to make a product" just let thousands and millions of entrepreneurs just try it. Those of them who do it wrong (= differently than people want) will go bankrupt (and go do something that will benefit society more). On the contrary, those who do it right (= as people wish) will prosper. Every service (even product) can be provided in several correct ways (if different groups of people prefer different ways, quality and price); then those firms that fulfill consumers' wishes (i.e. follow any of the "correct" paths) will remain on the market.

Although almost all the insights we have presented in this chapter are rather intuitive and clear, I ask the reader to let them go through their heads and think about what interesting consequences for the organization of society follow from them. Indeed, it is remarkable that although practically everyone is willing to agree with more or less all the statements found in this text, almost no one is able to see the consequences resulting from them; we will deal with them in the next chapter, within which we will refer to this one.

name: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text:
Perhaps everyone knows by now that socialist central planning is failing; you don't have to look far for examples from history. Now, dear readers, please stop for a moment, think, and answer in your mind the question why this is so. How would you describe it in one sentence? If your answer is that everything was owned by the state, so no one had an incentive to look after it as their own, plus everyone stole everything, this chapter will probably give you a new perspective.

This - probably the most common - answer is true, but it does not describe the biggest problem of central planning. Motivating managers of state-owned enterprises to make the same effort as managers of private enterprises is not an insurmountable problem. The theft of property cannot be completely eliminated, but it can be limited by various measures. Because the problems of motivation and theft are often seen as practically the only ones, many people still advocate partial central planning. However, central planners encounter another – much more serious – snag, which, although not so notorious, is practically (and theoretically) unsolvable.

In the last chapter, we described how the invisible hand of the market guides people to properly allocate scarce resources: When something is expensive, the market, through price information, will limit the use of that resource; and vice versa. Indeed, market prices express the relative scarcity of resources, thereby effectively coordinating human activity. In socialism, market prices do not exist, there they are replaced by prices set by the government, which have nothing to do with the scarcity of resources (the consequence is the chronic shortage of some - and surpluses of other - goods, known to many). My favorite author and thinker Murray Newton Rothbard brilliantly described this phenomenon in his book "Power and Market" (or "Man, Economy and State"), or the great economist Ludwig von Mises in his famous book "Bureaucracy". For central planners (even democratic ones), this phenomenon results in several fatal problems, which we will discuss in turn.

The first problem is the need for constant monitoring of possible resource shortages. A central planner would have to be aware of the potential deficiencies of hundreds and thousands of different resources; and not only with the fact that something is happening, but also with how much and how fast it is happening. In a free market economy, all these questions are automatically answered by the price system - there is no need to pay anyone for it, everyone does their small part of this work only as part of the effort to achieve the highest possible benefit.

The second problem is that even if the central planner gets all this information, it has to choose a solution. Even on a very general level, there are several of them: invest in making that resource easier to obtain, import from a greater distance, use a substitute, raise the price. These solutions can be combined, and each of them has countless ways of execution. Free market entrepreneurs each try what they think is best; some of them will do well and become rich, others will choose poorly and go bankrupt. Even if we completely ignore motivation (when an entrepreneur makes a mistake, he loses a lot - unlike a politician) and expertise (businessmen often - unlike politicians - understand their fields), the biggest difference is that when many entrepreneurs try many solutions, they will take the ones that people appreciate the most (and the losses for bad solutions are borne by their authors), but the central planners will simply try to solve the problem somehow, and it is not even clear how to know whether the solution is good, because there are no other realized alternatives to compare (and if the solution is bad, the costs are borne by the subjects).

The third problem is the wishes and demands of consumers. The price system conveys this information to entrepreneurs on the free market. The central planner must spend resources (who pays the cost, the reader will surely guess) to find out the same information, and what it finds out will always be biased; if some central planner had done a survey in 1975 on how many people wanted/needed a computer at home, they would have found that practically no one (considering that no one - not even those who invented and manufactured computers - could imagine their use back then), so there is no need to spend any precious resources in this direction.

The fourth problem is that even if the central planner somehow magically got information from people about what services or products they actually want, it has no way of finding out the ratio in which these goods are in demand: "Mr. Novák, would you rather have an ambulance travel time of 4 minutes, half a kilo of beef a week, a new subway line and go to the movies once every two weeks, or would you rather have an ambulance travel time of 7 minutes, a kilo of beef a week, a repaired highway and go to the theatres?' When we imagine the immense number of properties that Mr. Novák is asking for, and the countless combinations in which he can ask for them, we realize that it is simply impossible to compile such a list realistically. And now let's look at the absurd role of the central planner, who theoretically should find this out not only from Mr. Novák, but from millions of citizens! Even if he could somehow magically do it, it is only the beginning - he would have to somehow find the optimal result based on the demands of all his subjects. To do it really as well as entrepreneurs in the free market, he would have to deal with questions like: "Is Mr. Procházka's request for a tourist trail around Prague or Mrs. Vodičková's request for a swimming pool in Pilsen more beneficial for society?" To answer each such question, he would have to solve a lot of sub-questions such as: "Does Mr. Procházka's vote have the same weight as Mrs. Vodičková's? And does Mr. Procházka want the hiking trail as much as Mrs. Vodičková wants the swimming pool, or does one of them want more?" Let us realize the astronomical number of combinations of all relevant persons and wishes that must be compared; at the same time, neither one is easily solvable, because it is impossible to reliably compare the preferences of two different people other than to let them show themselves how much they are willing to sacrifice time and effort for the fulfillment of their wishes. But, as we have already shown, the best universal means of general expression of time and effort is money, and the only way of arranging things according to individual people's preferences remains to let these people freely choose and buy what they think best.

Unfortunately, central planning is not just what some of us had the opportunity to see during totalitarianism. Partial central planning is attempted by every state; some more, some less. It must be remembered that every regulation, every state enterprise, every "consumer protection" law and even every tax are all elements of central planning that run into the above problems.

If the entire market is in the hands of the state, citizens live in poverty and scarcity (take the USSR as an example). When the state frees up a part of the market for free entrepreneurs, it starts working like a magic wand in the image of consumers (for example, a part of the current market that the state regulates relatively little: IT, hospitality, tourism, retail and others). On the contrary, the part of the market that the state has kept works desperately (education, social system, healthcare, judiciary and so on).

Let's imagine that we have two ways to control the course of events: First we will control everything in one way, nothing will work, so we will try to do maybe half of the things in another way - and they will suddenly start working, while the other half still does not work. Who, other than a complete fool, would not try to manage everything the other way in such a situation? Nevertheless, we foolishly believe that the state simply has to do some things. Why? Because that's what they tell us in (state) school and what (state) politicians tell us. During totalitarianism, we became convinced that the state was desperately unable to handle the production and import of food (a shortage of meat, queues for bananas), the production of cars (car directories), the production and sale of drugstore goods (a shortage of pads, toilet paper) and electronics (television directories, refrigerators), which the free market can handle with ease and without problems. On the other hand, we foolishly believe that, for example, education and healthcare in the hands of the state is the right choice (although we see sad results). We assume that an institution incapable of solving problems as utterly trivial as the supply of toilet paper will somehow be successful at something as incredibly complicated as educating our children.

There will probably be more reasons for such an absurd belief. I consider propaganda, which is served to us since primary school, to be the most fundamental. In the second place, however, I see the fact that even today we have some "private" entities that do not work very well in some markets overregulated by the state; definitely no better than the state ones (especially private schools or hospitals). It is then easy to point to them and say, "Look, a private institution doesn't work any better than a public one."

The careful reader will surely understand by now why this argument is flawed. Such private institutions, which do have a private owner, but otherwise have to do practically everything the way the state wants, do not have much in common with the free market - that is, it solves the (small) problem with motivation, but it does not solve any of the (big) problems mentioned in this chapter (when the state says how private companies must work, the moment when many of them try it in various ways and those who did it right will stick). Competition issues notwithstanding; in the last chapter we explained that those who do it badly go bankrupt, which means that those who do it well take over their clients - but the state does not get money from customers paying it voluntarily, it collects it through taxes, ergo state institutions can waste scarce resources as much as they like, but they still do not go bankrupt (and when they expand throughout the market, those who do better go bankrupt instead). Finally, the state imposes high barriers to entry in similar markets, thereby artificially reducing competition and harming consumers.

Thus, the free market is more efficient than central planning; which cannot be avoided by the state increasing the motivation of managers or reducing corruption and embezzlement, because the fundamental problem lies in something else entirely. Let's note that this applies in general - to all fields of human activity. There is no reason why some should be an exception; however, many think otherwise, so we will discuss these individual areas in the coming chapters.

chapter: 2. Why does central planning fail?
name: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text:
The phenomenon dealt with in the second chapter is called "the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning". Since this is one of the most fundamental things on which many theses throughout the book are based, I decided to expand this chapter somewhat. A deep understanding of this topic is probably necessary to fully understand the rest of the book.

Let us imagine a centrally planned society and its government, which may be formed by an individual, or even by a group; unless this society is at a completely primitive level of technological development, it cannot be considered realistic that these rulers understand all the fields of human activity that their subjects engage in. They must therefore necessarily create a hierarchical structure of individuals, which can be imagined as a pyramid, the foundations of which are made up of, for example, workers, above whom are their superiors, and above them, in turn, their superiors; and so on up to the government, which is at the very top.

To show that the problem of central planning of society is absolutely fatal even under absolutely ideal (unattainable) conditions, let us assume for all the reasoning in this chapter that all members of a given society are unreservedly honest, put the welfare of the whole above their own welfare at all times, never steal, and have nothing at heart but the building of a better tomorrow, for which they will toil from dawn to dusk. Very often one can come across the opinion that central planning does not work precisely because people do not have the above-mentioned characteristics; however, I intend to prove that even if they had, central planning would still remain a woefully inefficient way of running society.

Of all the thousands and millions of resources that need to be coordinated and distributed, we will focus on just one: titanium. The applications for this silvery white metal are – thanks to its remarkable properties – many. Leaving aside that it is used to build the casings of space probes, satellites and stations, which we will not deal with here, there are enough other uses left, of which we will focus only on the production of ship propellers and chemical reactors; suppose there are some shipyards and a highly developed chemical industry in our centrally controlled country.

In accordance with the initial assumptions, let's assume that all relevant positions are staffed by top professionals whose goal is nothing other than the welfare of society. The chemist knows exactly and can describe the advantages and disadvantages of a titanium reactor compared to another. The boat designer, on the other hand, understands and can explain all the pros and cons of titanium boat screws. Both will communicate these conclusions to their superiors, who will understand them in everything, as they are also experts taken at their word. So they calculate how much titanium they need for their entire industry and apply for it. However, let's assume that the metal is in short supply, so a wise central planner summons everyone who requests titanium, as well as the person responsible for its production (in the real world, of course, this will work completely differently, but here for simplicity we assume ideal conditions free of cronyism, ignorance and the like).

How will such negotiations take place? We must not forget that this is a centrally planned society in which there are no market prices. So everyone gets together, the applicants explain why they need titanium; the person responsible for its production will tell you what resources are needed to make more titanium. The central planner must now make a decision; but how? What factors should it even include? If it was clear how many chemical reactors and ship propellers "are needed", he could at least investigate where it is less expensive to use a substitute. But the "need" depends on, among other things, how costly the resulting solution will be; the more complicated the construction of the ship, the more it pays to have fewer of them and use other means of transport (not to mention that the wishes of millions of consumers come into play here, who sometimes don't even know what they want until they try it). It is also possible to increase production, which of course costs other resources, but of course there are many other uses for them; one problem leads to another. And this is just the beginning, because titanium itself can still be used, for example, in the health sector, the aviation industry, some people want to make watches out of it, and so on; above all, it is necessary to make similar decisions not only for one metal, but for each of the countless sources.

One might argue that a central planner can solve the whole problem by setting the prices of individual goods. However, prices are the result of market processes; then they express the scarcity of resources and human preferences. If one establishes them arbitrarily, one does not avoid the above problem, it only shifts it elsewhere; in fact, he will face questions similar to those from the previous paragraph in the framework of price creation, since in this process he still has to compare the relative rarity of all goods (and confront this with the demand of buyers). Another major problem with arbitrary pricing is that the state of the world is ever-changing and the pricing process should be inherently dynamic and never-ending.

The market, on the other hand, can solve these problems arbitrarily, since the prices are created by the trading individuals themselves in an effort to maximize their profits; the whole process is very robust, reacts to changes over time, reflects the preferences of all participants in the market process and the scarcity of resources. All the decisions described above are not made by any central authority, but by all buyers, sellers, producers, consumers, employees and employers. If the free market is not distorted in any way (for example, by state interventions), then maximizing the profit of each individual is equivalent to maximizing his contribution to society (because on the one hand, providing the most requested services means the highest income, and on the other hand, reducing costs means saving scarce resources that can then be used by others).

It is often objected that giant corporations are also centrally planned, which should be proof that a centrally planned society could function in the same way. The difference, however, is that even a very large corporation can orient itself in the market environment with the help of prices. It can be divided internally into individual divisions and departments so that the results of their activities can be converted into money, which can serve as a key to the distribution of scarce resources. If the economy as a whole is centrally planned, then it has no such possibility, because market prices arise only and only through the unregulated interaction of free (ie not centrally controlled) individuals. The above-mentioned corporation thus orients itself with the help of prices from the outside; however, if the entire company is centrally controlled, it loses this option (or it can be guided by foreign prices, which will probably be better than nothing, but definitely grossly inefficient). However, if a private entity were to grow up in a territory of the size of a state and become a dominant player in so many areas, it would begin to face the same problems; but crucially, as long as people can refuse its services, it can go bankrupt, giving way to more efficient competitors. This will hardly happen in the case of the state, as taxpayers do not have much of a choice.

The vast majority of states are, of course, governed by some combination or compromise between the free market and central planning; however, it is important to realize that the above conclusions apply to every field of human activity, so that when the state usurps an industry, it necessarily introduces inefficiency into it. Therefore, the larger part of the market the state controls or regulates, the more centrally unsolvable problems discussed in this chapter will manifest themselves.

In conclusion, I would like to point out that the search for all sorts of compromises of the free market and central planning only leads to the fact that the more deviations from the undistorted market there are, the more noticeably the efficiency of the given society as a whole decreases. And if we ask the government for help because of this, we will get lost in a vicious circle: The worse it is, the more intensively we call for state interventions, which, however, cause further deterioration of the situation.

chapter: 2. Why does central planning fail?
name: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text:
Since I definitely refer to the second chapter most often in this book, I believe that the given topic deserves one more expansion, because it is really absolutely essential. So far we have looked at the problem of economic calculation only from the point of view of the central planner; however, I would like to show how the consequences of the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning look like from the perspective of his subjects.

The key is to realize that each individual has limited resources that they use to meet their needs. These needs can be completely arbitrary - material, spiritual, hedonistic, ascetic; in any case, the priority of these needs is always best known to the person concerned. No one can, in general, decide for another what will make him happy, more thoroughly than he himself. Of course, it can sometimes happen that an individual chooses the wrong means to satisfy his needs, so that the result will not correspond to what he originally intended. Just as it is possible that someone else could choose the appropriate means to achieve the same goal. Unfortunately, however, we can never say it with certainty in advance, and even retrospectively it can only be evaluated on the assumption that we know the actual (not only declared or estimated) goals of the person in question, which in principle we never know with certainty.

Therefore, the absolutely essential knowledge is that no one can generally make decisions for another as well as if he were to do it himself; and while it may occasionally work out for a decision, there is no way anyone can know beforehand, and certainly not afterwards, so it's always a game of hidden cards. The principles briefly discussed in this chapter are the measure of the life's work of the great economist Ludwig von Mises; his book is called "Human Action" and belongs to the basic works of economic theory, because the ideas contained in it are necessary for a real understanding of economics as a science and not only as a field based on what is just modern and desirable for the current social and political demand.

Each of us will therefore, from the resources available to him, satisfy those needs which appear to him to be the most urgent; this is always the case without exception, no model of a perfectly rational and informed individual is needed. In practice, this means that we take our resources and our time and do with them as we see fit; we'll buy what we think is best, we'll do what we think is best to achieve our goals (yes, even a junkie who goes to hit another high does what he thinks is the best means to his goals; and none of us can say for sure that it's wrong, because we don't know what the junkie's goals are, and even if we did know, it's not up to us to evaluate them in any way or consider them objectively inferior to ours).

However, what happens when someone (and it's usually the state) takes part of an individual's resources and uses them as someone else sees fit? In the ideal and very unlikely case, it will hit exactly what the person wants to buy anyway, thereby not harming him, but not helping him either. In other cases, he gets something for his money that he would rather buy something else instead, if left to his choice. This is exactly how taxes work.

Regulations have an effect very similar to taxes. Their purpose is supposedly to "help ordinary people" by limiting someone's choice somewhere. But the truth is that when all impacts are included, regulations will at best help some group of people at the expense of others; in a typical case, they harm the group they are supposed to favor, or you can even find one that harms practically everyone. The classic and probably the most common example of regulations that are supposed to "help the poor" are all kinds of quality control of goods, which are supposed to protect poor customers so that merchants do not sell them "scum". Even if such a regulation really fulfilled its purpose without other side effects (which is rarely possible) and simply cleared the market of low-quality products, it will certainly not reduce the price of quality goods (on the contrary, it will quite possibly increase it, because those who bought lower-quality products are now forced to buy better ones, so the demand will rise and with it the price), so the poor who were supposed to be helped, because they were only deprived of the opportunity to buy low-quality goods cheaply, so often they can't afford anything at all instead of "scum".
