Some may argue that this situation "forces" them to wait and buy something better later instead of buying lower quality items, but this brings us exactly to what was stated at the beginning: No one can decide for these individuals better than themselves whether it is better for them to have nothing first, so that they can then buy something of better quality, rather than having at least a lower quality item all the time (with all the resulting disadvantages).

Another objection to central planning (and thus to the free market) tends to be the redistribution of wealth; that some services are supposed to be paid by the rich to the poor. This, on the one hand, does not change anything at all about the above, i.e. that it would be much better for the poor if the rich gave them this money directly and they chose what to buy with it, rather than someone else deciding it (if we even admit some immoral and disgusting compulsory redistribution); but especially the whole forced redistribution thing doesn't make much sense, since wealth is a free market measure of how much a person has done for others according to their own rankings of values. Directive redistribution (and any violent distortion of the market, i.e. not only the state, although it is by far the most common) then favors individuals less beneficial to others at the expense of those more useful.

In conclusion, I would like to emphasize again that an understanding of the second chapter and its subchapters is key to understanding most of the economic arguments contained in this book. A detailed and comprehensible explanation of the phenomenon discussed here is offered in particular by the book "Bureaucracy" by Ludwig von Mises; if you don't want to read the whole book, I can recommend a different view of the matter in the very high-quality article "Neglected economic calculation" by Petr Málek, one of the founders of the Ludwig von Mises Institute (the text is freely available on the Internet). As a test of understanding of the given issue, each reader can try to refute for himself the favorite argument of statists (supporters of the state): "If the state did not pay for this or that, people would not voluntarily give money for it." Why can this sentence never be a valid argument for the preservation of the state? Although this question will be answered in one of the final chapters of this book, I sincerely hope that everyone will find it for themselves before reading the answer.

name: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text:
In the previous two chapters, we have shown why the free market is generally better than state central planning in meeting human needs. Many people are willing to agree with this, but they argue that the free market economy is efficient but heartless, amoral, unethical and unfair. Is that really the case? Does a really big state mean less efficiency, but more justice? Let's break down and answer these questions.

Every human society in history recognized some set of rules that determined what was right and what was wrong. We call such a list of rules (laws) law. There are countless different laws: common law, currently valid laws of the Czech Republic, the codex of King Hammurapi or perhaps the code of the Third Reich. However, if something is legalized by law, it does not have to be moral and right - even if one considers the laws of the Third Reich to be ethical, it is easy to see that different concepts of rights, the meaning of which contradict each other on fundamental moral issues, cannot be right at the same time.

What should "correct law" look like? A tough question. So I will try to summarize at least some minimum, which I assume most people will not have any fundamental objections to:

• No one should have the right to initiate violence against others.

• Everyone should have the right not to be robbed by others.

• The law should apply equally to everyone.

• The law should be clear and understandable; After all, if everyone is to live according to it, they should understand it and carry it in their heads. The absurd thing is that, although most people probably agree on this minimum, not a single one meets our right from the above points.

The first point can be crossed by the police. For example, it has the right in some cases to forcibly seize the cars of drivers who are not involved, or – even worse – to use these innocent drivers against their will in their cars as roadblocks and human shields (relatively well-known cases took place in May 2011 in Legerova Street in Prague or in March 2013 on the D1 highway). Less obvious - but much more frequent - violations of this rule are demonstrated by the police during house searches, taking suspects into custody, and the like. Whenever an innocent person refuses any of the above, the police may use violence against him.

The second point is violated by taxes, which are nothing more than robbery legalized by law. The state says: "Subject, give me the money, if you deal with evil, and we will take even more by force." It is basically the same as a robber saying to us, "Money or life!" The only difference is that the state will give us some counter-service for this money, the robber typically will not. On the other hand, it is difficult for a robber to take so much from us (and so often), but especially even if he buys something from us with the stolen money, it does not change the robbery and he does not stop being a robber because of it.

The third point is most obviously not fulfilled by the politicians with their parliamentary and other immunities, with which they tell us "out of the blue" that we are not equal before the law. Furthermore, different laws apply to police officers on duty (and other public officials) than to ordinary citizens.

The fourth point is particularly interesting in combination with the fact that ignorance of the law is no excuse. When even lawyers are routinely represented by specialized colleagues in their disputes that do not concern their specialization, there is probably no one in our country who knows all the rules perfectly. Isn't having to live by a thousand rules that virtually no one understands something that could be written about in a comedy that would be seriously hilarious if it weren't our reality?

The overwhelming majority of the legislators of almost all contemporary and historical states could be subjected to similar criticism. This is not a coincidence. On the one hand, the very existence of the state in principle contradicts equality before the law (different rules must apply to state representatives than to subjects), and on the other hand, the state must rob (collect taxes) in order to earn its existence.

One of the few concepts of law that meets these (and many other) requirements, and at the same time probably the only one that respects private property and according to which some human communities have long-term framework functions in history, is called natural law. Throughout history, many philosophers have touched upon various areas of natural law in their works: in antiquity, for example, Heraclitus or Aristotle, whose works in the Middle Ages were the basis of Thomas Aquinas, and modern thinkers such as John Locke; it was most comprehensively and, in my opinion, best described by my favorite author and thinker Murray Newton Rothbard in his book "The Ethics of Liberty" and partially also in the manifesto "For a New Liberty", where he formulated natural law as the so-called principle of non-aggression, which is then written about in detail by contemporary authors such as Walter Block or Hans-Hermann Hoppe, while such Clint Eastwood summed up the principle of non-aggression very aptly in a single sentence: "Everyone leaves everyone else alone." I would describe the principle of non-aggression like this:

1. Ownership is a relationship that assigns physical objects to people (a person can be the owner of an object). No one may deal with an object that has an owner without his permission, except in cases where it is necessary to correct a situation in which the owner himself has violated someone else's property or violated a contract.

2. Ownership can be freely transferred and exchanged if both parties to the transaction agree (without coercion); transactions can be implemented using contracts.

3. Each person owns himself until he transfers that ownership to someone else (some libertarians argue that self-ownership is inalienable; others—including me—are of the opinion that a person is free to do with himself as he pleases).

4. Something that no one owns at the moment, someone can start to own by starting to use it (mixing it with his work, so-called homesteading, see the work of John Locke). Homesteading addresses the issue of initial appropriation; when something doesn't belong to anyone (like newly discovered land and the like), anyone can get it by being the first to start using it. The principle of non-aggression corresponds to a certain minimum of what most people consider to be right, moral, ethical and fair: It follows from it in particular that people should not rob each other, attack each other (they can defend themselves) and kill; murder is a violation of the victim's property rights to his body - and as the astute reader will surely have noticed, natural rights, formulated as the principle of non-aggression, are actually property rights.

Although perhaps everyone agrees that the principle of non-aggression corresponds to some minimum of what is right, many will argue that it is not enough; that it would be moral if the right included more things, such as necessary medical care. No matter how noble such an idea may seem, its inclusion in the principle of non-aggression is simply impossible. Why? Well, someone has to provide and pay for such health care; but if no one could be found who would do it voluntarily, he would have to be forced to do so by force, which would be a violation of property rights (and therefore aggression).

When we think about it more deeply, we find that adding anything else - however noble - to this system of law contradicts its meaning, or creates inconsistencies in it (which, after all, contains most legal concepts). In addition to the right to health care, there is also the right to education, a dignified life, a pension, housing - all these rights (if they are defined positively, i.e. not for example "everyone can get an education", but "everyone must be provided with an education") contradict the simple "you shall not steal". I certainly don't mean to say that people shouldn't help each other; it's just that no one should force them to do so. In all known historical societies, whose law was based on the principle of non-aggression, there was a considerable degree of voluntary solidarity (this is logical - when you know that you have a "right" to have someone help you in a crisis, you don't have to worry too much about others; on the contrary, if you depend only on them, you will help, for example, so that you can get help next time).

Despite the simplicity of the principle of non-aggression, answers to complex questions can be derived from it, for example regarding freedom of speech, labor relations, disputes over "public spaces", freedom of religion, but even the rules of transport, carrying weapons, abortion, prostitution and general management of society (which states formulate into thousands of confusing laws). Although anarcho-capitalism is in full agreement with the principle of non-aggression, this does not mean that this principle must be followed in every situation without exception in an anarcho-capitalist society, as there are no universally valid collections of laws; among the favorite pastimes of statists is inventing improbable and even absurd scenarios that show strange results after the literal application of the principle of non-aggression, while completely ignoring the fact that if someone acts contrary to the principle of non-aggression, but in accordance with common sense and generally accepted ethics (which, moreover, hardly happens), people will probably accept his behavior (therefore, we will not encounter arbitrary punishment for completely understandable behavior with reasoning that "the law is the law").

Although it cannot be assumed that the principle of non-aggression in a real anarcho-capitalist society would be followed unconditionally by everyone (after all, even the laws of today's states are not always observed), they are related as follows: First, anarcho-capitalism as a school of thought is derived from the principle of non-aggression, and secondly, in practice in places where real (even if not formal) anarchy reigned in some historical period (for example, medieval Iceland or the USA during the time of colonization), society governed by rules that were very close to the principle of non-aggression.

Why the concept of law described above is sometimes called natural law is a rather philosophical question. Some claim that we all have them somehow encoded in our brains (because they are property rights and owning things is natural for humans) or that it is given by God. In my opinion, however, it is more important that it is a moral, ethical, consistent and non-arbitrary law (applying equally to all). I leave the evaluation of these approaches to the reader - as well as the comparison of the principle of non-aggression with the law imposed on us by the state. It probably did not escape anyone's attention that we only dealt with the law as such, not with its enforcement, i.e. putting it into practice; we will get to both of these in chapters fourteen and fifteen of this book, while the next one will focus on state protection of the irresponsible.

name: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text:
“He who sacrifices liberty to gain more security loses both and deserves neither,” said Benjamin Franklin, eighteenth century American thinker and scientist; I begin the chapter with this quote, which will be dedicated to state interventions that aim to ensure people's safety and protect them. What can we say about such interventions?

It follows from the first chapter that they are not needed; on the other hand, that they are not effective; from the third, moreover, that they are not moral; and now, in the fourth chapter, we will show that, regardless of their unnecessaryness, ineffectiveness and immorality, the consequences of these interventions are negative for the very subjects for whose sake they allegedly occur.

First, I will list a few state interventions that promise people safety in exchange for freedom, so that everyone can imagine what I am actually talking about: unemployment support, legal arrangements for contracts "noticeably disadvantageous to one party", social benefits, consumer and employee protection and many others.

What is the problem? Well... except that the market will provide all this better than the state (the general principles are described in the first two chapters, we will deal with this specifically in the following chapters) and that it is immoral, because in order for the state to provide any of the above, it must first rob. Even if this were not a problem for someone - what will people do who are assured (or create the illusion of assurance) that they cannot be cheated, that they cannot starve, that they will be provided for in their old age, that their children will always be taken care of? Well, they probably won't behave in the most responsible way.

One of the supposed "functions" of most states is to take care of the poor and helpless; it is realized, of course, by forcing the subjects to take care of someone by force. For a smooth enforcement, of course, people still need to be made to feel that no one would do it otherwise (Vladimir Putin perfected it in 2013, for example, with his effort to outlaw Yevgeni Grekov's charity organization, which "threatened the motherland" by building a hospital). However, charitable associations existed even at a time when the state had not intervened in this area at all (we can read about the details of how such associations functioned in the Czech lands, for example, in the research of Professor Karel Engliš).

So what is the main difference between the charity of voluntary associations and the state? On the part of the payers, it is understandably either a matter of charity or of being robbed; but let's look at the side of the recipients. While voluntary associations choose well whom, how much, how long and in what form they will help, the state guarantees the "right" to help. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk saw it this way in 1919: "In the Czechoslovak Republic, there will be no more place for the old charity, which was always considered a grace, which always humiliated the poor recipient and dulled his human consciousness. Today, we put social duty in the place of humiliating grace."

But what is the natural consequence of the fact that if a person in need does not have to ask for alms, it will not humiliate him, the poor man, but it will be his "right"? People will definitely not be so embarrassed to reach out. Those who reach out will then not try so hard to improve their situation. And most importantly, all people in the whole society will not be so worried about getting into such a situation.

In discussions on this topic, many object to me: "Just look around you. Look at the people on the street. Look at those demented people who take out holiday loans again and again with ridiculous interest rates, they only care about beer and TV, they choose Paroubka or Babiš for a free sausage or doughnut, they are unable to take care of themselves because they have no idea how the world works, because they just don't care, they don't care. How will these people take care of themselves without a state?' Far better, I say! They are not interested in anything simply because they have no motivation to do so. The state declares that it will take care of them; they believe him (and for the purposes of this discussion whether it is true is irrelevant), ergo they have no reason to care. Economists call this phenomenon rational ignorance (when people believe that the state cares, then the expected benefit of knowing some information about how the world works is often lower for them than the effort expended to obtain that information).

Another example of rational ignorance is democratic elections. In order to make a truly well-founded choice between the candidates, one would have to read election programs, politicians' statements, familiarize themselves with the opinions of each of them, follow their past and estimate from it how sincerely the person in question means his promises, and so on. Such a study costs dozens or small hundreds of hours. And what does one get for this time? Almost zero chance of his vote making a difference when everyone else is throwing in whoever gives them a free hot dog and beer anyway. Coughing it up can then be a completely rational and logical choice.

Let's say you have a roof over your head and something to eat too. You know that if you take out a loan that you're going to have a hard time repaying, or lose your job, it'll all "work out" anyway, and you'll probably still have a roof over your head and food to eat. What is your motivation to behave responsibly? Compare that to a situation where you know that if you do something similar, maybe once or twice a charity will help you, but then you'll lose a roof over your head, you'll be cold, you'll be hungry, you'll lose everything. What is your motivation to act responsibly now?

We see the consequences everywhere, including in the labor market. The modern state tries to increase the number of people with university degrees, education is set up like this, demands are reduced; Nowadays, almost anyone who wants a little can have a university. What does it lead to? On the one hand, the employment offices are overwhelmed by social anthropologists with diplomas from anywhere in Upper Lower Saxony, whose number exceeds the demand, so they cannot find work, which is why they receive benefits. On the other hand, a programmer from Matfyz puts up a CV on the Internet and is overwhelmed with job offers literally within a few hours, not to mention the fact that it is becoming more and more difficult to find an electrician or a plumber, because there are fewer of them than are needed. That magical "how many are needed" means exactly what no mortal has a chance to count; the answer is only the market (the same applies in the labor market as in any other - it is about the principles we described in the first two chapters). This situation is a typical consequence of central planning in education, but it also has another cause: If we look at the average student in the last year of high school, who chooses a university, he decides according to what he likes and what he likes, or which school is the best place to hang out, while the criterion of "applying in the field" is usually secondary and unimportant. The question is whether this would be the case even if those concerned knew that if they studied a field in which they were not interested, they would have existential problems, would not be able to start a family, and so on; the attitude of the parents of the students concerned would probably change accordingly.

Some will argue, "Okay, but what about people who try but are just incapable?" Something similar applies to incompetence as well as to lack of motivation. The world is a wonderful place whose great qualities include a huge degree of predictability: You reach into the fire, you get burned; you do it again, the result will be the same. This enables all thinking creatures to learn and develop; if the world worked completely randomly, nothing like this would be possible. However, this predictability is far from being limited to the laws of physics, it also works quite well within socio-economic relations and, in fact, almost everywhere. Thanks to her, we can learn from our mistakes; however, when the state mitigates the consequences of these mistakes, it makes it difficult for us to learn, thereby creating not only the irresponsible, but also the incompetent (not that they would not exist without the state, but in far smaller numbers).

In general, then, it can be said that the more the state supports the irresponsible and incompetent, the more there will be; and these will hardly raise responsible individuals from their children, so their number will increase with each generation and their dependence on the state will deepen. This creates an artificial argument for why the state is actually needed. Why artificial? The human instinct for self-preservation is still quite strong; at the moment when something is really at stake and people will be seriously faced with the choice of whether to start behaving responsibly or starve and freeze, it can be assumed that most of them will - for purely existential reasons - prefer thinking over freezing (although both sometimes hurt). And the more we buy into politicians' rhetoric that people can't take care of themselves, so the state has to do it for them, the more we'll see around us that it's true; but as soon as we say no, and we stop supporting irresponsibility, we will witness its decline.

Inextricably linked to this is a phenomenon I call the "deadly cycle of democracy": A politician promises voters protection from the consequences of their mistakes; they elect him, he fulfills his promise (at least partially), the state mitigates (obviously at someone's expense) the negative consequences of some bad decisions; it will start to pay less to be responsible (the costs will remain, but the price we already pay for irresponsibility will decrease), so there will be more irresponsible and dependent on the state (including civil servants who implement the politician's promises); these people (and in subsequent generations their descendants) will typically vote for politicians who promote a strong state. This completes the circle; democracy inherently tends towards socialism, as it creates people dependent on the state the more the more such voters there are.

However, I am certainly not saying that we should not care for people in need (I do so abundantly myself); and history shows that those who care are not few, they just choose who to help and who not to (typically they don't help those who get into bad situations repeatedly and don't try to get back on their feet as soon as possible). On the contrary, the state claims that everyone has a "right" to help in an emergency, which leads to a huge increase in addicts who do not even try to actively solve their problems.

This chapter concludes the first part of the book, which deals with the general principles of human action, economics, the market and the state. In the following chapters, we will analyze the individual areas of human activity, which are now held by force in the hands of the states. We will consider how they could function without violence based on the actions of free people; in the very next chapter we will focus on state-controlled money and banking.

name: 5. Money
text:
I will preface this chapter with a well-known quote: "Give me the power to print and control the money, and I will not care who makes the laws," authored by none other than Mayer Amschel Rothschild, who, in my opinion, omitted one very important fact when formulating this sentence; any of the readers may be wondering why Mr. Rothschild could possibly not really care who makes the laws?

Almost all of us already perceive it as a completely natural thing, so we often forget that the state has a monopoly on money enforced by force. So what would happen if Mr. Rothschild started merrily printing and controlling the money, but the law makers abolished the legal obligation of the citizens to accept the currency? Apparently what happened virtually any time in history when the state gave the people the option or when state money failed (typically too much was printed, leading to massive inflation): Private money spontaneously arose in the free market, usually backed by a precious metal. People would rightly say, "Why should this Rothschild be allowed to print money, devalue our savings, and live comfortably off it? Away with his money! Let's start using others!"

In the first chapter, we described why and how money was created. People exchanged goods and services. When two people each possessed something that was more useful to the other than to themselves, they voluntarily exchanged these goods, increasing the welfare of both without producing anything new. The complication arose when one had something to exchange that the other did not want; then they had to find some chain of people through which they exchange their goods (for example, exchange bread for potatoes, which can then be exchanged for steak, because the person who has steak is not interested in bread). This is, firstly, complicated, and secondly, it is not very clear which offer is the most advantageous, if there are several such exchange methods.

This problem was elegantly solved by the free market: Some commodity spontaneously established itself as the universal medium of exchange. People began to accept it even when they had no direct use for it, but knew that they would be able to exchange it easily. The prices of all goods were then expressed precisely in proportion to this currency. Examples of such universal means of exchange were especially precious metals, iron, cloth scarves, leather, grain and many others. Of course, these commodities continued to fulfill their normal function (which, incidentally, made counterfeiting problematic: if, for example, the currency is grain, then "counterfeiting" means that you grow grain; this is not a harmful activity, you simply become a farmer).

Over time, precious metals became established as currency almost everywhere: They could be easily divided and melted together again, they did not spoil, it was possible to store a lot of value in small volumes and, above all, their total amount on the market only changed unexpectedly or in leaps and bounds (for example, when the Spanish fleet with gold cargo was sunk).

Many people made their trades in metalworking: goldsmiths and jewelry makers, but also coiners and makers of private money (people brought their precious metals to them, which were processed in mints into coins on which the weight was stamped, facilitating transactions where the precious metals did not have to be divided and weighed again). Over time, institutions operating in this sector began to function both as lenders and as depositories: So that people did not have to carry precious metals directly with them, they deposited them with trusted goldsmiths, from whom they received confirmation of deposit; they then began to trade these confirmations as precious metals themselves—and paper money was born.

Since the same institutions that issued certificates of deposits of precious metals (i.e. paper money) often also made a living by providing loans, loans were often made in such a way that the borrower did not receive the coins directly, but these certificates (paper money). This naturally tempted individuals endowed with a higher degree of enterprise and a lower degree of morality to lend more than they actually had. It was simple: The person issued a certificate of deposit of more precious metals than he owned. That usually worked until he overdid it and word got around. They then quite understandably started asking for precious metals for their confirmations; the cheater didn't have that much and the cage fell. He was dealt with according to local customs, which in the best cases meant hanging; in worse burns, flaying and similar pastimes.

As is often the case, when the state sees an evil, it does not take long to establish a monopoly on it. It was the same with lending money that doesn't exist. In the vast majority of cases, the historical development was something like this: The state issued paper money as a confirmation of the deposit of gold in the state bank, then started a war that there was nothing to finance, so it printed more money than it had gold as a "temporary measure". The subjects were simply told that the state money was no longer backed by gold; of course, this was not met with enthusiasm, and citizens preferred gold to worthless paper, but this did not usually pose much of a problem for the state, which had a monopoly on violence: Failure to accept the state currency was often punishable by death (somewhere "only" by prison). Although in the beginning it was always necessary to impose state (uncovered) money on the people by force, it was not such a problem during a few generations of brainwashing to convince the subjects that it doesn't really matter; and a new way of legalized robbing was born.

How exactly does such a robbery take place? Actually, exactly the same as counterfeiting (only when the state is counterfeiting, it is called quantitative easing). If the amount of money in the economy increases, its value falls, so prices rise (money is a commodity like any other; when there is more of it, it is less scarce, so its value falls relative to other goods, see chapter one). As a result, everyone who has savings in a given currency transfers part of their value to the counterfeiter (state, banks). The nominal value of savings will remain the same, but their owner will be able to buy fewer goods with them, so their real value will fall. So when someone prints a billion crowns, they actually steal everything they buy with that billion from all holders of that currency (they are robbed in proportion to how many crowns they have).

After government money was forced upon the people, the masses - with the help of heavy propaganda - got used to it over time. The majority of states then relaxed their repressive strategy: Although the law imposes the obligation to accept state currency, in theory private currencies are not prohibited in many states (however, they are disadvantaged by the fact that everyone must accept the state currency by law, and in addition, taxes are collected in it). However, when someone tries to succeed in this market in practice and starts to do well, he is somehow cleared by the state anyway.

In 1998, Bernard von NotHaus created the Liberty Dollar, a silver-backed private currency. Within a few years, over seven million US dollars worth of silver (in the form of Liberty Dollars) had entered circulation, and the Liberty Dollar was becoming more and more popular. The United States government was frightened by the potential competition, so it had to be nipped in the bud. In 2007, the FBI launched a crackdown on NotHaus, only to have him indicted in 2009 and sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2011 (the trial lasted just 90 minutes) for conspiracy and counterfeiting. The plot was to create competition to the US dollar, and the alleged counterfeiting of money was even more absurd: One of NotHaus's coins was said to resemble a US quarter (although the quarter has a male likeness, the Liberty Dollar has a female likeness); even if the likeness actually existed, the alleged "forgery" made of silver was worth 160x more than the quarter it was supposed to fake. Imagine expecting a quarter, but a rogue counterfeiter slips you a coin worth 160x more, or $40; wouldn't that make you angry?

And so Bernard von NotHaus became another victim of the regime; although he was released after several years, the government sent a clear message. The state simply took all Liberty Dollars from him - and his innocent customers - by force. And what did Bernard von NotHaus actually do? What crime did he commit? He minted silver coins and sold them. No one was forced to buy those coins. The man was merely satisfying market demand, nothing more. Who did he hurt? To no one. Unlike illegal drugs, which the government bans under the pretense of protecting ourselves, these silver coins didn't hurt their own owners (the government did when they seized the Liberty Dollars), they just gave them a choice in what to do with their money. So why are governments all over the world usurping a monopoly on money? Well, simply so that they can rob the subjects. There is really no other reason here, it cannot even be said that they would protect citizens from anything. Free entrepreneurs in the money market have operated for hundreds of years to everyone's satisfaction; but then the states saw another way of subtly robbing their subjects, and immediately seized upon it.

In conclusion, it should be added that states usually do not do these machinations with money themselves, so that it is not too messy. In fact, they use banks to do similar shenanigans, which create money out of nothing in a relatively sophisticated way (they get permission from the state to do this; profits are shared between governments and banks using other complicated and non-transparent mechanisms). A detailed description of these practices would probably take up many books. However, we don't have that much space, so we'll just show the two most fundamental consequences of the above actions: constant inflation and economic cycles (which are the cause of economic crises). A more demanding reader can read about the principles of how economic cycles arise, for example, in the book "What has government done to our money?" from my favorite author Murray Newton Rothbard, or "The Theory of Money and Credit" (published already in 1912!) by Ludwig von Mises, or search the Internet for "Austrian business cycle theory"; a less discerning reader will perhaps be satisfied with the reasoning that there was no such thing as economic cycles or constant inflation until states began to control money. I would really like to go into more depth on this subject, because the instruments by which governments, with the help of banks, control money are almost diabolical; however, their detailed description would take another separate book. Now let's turn to something that fills me with hope - and that is cryptocurrencies.

chapter: 5. Money
name: Cryptocurrency
text:
In 2013, when the Money chapter was created, the fundamental importance of cryptocurrencies was not yet completely clear to me, and therefore I did not include them in it; however, I would consider it a significant omission if I did not mention them even today in the second edition. Cryptocurrencies are digital money whose existence and transfers through cryptography are ensured by decentralized networks instead of central authorities; this means that they do not need any central bank, but at the same time they provide all the advantages of online means of payment.

The consensus among economists is that in order for an asset to be classified as money, it must fulfill three basic functions: store value, serve as a universal medium of exchange, and fulfill the role of a unit of account (that is, be a measure of the prices of goods and services in the economy); I personally believe that a unit of account cannot be anything that is not a universal medium of exchange, so the second described function is redundant, as it directly follows from the third. History shows that these functions are performed by commodities that have the following six properties: rarity (limited quantity), durability, fungibility (ideally the indistinguishability of the units of a given item), divisibility (possibility of being "exchanged" without loss of value), easy transferability, and distinguishability (verification of authenticity). Not everything that possesses these attributes automatically becomes money; good money, however, must meet all these parameters (at least to a considerable extent).

All six characters are very well fulfilled by a number of assets that are commonly called cryptocurrencies; some of them serve as great stores of value, but none of them is yet widely used as a universal medium of exchange, and therefore not even as a unit of account. State (fiat) currencies meet most of these six criteria more poorly, but their acceptance is enforced by law (in addition, there is an obligation to pay taxes and keep accounts in them); as a result, they function as units of account as well as mediums of exchange, but fail as stores of value (since there is no guarantee of their rarity when banks keep issuing new ones). Therefore, no cryptocurrency (due to insufficient liquidity) or fiat (due to a persistent decline in real purchasing power) fulfills all the functions of good money today. For cryptocurrencies capable of long-term storage of value, I prefer the term cryptomoney, thereby distinguishing them from liquid - but constantly depreciating - sovereign currencies, as well as from the vast majority (over 99.99%) of cryptocurrencies, which are called by the established term "shitcoin" in the crypto community.

Bitcoin is the oldest, most widespread, most liquid and, for many (so-called Bitcoin maximalists), the only cryptocurrency. This protocol for an open-source peer-to-peer payment network was defined in late 2008 by a person or group of people using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto; On January 3, 2009, it was launched to initially serve as a toy for a few enthusiasts. A year and a half later, for the first time, someone used it to make a purchase - programmer Laszlo Hanyecz ordered two pizzas for 10,000 BTC; little did he know at the time that in honor of this transaction, crypto-anarchists would start celebrating May 22nd as "Pizza Day" a few years later. Today, for the same number of bitcoins, we could buy, for example, a large private island with a luxurious palace, a power plant, an airport, a port, a jet, a helicopter, a yacht, and perhaps even a submarine; at the same time, we wouldn't have to worry too much about the budget - there would be enough left over for operating costs for the rest of our lives. How could the price go up so much? More and more people understand that Bitcoin is a great store of value; far superior to any current fiat currency.

From the point of view of a (crypto)anarchist, I see the absence of any central authority as the most important feature of Bitcoin; it is a decentralized network that anyone can join at any time and start participating in its operation. While records of current account balances are managed by banks (and can therefore be frozen and similar), all Bitcoin transactions (including the complete history) are simultaneously stored by tens of thousands of computers located around the world; and if by chance someone decides to block my funds, the request for their transfer will simply be handled by another. Bad language people claim that the secret services of some of the great powers may be hiding under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, which I do not consider very likely; however, the beauty of decentralization is that it's completely irrelevant - even if it were true, the creator of Bitcoin has no actual power over it (and not even a backdoor, since it's open source software).

On the contrary, I consider Bitcoin's greatest weakness to be that it is not fully anonymous; although it does not show who owns which funds, but their transfers can be tracked - the history of all transactions is public (although they cannot be linked to specific people without additional information, states are gradually beginning to spend more and more resources to obtain this "additional information"). Although this problem can be solved in most cases and privacy can be protected, it requires an advanced level of understanding of the functioning of the entire network as well as blockchain analysis tools; not to mention the fact that anyone can simply make mistakes, which unfortunately has led to many seasoned crypto-anarchists knowing the inside of a prison cell. In response to this, for example, the Monero project was created - it can be imagined as the "younger brother" of Bitcoin, which, however, operates in complete anonymity and no one can monitor third-party transactions in it without the permission of their author; this is also why it is commonly used on illegal darknet markets (although it has other limitations). For the sake of completeness, I state that Bitcoin has tens of thousands of different "siblings"; however, almost without exception, these are broken or outright fraudulent projects (the aforementioned "shitcoins") in which you can easily drown your savings - but their existence provides much-needed competition that separates the wheat from the chaff (and some of them I still consider more trustworthy than sovereign currencies).

As I mentioned a few paragraphs ago, no cryptocurrencies yet fulfill all the necessary functions of (good) money; and due to the inflationary nature of absolutely all fiat currencies, I dare say that unfortunately there is no such thing as good money in the world today. The six properties that constitute a necessary (but not sufficient) prerequisite for a commodity to become such money are currently, in my opinion, best fulfilled by Bitcoin and Monero. Let's do a quick comparison of these cryptocurrencies, precious metals and sovereign currencies:

Rarity

Bitcoin: Excellent - given maximum number of coins

Monero: Very good - low predictable inflation

Precious metals: Good - potential new deposits

State fiat currencies: Bad - unpredictable central bank inflation

Durability

Bitcoin: Excellent - Distributed Database

Monero: Excellent - Distributed Database

Precious Metals: Excellent - tangible physical goods

State fiat currencies: Good - central control of account balances

Interchangeability

Bitcoin: The Bad - Public History of Coins

Monero: Excellent - invisibility of coins without keys

Precious Metals: Excellent - indistinguishable coins, bullion

State fiat currencies: Very good - digital footprint of cashless transactions

Divisibility

Bitcoin: Excellent - easily divisible "to dust"

Monero: Excellent - easily divisible "to dust"

Precious metals: Very good - divisible almost "to dust"

Government fiat currencies: Very good - easily convertible

Portability

Bitcoin: Excellent - portable keys in your head

Monero: Excellent - portable keys in the head

Precious Metals: Good – tangible physical goods

Government fiat currencies: Very good - physical cash, bank controlled accounts

Recognizability

Bitcoin: Excellent - Public Blockchain

Monero: Very good - complex cryptographic verifiability

Precious metals: Good - chemical testability

Government fiat currencies: Good - anti-counterfeit features of notes and coins

I feel it is important to add that not all properties are equally important; for example, the poor recognizability of money may not be such a fundamental obstacle (for example, if the commodities for which it can be exchanged are also rare), while the minimal rarity or extremely short durability of the good essentially makes its monetary use impossible. In addition, it is not the case that the item that best meets the above-mentioned parameters must always become money; changing money entails high transaction costs, which is why people only give it up when they stop fulfilling the necessary functions - not just because something could fulfill them a little better. For example, Bitcoin has (and has always had) the highest market capitalization (that is, the product of the number of Bitcoins and the current unit price) of all cryptocurrencies; because it serves as a good store of value, which allows it to be quickly and cheaply transferred between individual holders at essentially any distance. Although other cryptocurrencies (such as Monero) later brought certain advantages (such as anonymity), the time-tested trustworthiness of the first and oldest open-source peer-to-peer payment network is clearly more important to most users; for this reason (at least for now) it does not seem that Bitcoin should lose its position as "number one" (at least in the foreseeable future).

If (any) money ceases to be scarce, its value decreases, which may lead to people refusing to accept and use it as a universal medium of exchange; in the case of state currencies, this fate can to some extent be delayed (or even averted) legislatively - for example, by enacting their mandatory acceptance by merchants or by not allowing taxation (or accounting) by other means. Even these steps are understandably not a panacea; for example, during hyperinflation, debased money alternatives typically come into play. However, until the situation is unsustainable, the state successfully enforces the use of bad money by force, thereby harming its holders; inflation (of virtually all current fiat currencies) is a hidden form of taxation.

It probably won't surprise anyone that as a (crypto)anarchist I prefer cryptocurrencies over state ones; above all, however, I am a supporter of full voluntariness, freedom of choice, and therefore a free money market - I consider this to be far more important than my personal preferences for Bitcoin (or Monero). I believe that the only way to know really good money is to let people choose the ones that suit them. Even if centrally controlled inflationary currencies should turn out to be most desirable (which I think extremely unlikely), I will humbly accept that choice, unless it is conditioned by violent coercion; although for many reasons I consider Bitcoin to be the money of the future, I don't want to impose anything on anyone - let everyone decide for themselves what they (don't) want to pay for.

If you don't know anything about cryptocurrencies and would like to change that, you can visit the website krypto.urza.cz.

name: 6. Firefighters
text:
Private firefighters. Absence of state firefighters. When a person says something similar in mainstream society, the reactions tend to be different. Mostly very emotional, we are often treated to various colorful images featuring burning houses, from which paying customers are rescued, while others end up in flames, jumping out of windows like living torches. Since these emotions are exactly what the state manipulates its citizens with, let's try to put them aside for a moment and think about things more deeply.

Since in this chapter we will talk about the method and quality of fire service provision, it should be mentioned at the outset that this quality depends a lot on their price; in general, for almost every condition, it can be said that for some extra money it is possible to achieve an increase in quality. One extreme corresponds to the fact that fire services will not be provided by anyone and in any way, so that all costs will be equal to zero. The other theoretical extreme may look approximately like that a fully equipped fire station will be located near every house. Between these extremes there are many intermediate states, which correspond to a network of varying density of the most diversely equipped stations. It is obvious that by adding money to such a system, quality improvements can be achieved - for example, by buying better equipment, reducing travel times, and so on.

Common sense, the famous book "Human Action" by Ludwig von Mises, observation of the environment and the first two chapters of this book suggest that people have their needs, which they satisfy in order from the most urgent to the least urgent (resources are limited, so they cannot satisfy all of them). What this means in practice is that a person typically knows that they need to eat, live and go to work, which will be the things they buy first (so they will pay for food, housing and transport to work first with their money); furthermore, for example, he knows that he would still like to go to a concert and have a couple of dinners in a good restaurant (he will pay for this with the money that is left over); then, for example, he knows that he wants to go to the beach in the summer and buy a car in a year (from the money left over after food, housing, transport to work, concerts and dinners, he will put some aside for savings); and finally, he would also like to go to the cinema, but for example he may find that he has no money left for that - that is, he will not go to the cinema because his other needs are more important. Each of us thinks approximately in this way: They prioritize their needs and desires and satisfy the most urgent, the biggest ones. Some may argue that there are also people who do not plan it directly like this and act more impulsively, or are too lazy to think about it and make some reasonable calculations; in short, one can answer these objections that for these people, impulsiveness or laziness (whose manifestations are also needs in a way) is more important than satisfying some of the needs mentioned above (for whom this answer is not enough, I refer to the above-mentioned book "Human Action", in which Ludwig von Mises describes this action in great detail).

How does this relate to firefighters? Well, fire protection is among the needs of the vast majority of people; and everyone feels this need to varying degrees. Someone is willing to pay a lot for very high-quality services, while others would prefer to pay little for inferior services. What happens when the state sets some fixed quality of service? Those for whom the quality is not sufficient will typically buy something better; after all, many industrial enterprises and more valuable real estate are today protected against fire by private fire companies (the owners of protected buildings, however, still have to pay for state fire protection in an absolutely immoral and senseless way). But there are also those among us for whom state fire brigades are too expensive and would be satisfied with a cheaper – but worse – option. These people are forced to pay something they don't want. The state simply takes one of their less urgent needs and forces them to satisfy it at the expense of a more urgent need, for which the person may no longer have sufficient resources.

So this (and, of course, the fact that forcing someone to pay for a service by force is extremely immoral) are the main - and quite fundamental - reasons against the existence of state firefighters. So if we assume that the fire service will be provided by a purely free market without state interventions, what could such a thing look like? Given that market solutions to problems are the result of the interaction of vast numbers of free individuals, it is impossible to say exactly how this will work off the table, but one can guess a lot. So I'll outline one way the free market could provide fire services - it's likely that the reality would be even better, as millions of entrepreneurs around the world will surely come up with a much more efficient solution.

Considering how private fire departments have operated historically and now, one can assume that payment for these services would be similar to insurance. Entrepreneurs will set up fire stations in various places, and people in the neighborhood will pay for their services at a flat rate: They will pay a small amount every month, regardless of whether there is actually a fire in their place or not; then when it really burns, the company in question intervenes. It is reasonable to assume that entire houses would be insured in this way (it is difficult for individuals, who are practically impossible to locate in time during a fire), thus eliminating scenarios where firefighters pull paying customers out of a burning house and let the rest burn (the insurance will probably cover the whole house and all the people inside - a fire company that would protect property but let people burn would probably not have many customers).

Another huge advantage of this principle is that the price for fire protection would be set individually - it would be higher for buildings with a higher probability of fire and lower for those with a lower probability. Similar to the price of flood insurance today, the location of the house plays a role (it is more expensive in flood zones). For houses better secured against fires, the fire protection fee will be lower. When these services are provided by the state and their price is independent of the risk of fire, there must be clouds of fire regulations that no one has much incentive to comply with (and those who build houses have little reason to do more than the bare minimum). If the price of fire protection is market-based, compliance with (and creation of) "fire codes" will be economically beneficial to those who build buildings, as well as those who maintain and live in them. No one will have to force anyone to do anything, people will be motivated by simply saving by following certain rules.

Let's admit that some people don't take out fire insurance. It is very likely that companies that provide firefighting services on a regular fee basis will be willing to fight a fire even for a direct payment, which will logically be much higher than the payment of that regular insurance; in any case, considering that the house is extinguished, it is practically always worthwhile for the owner to pay such a fee, since the price of the house is typically higher than the price of its extinguishment. Therefore, it cannot be argued that the poor will not be able to pay for fire protection: Whoever owns a house or an apartment also has money for firefighters; even if he chooses not to pay the regular fees, he can still call a company to extinguish the property in the event of a fire - he will be paid for practically any amount that is less than the price of what is left of the property after it is extinguished.

Other free market options are, for example, company firefighters (the factory has its own fire brigade, which also extinguishes the surrounding area) or volunteers (this profession brings social prestige), for example in Austria these cover a significantly larger part of the market than the state ones; in Denmark, most fires are extinguished by commercial companies. Historically, too, private fire brigades have proven themselves. State-funded fire departments are a relatively recent phenomenon; they mostly didn't start appearing until the end of the nineteenth century, when they didn't cover nearly as much of the market as they do today (which only came in the twentieth century). Previously, fire services were provided and paid proportionately

differently. In London, for example, the first professional fire brigades were established as early as the seventeenth century; they were paid by insurance companies and were very successful - in a city that was practically entirely wooden, they intervened several times a day and put out hundreds of thousands of fires (for those who are interested in the details, they can be found, for example, in the book "An Economic History of London 1800 - 1914" by Michael Ball and David Sunderland). In the territory of the Czech Republic, fire brigades were rather voluntary and financed on the basis of charity or they were factory fire brigades (their primary task was to extinguish possible fires in factories, but they typically also protected the surrounding area); the means for their operation were sufficient even without state intervention (more details can be found, for example, in the book "History of Moravia. Part 4, Free State and Occupation" by Josef Bartoš).

Market prices will also ensure adequate salaries for firefighters (what they deserve, which is what people are willing to pay them voluntarily) and the "right" number of them. Everyone has already heard from the mouth of some politician that they will stop the slimming of fire brigades, or take care of an increase in their numbers; we keep hearing about the fact that there are too few civil servants and they are not able to do their job to the required extent. How often, on the other hand, do we hear about directive increases in the status of bakers, programmers, workers or salespeople? None of this is necessary, as the invisible hand of the market can ensure the right number of them (if there are few people practicing a profession, their wages rise, which attracts more people to learn the profession, and vice versa - these principles are described in more detail in the first two chapters of this book). It would be exactly the same with firefighters - if the state stopped regulating the industry and left room for the free market.

Although fire protection is generally seen as a good that should be provided by the state because "otherwise it wouldn't work", on closer examination we find that it worked a long time ago and still works today in some countries; plus, there's really no reason why it shouldn't work. On the contrary, there are many arguments why private fire services are not only more moral (no one forces anyone to pay for them), but also more efficient. Unfortunately, we have no choice, the state forces us to pay for its services by force; the same can be said about the subsidization of culture, which we will pay more attention to in the next chapter.

name: 7. Art and culture
text:
Culture - and art in general - enriches a person spiritually and mentally, it is beneficial to society; therefore, it should be subsidized by state subsidies, otherwise many beautiful things would disappear from our world. Some art will pay for itself, others would disappear without subsidies; after all, we must protect such from extinction. Most people say something similar when we ask them what they think about state funding of culture. But let's think more deeply about the implications before jumping to any conclusions.

At the outset, I want to say that I am definitely not an "art opponent". People often tend to think that when someone condemns the subsidization of culture, they are against art as such. That may not be true, and in my case it certainly isn't. I consider both art and culture very important because they really enrich individuals and make them happy; me personally, for example, especially rock and classical music.

Defenders of cultural subsidies from public budgets justify their positions mainly by the fact that without subsidies, many artists would not be able to create, theaters would disappear, "non-commercial" cinematography would not support itself, exhibitions and museums would not cover costs from admission fees alone. To begin with this objection, it is necessary to note that many great artists created without state support; for example (across various types of art): Shakespeare, G. B. Shaw, Beethoven, Mozart (who, as part of his eccentricity, refused to serve the masters and became a free artist), Queen, Pink Floyd, Deep Purple, The Rolling Stones, Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Vincent van Gogh, Picasso, Dalí...

Above all, however, it is necessary to realize what it actually means when, without state subsidies, an artist cannot create, a theater ceases to exist, a film cannot be made, or a museum cannot cover operating costs. When such art does not support itself, it is because people voluntarily (without state coercion) do not want to pay enough for it, so that the cost of running such art is greater than what people are willing to pay for the result. However, we know from the first chapter that such a state means that someone is wasting precious resources (for example, an artist's time, a theater building, a canvas or paints, musical instruments); people value these resources as something more valuable than what is produced from them (if this were not the case, the art in question would be profitable). This means that the utility of such an artistic act is negative for people.

I can imagine readers who will indignantly object at this point that art and beauty can't be calculated only in terms of money! Please, let's recall the opening few chapters of this book. What is the main function of money and prices? After all, transmitting information about the rarity of goods and their benefits. Converting something to "mere" money means converting it to the benefit and satisfaction of people at the same time. Of course, the fact that it would be necessary to spend more money to implement a project than what people are willing to pay for it is not important. What is important is what this information tells us: People do not want such a project. It is necessary to remember the cost of the sacrificed opportunity - in addition to the benefit that the above-mentioned project brings, it is also necessary to take into account the fact that other things could not have arisen due to its creation; the people involved in the project could have done something else, the material could have been used differently - even the value of the time of those people and the material used is higher than the value of the final work (although the value is numerically expressed in money, but of course it is a benefit for society).

Most people live with the idea that the "value of art" is something that only experts or critics can determine, because many ordinary people "don't understand art". But what is the purpose of art or culture? After all, the purpose is to enrich a person in spirit, in heart and mind, to make him happier, to evoke pleasant feelings, to make him think. But what kind of person? Everyone! Not just a few insiders. He who "does not understand art" is not enriched. But he is no less a man than those who understand; his wishes, desires, feelings and dreams are no less important - and therefore it is monstrous to force him to pay for something he has no interest in. I am not suggesting that "quality art" is that which earns itself; I just don't want to force anyone to pay for it.

One can often meet the objection that if the state did not support art, only "commercial" and "junk" things would survive, but some truly "valuable" things would not; that, for example, stupid TV series or monotonous pop music would be enjoyed, but some really deep works would have a problem with it. But what does that mean? That the monotonous pop music and stupid TV shows that make money for themselves make people happier than those works that can't support themselves without state subsidies! The objection that this is because "they are uneducated barbarians" may be true, but irrelevant - why should the happiness of a "civilized man" take precedence over that of an "uneducated barbarian"? I also don't understand how someone can prefer, for example, Michal David over Brian May, Freddie Mercury, Beethoven or Vivaldi, it seems completely crazy to me. Nevertheless, such people exist. And nothing gives me any right to force them to pay what I like at the expense of what they like. If someone is happy with the series "Rose Garden Surgery", it is immoral, unethical, monstrous and inexcusable to force them to pay for the series "Italian classics of the second half of the 20th century", which he does not watch and does not bring him anything; regardless of my opinion of his taste (I'll leave it to the reader to decide whether the greater barbarian is the one who peacefully watches his favorite soap opera or the one who forcibly forces him to patronize his favorite theater).

In addition, the choice does not always stand as it is presented to us and as I did in the previous paragraph. People who do not pay for a theater or museum do not automatically donate this money to some "fallen waste". They often don't dedicate them to any form of art at all, but use them to buy a house, educate their children, eat, or donate them to charity. And even if experts in the field of culture were able to decide (and for others) which art is mere cinders and which, on the contrary, is of sufficient quality to "deserve" government subsidies, perhaps no one can seriously believe that there could possibly be an expert in everything who could decide for others whether theater or food is more beneficial for them, or whether an exhibition of paintings or a charity collection brings more benefit.

If anyone is worried that art would cease to exist without government subsidies, then they can rest easy. Art has always existed; this human need is much older than any state. Throughout history, artists have created regardless of whether they had to support themselves or were supported by a patron or government. There is no reason to believe that right now culture needs the state to exist. After all, governments take money to subsidize culture from citizens' pockets; if they didn't, people would have more money to pay for, say, a more expensive theater ticket (or other art or whatever; just whatever gives them the most benefit). Not to mention that, according to the CZSO, even at present (research from 2011), the state participates in the financing of culture by less than fourteen percent; the remaining eighty-six were paid voluntarily.

In addition to subsidizing contemporary artists and cultural institutions, governments often care about the preservation of older works of art and historical monuments. Why will this also ensure a free market to the greater satisfaction of the people? When works of art are not managed by the state, this role falls to their owners. Who will these owners be? The free market will, over time, ensure that it is those willing to pay the most for the thing in question to whom it has the most value; such owners can be assumed to also take care of the work (or historical monument) in question when they have paid dearly for it. And these owners do not have to be only rich individuals, it can also be a voluntary association of many people who have the same interest and are willing to agree to it.

Common objections to abolishing state supervision of works of art or monuments are something like this: "What if someone bought St. Vitus' Cathedral and opened a supermarket there?" "Who's to stop someone from buying the Mona Lisa and destroying it?" The answer is easy: Why would someone pay a fortune for a painting that they then simply destroy? In the case of the supermarket in the St. Vitus Cathedral, it is similar: If someone wants to have a supermarket in the center of Prague, why would they pay huge money for the cathedral, which many people value much more for other purposes, when they can buy some other object in a similarly lucrative location for less? Even if someone already owned the temple and wanted to open a supermarket, it would be worthwhile for him to sell it as a temple and buy a cheaper object with the money taken (and make a profit on the difference). It can be argued that none of the above are 100% guarantees, but neither the state gives us these; for an example, you don't have to go far, just remember how many works of art and historical monuments were damaged or destroyed by the state in the Czech Republic between 1948 and 1989.

Many also object that if works of art and historical monuments are owned by the rich, they will not be able to be enjoyed by the general public. On the one hand, this may not be true, because even private owners can exhibit their property (either for free or for a fee), or lend it to various exhibitions (they have always done this to varying degrees and still do today). But if the owner is not willing to do anything like that, people can always get together and put together such a sum to buy the work of art or historical monument from him. If they fail to collect such an amount voluntarily, it means that the current owner values the thing in question more than the general public, who understandably has no right to take the thing from him by force.

When thinking about government subsidies for culture, we must never forget that no matter how wonderful the art might not (or could) pay for itself, government subsidies always mean the forced extortion of money from people who want to use it in other ways (otherwise they would fund the art voluntarily). Works that people are not willing to pay for themselves and voluntarily bring them less benefit than what it costs them money. If culture is left to the free market, only art will emerge that brings more to people than it takes from them; which no one else can decide for them but themselves.

name: 8. Education
text:
Schooling and the educational system have been - at least in our territory - inextricably linked to the state for over two hundred years. Today, this means that the "rules of the game" in education are determined by the government, which decides what must be taught, how it can be taught, who can teach it, who can learn it, who must learn it, how long it must be taught, how it must be assessed, and what punishment awaits anyone who goes against any of the above regulations. And this chapter was written especially for readers who find the above reasons alone insufficient for the abolition of state education.

The Achilles heel of our public education is... our public education. Practically nothing works well in it (except for a few individual schools). Critical thinking is punished, individuality is suppressed, students' attitude towards authorities is distorted, they are required to memorize completely useless information, graduates of many schools lack useful knowledge, students allow themselves to be teachers more and more, some teachers tyrannize students, teacher salaries are low, many lousy teachers just hang around in schools and are overpaid for doing nothing, students are not interested in teaching.

Do you feel that some of the solutions to the above problems may contradict each other? That feels right to you. So isn't such criticism of state education unfair, when it can demand something and at the same time the opposite of the same thing? It is not, on the contrary - it quite correctly points out the first fundamental problem of state education, which the free market can solve: In state education, there are some uniform rules that differ in certain details, but their basic direction is determined uniformly (see "National Education Program"). There is no such thing in the free market. Each school can teach what customers want.

Not all parents have the same idea about raising their children. For some, education about religion (of which there are many) and, for example, sexual abstinence is important; others want to protect their children from religion and are comfortable with today's modern concept of sex education. For some, conformity, discipline, obedience and submission to authority are more important; still others emphasize individuality, own opinion, searching for the causes of rules instead of automatically following them and following only such authorities as their descendants choose for themselves. Some of us prefer friendship (anti-manipulative education) to classical education. There are countless approaches; and since we are not all the same, it cannot even objectively be said that any one of them is the universally best for everyone. And why look for compromises or golden middle ways when there can be different schools with different rules and different teaching? And this is something that the free market, by its very nature, will offer incomparably better than the state, which simply cannot provide such a thing to the required extent (due to the impossibility of economic calculation - see Mises' book "Bureaucracy" or - for short - the second chapter of this book).

Another intractable problem of public education is the fact that there is - and cannot be - any way to distinguish a good teacher from a bad one. Virtually anyone who gets the appropriate diploma can go into teaching. The government then supervises (poorly at that) only to see if any teacher is so extremely bad that it is obvious (for example, drunkenness at work). Apart from such marginal cases, the state simply does not know how to differentiate teachers according to quality. And considering that the quality of a teacher cannot be measured exactly, and different teachers are good or bad for different students, this task is impossible for central planners. The market will solve this problem quite automatically, just like in any other industry: The better someone is at what they do, the more people are willing to pay for their services. There is no need for any central algorithm to determine the quality of architects, programmers, graphic designers or even chefs (a good chef wins customers for his restaurant and vice versa). The same would be true for teachers in a free market.

The logical consequence of the impossibility of assessing the quality of a teacher is tabular salaries. And what happens if an employee receives the same amount of money for a job well and poorly done? That it motivates everyone to slack off is probably obvious at first glance. Moreover, another consequence must be realized: For capable experts, learning is a poorly paid job, because they can get more elsewhere; on the other hand, for budižknic people who are able to get a diploma at some lousy pedagogical school with great difficulty, such a job is well-paid, because they won't be able to get more elsewhere. Unfortunately, it follows that the more capable a person is in a certain field, the less motivation for learning state education gives him (and vice versa).

A fairly typical objection to free-market education is that allegedly some poor (or miserly, or those who do not understand the value of education) parents would not pay for their children's school, which could lead to the fact that some - perhaps talented - children would not receive an education. Well, if a child is really capable, it pays for schools to teach them for free (or very cheaply), because such students raise the level of the school (on the one hand, they "pull" less talented classmates up, and on the other hand, they improve the school's statistics of successful graduates) and make good advertising (this is not an empty theory, this is already happening in many private schools today). Another solution is offered by home or community teaching, charity, or company schools, whose graduates can then become employees (which can also be anchored in a contract).

Of course, these solutions require at least minimal cooperation on the part of the parents, which at first glance may appear as a disadvantage; however, upon closer reflection, it is obvious that if the parent is an ignoramus who simply does not care about his child, the state will not help him much anyway (although he usually gets the child into school, but it typically gives the student in question practically nothing; on the contrary, he often spoils the lessons and enriches his classmates with things that their parents - or teachers - don't really care about). If someone now objects that even a slight increase in the chances of a good life for a "problem child" is worth the effort, I ask him: "Are the chances for problem children so important to you that you would not mind if their classmates - and often the targets of bullying - were your own offspring?" Because it has to be someone's children. In addition, the state quite possibly does more harm than good to them as part of "giving chances to problem children", who are placed in an environment where everyone shows them their inadequacy (see the fourth chapter).

A common objection to leaving education to the free market goes something like this: "Even now we have private schools, just look at them, they are mostly worthless and often just sell diplomas." Here it is necessary to note that even if the school is owned by a private person, the state dictates to it what it cannot, must and must do, ergo it has practically nothing to do with the free market (regardless of the artificial competition in the form of state schools). In such an environment, it can be really profitable to simply teach poorly and hand out diplomas. However, the value of the diploma in the free market would correspond to the reputation of the given school (and if anyone can easily get it, it will become worthless - just as today the value of certificates from educational courses is determined by their quality); in addition, it can be assumed that there would be certification companies that would assess the education of students independently of the school from which the person concerned came. The motivation of such certification authorities to do their job well is clear: If they certified (perhaps for a fee) everyone, their certifications would then lose value, so there would be no interest in their services.

However, the main advantage of the free market, which today's private schools under the baton of the state lack, is the possibility of choosing to learn in their own way. That is the main power of the free market! Millions of people start schools, try all kinds of teaching methods; the good prosper, the bad fail. The state has no room for such a thing; on the one hand, he cannot try an inordinate number of possibilities at once, and on the other hand, he cannot afford too much experimentation.

Throughout the chapter I refer to the fact that the state allows schools to teach basically only one way and restricts them too much. Despite this, our laws allow schools to specialize in different fields, within which they can have significantly different hourly subsidies for individual subjects, so what's the problem? Such reasoning shows that we are already so bound by the practice of state education that we cannot imagine anything else. But with a little imagination, we can ask ourselves, for example, the following questions: Is it necessary for any subjects to be taught in school at all? Do students have to be assessed (at all)? Is age segregation into classes necessary? Do teachers have to motivate children to learn? While we may think we have the answers to these – and all other – questions, how can we know for sure until someone tries?
