There is also a theory of education that describes a school that would function like this: Students would not be segregated by age in any way, there would be no classes, although the age range is planned to be quite large (from about four to nineteen). No subjects would be taught in the school. Students would have available tools and things (computers, playground, library, workshops, tools, notebooks, stationery, garden...) for free use. No one would even force them to learn to read and write. There would be no grades, no exams, no tests. The teachers would not give directives, they would only help if the children asked them. But the impulse must always come from the student, no one can force anyone to do anything. All important matters in the school, which cannot be individual and must be decided somehow, are decided by simple voting, where the votes of students and teachers have equal weight; so the voice of a four-year-old is the same as the voice of a nineteen-year-old, which in turn is the same as the voice of a teacher. This vote would include, for example, deciding which teachers will get a contract for the next year.

Would you choose a similar school for your children? I do. If there were more of us, perhaps the market would show that this education system makes sense. However, no one would have to participate in this experiment against their will. There is nothing wrong with someone having a different idea about raising their children. At the same time, countless different solutions can be implemented in the free market, as it is not bound by any central planning by the state.

chapter: 8. Education
name: Education and freedom
text:
I ended the previous – i.e. the eighth – chapter by presenting a non-standard and very free educational model, which describes another possibility of how a school could look like. Does it seem unrealistic to you? Have you ever thought that I can't even be serious about this anymore? Is this just salon theory that has no basis in practice? Is this a concept that could never work with real children?

When I first read about this educational model, these are the thoughts that went through my head. Whenever I discussed the topic with a teacher, the reactions were basically always negative. It is precisely one of those methods of teaching which no government would dare to introduce, because it contradicts everything we know about education; so of course it can never work.

But Hanna and Daniel Greenberg were of a different opinion. In 1968, they decided to found just such a school. Sudbury Valley School, in which there are no classes, no subjects are taught, no one forces students to do anything, does not know them and does not evaluate them in any other way; they are just given space to do whatever they want. They don't have any classes there, they don't segregate children by age; on the contrary, they leave everyone together - from four-year-olds to nineteen-year-olds. Decision-making (including which teachers will and will not have their contract extended) is decided by voting, in which the votes of all (four-year-olds, nineteen-year-olds and teachers) have equal weight.

The results? Excellent. Over the fifty years of its existence, the Sudbury Valley School has produced hundreds of successful graduates who, among other things - surprisingly - are able to enter public education: Eighty percent of them received a university degree. Over the years, there has not been a single graduate of this school who did not know how to read and write (although this is a very frequent objection of opponents of this style of teaching). Sudbury Valley is also free of bullying. Psychologists who have dealt with this phenomenon explain it in two ways: First, they believe that the absence of age segregation has a big influence on it, thanks to which weaker children (frequent victims of bullying) are not forced to compare themselves with their peers, but can spend time with younger ones (in addition, it often happens that the older ones stand up for the younger ones). And secondly, they believe that children often adopt patterns of behavior that they see around them. This is also why bullying is rampant in schools where teachers treat students authoritatively (the same can be observed on a more severe scale in the military), not in Sudbury Valley, where no one encounters such behavior. You can read more about this school, for example, in the publications of psychologist Peter Gray, or just search the Internet for "Sudbury Valley".

Although Sudbury Valley is probably the most popular and well-known of the independent schools, it is not the only one or the first. The oldest known similar project in modern history was started by the anarchist Francisco Ferrer Guardia in 1901 in Barcelona; five years later, however, he was arrested for allegedly collaborating in another anarchist's attempt to kill the king, which the state did not prove, but still imprisoned him for over a year, during which his school disappeared. The first still functioning (and extremely successful) educational institution of this type was founded by Alexander Sutherland Neill in 1921 in Germany, from where it moved to Austria, and since 1923 it has been based in England.

The successes of these schools inspired many other enthusiasts and entrepreneurs; dozens of similar institutions were founded in several other countries of the world. Their results are very similar to those I described above for Sudbury Valley. Despite these demonstrable and fascinating successes, the legislation of many states rejects such schools. This means that if, for example, someone were to open such an institution here in the Czech Republic, the state would not recognize it as a school, which would lead to the fact that the students' studies there would not be recognized as part of compulsory school attendance, and their parents would have problems with social welfare, like those who do not take care of their children. Makes sense, right?

I consider it important to emphasize that I definitely do not claim that all education should look like this and that all schools should function according to the Sudburg model. I assume that for some children such a method of education is suitable, for others it is not (after all, the same can be said about any system, including the current one). But this does not mean that it should be banned across the board. People are different; why then suppress their individuality and try to indoctrinate them under the threat of violence and do everything possible to cram their education into some uniform pattern created by the state?

But as long as the government determines the rules of the entire education system, many good ways of education will never have a chance to emerge. After all, when someone comes up with rules for a school like the one they have in Sudbury Valley, the vast majority of people (and especially educators and all kinds of education experts) say it could never work. So no one tries it and the concept remains a barren theory. Of course, it's not just a Sudburg model! There are countless different theoretical ways of education; and the only way to find out which ones work in practice is for someone to just come and try it (while of course no one will force any parents to send their children to such a school, that will be entirely up to them). However, until people are free to experiment like this, they cannot try, so many good educational models remain only on paper.

Unfortunately, one of the reasons why most countries have conquered education and the educational system is precisely the effort to ensure that each individual is properly indoctrinated and thoroughly instilled in him already in childhood that it is morally justifiable and justified for some to rule over others, that he is just a citizen who needs a ruler, and he should be happy that he can at least choose one. Don't you believe? Pick up any textbook on the basics of social sciences, or some civics education (the very name of the course suggests citizenship education). Still don't believe? It is enough to read the "National Education Program", where you will read about (I quote) education for democratic citizenship, strengthening of belonging [...] to national traditions, key competences focused mainly on [...] citizen education or about introducing elements of democracy into the life of schools. I completely understand and respect that some readers may think this is right, but please don't make me expose my children to it.

I have discussed the Sudbury model with many people. Often with educators. Even with two education experts who have dedicated their entire professional careers to teaching, learning how to teach, publishing textbooks and various work for the Ministry of Education. I have always started by describing the model as a theory and discussing it only hypothetically; those concerned had no idea that such schools really existed somewhere. Most often, I encountered approximately this answer (and the more experience the person had with pedagogy, the more categorically and confidently he uttered it): "It's a beautiful theory that sounds very nice, but it can never work in practice. I know what I'm talking about, students just behave differently." Sure, they behave differently! Not even when they are being educated in a completely different environment. The problem with every such pedagogue (or pedagogical expert) is that they only judge everything based on what they see in current education. But it is not reasonable to assume that if students behave in a certain way in one educational model, they will behave in the same way in a diametrically different model.

In connection with this, a parallel about the functioning of society comes to mind. When discussing a stateless polity, many people very often assume that people will behave in such a society as they do now. This is, of course, a big mistake. People now don't care about some things and don't do some things simply because the state does them for them. It is a mistake to think that if the state stopped caring, they would not change their behavior. It is just as short-sighted as condemning the Sudbury model on the grounds that if students behaved in it as they do in current schools, it would not work.

Give people shackles and they will be aggressive, distrustful. Pin someone to a wall, they will try to break free, be hostile, distrustful. Then unchain him from the wall, give him slightly longer chains. What do you notice? He will be even more aggressive, he will see a chance, he will try to escape even harder because now he can at least do something. What do you conclude from this? That more shackles and shorter chains are needed because a person chained to a wall is calmer than one who can at least move around the room? Because that's exactly how many think of the state: The more the state "loosens the chains", the more people allegedly start to misbehave and abuse it. But the completely obvious truth lies in the exact opposite. The solution is to release the person from the shackles and give him freedom. Because freedom is natural, then he will be satisfied.

I can observe it on myself. As long as I believed in the state, obeyed its laws, lived under the influence of propaganda, I was more interested in what was written than what was right. I followed the laws on principle - even when I had the opportunity to help myself by breaking them; it seemed to me that a good person respects the law. When I freed myself from this view, two things happened. For one thing, my mind is free. It's a wonderful feeling, believe me. And on the one hand, I understood that morals and ethics are superior to laws; I follow them either in cases where I voluntarily decide to do so, or when I would be punished for violating them; otherwise they mean nothing to me but shackles that I never consented to and that were forcibly imposed on me by a government I have no interest in and no longer chose. So I feel no obligation to respect her bonds and have no qualms about leaving them at any time. But that doesn't mean I've become a badass. On the contrary. I also got into situations in which I could have helped myself by simply appealing to the law, but I preferred to behave correctly rather than in accordance with the law. I no longer look at what is written, but at what is good and what is bad. And I dare say that this transformation has made me a better person than I was before.

I am certainly not saying that if the state did not exist, all people would start behaving honestly and correctly. It's clear to me that they haven't started. However, I am convinced that a non-negligible group of people would become more responsible because they would have to take care of themselves. And I believe that responsibility is a virtue that leads to other virtues...

chapter: 8. Education
name: Education and propaganda
text:
Sudbury Valley School is based on one of a huge number of different educational models; however, there are also those that completely reject any school (no matter how independent it may be) (so-called unschooling) and often include the complete voluntariness of the educated individual as a necessary condition for them to function at all, which of course excludes their legal application in any country with legislatively anchored compulsory schooling or compulsory education (ie de facto everywhere). Although I do not claim that every educational model is suitable for everyone, I see no reason why some (or indeed most of them) should be outlawed.

For example, in the Czech Republic, almost the only legal model of education is the so-called "Prussian cadet" (and its modifications), i.e. schools with teachers, lessons, classes, grades, discipline, age segregation, obedience and compulsory attendance; why is he sometimes called "prussian cadet"? Well, once upon a time the Prussian generals complained that the schools prepared bad soldiers for their needs, who thought too much and carried out orders too thoughtlessly; therefore, there was a reform, the aim of which was to change education so that it produced ideal obedient killing machines - and it is in this model (after some minor modifications) that our children are still educated today. In relation to this, it seems laughable when teachers talk about developing students' critical thinking, independence and the like, while trying to achieve all this within a system that was designed to do the exact opposite; it's like wanting absolute silence, going to a music festival in search of it, and being surprised that by adjusting the parameters of the earplugs we don't get the desired result.

An integral part of today's education is represented by teachers, who are typically not chosen by the students, but still have to listen to them and often even show them a kind of respect (one example for all may be standing up when the teacher comes to class); in this way, even young children are made to feel that it is desirable and right to submit to an external authority that they have not chosen for themselves. First of all, he is a teacher, who is replaced over time by the government, a politician, a policeman, an official, simply any oppressor that the state invents. One might argue that similar training is appropriate for future employment, since most people have a boss at work; but a person chooses such a place and is there voluntarily (not that he necessarily likes it there, but no one forces him to be there).

To be clear, I have no objection whatsoever to the natural authority that man chooses of his own free will and recognizes to the extent he sees fit; I consider it healthy and natural to respect someone, value them and learn from them. The key, however, is that everyone chooses for himself who is worth following for him; the imposition of authority, on the other hand, leads to a loss of self-confidence and unnecessary conformity simply because it is expected and learned completely automatically. It is precisely the forced imposition of authority and its voluntary acceptance that forms the boundary between "throwing away self-respect and learning to hunch our backs before anyone who is meant for us" and "accepting another person, respecting him, valuing him even with his mistakes and wanting to learn from him." I want my children to have the healthy self-esteem and perspective to be free to decide for themselves who deserves their respect, but I resolutely refuse to be forced to show it to whomever is assigned to them. What about you? Do you want your offspring to be primarily obedient citizens or good people? Do you want them to do what someone tells them or what they think is right?

The effort to enforce conformity by force where there is a lack of natural authority is not the only, and unfortunately not even the biggest, problem of state education; I consider the indoctrination of the youngest by state propaganda to be at least as insidious. How would you like it if, for example, a private company introduced the promotion of its products into compulsory education, which would not be labeled as advertising, but presented as objective truth? Do you find this completely unacceptable? If so, do you mind if the state does exactly the same thing? Without any discussion, he presents himself as the only solution where there is supposed to be "market failure"; sure, not everyone will agree on whether the market is failing or not, but even then, it's an open question, not a given, how these alleged "market failures" are presented. As a result, the atrocities of the state (the curtailment of our liberties and the use of offensive violence) are excused as a matter of necessity; and sometimes the means of such behavior include completely obvious lies.

Do you think I'm exaggerating? I can demonstrate my claim, for example, on the example of freedom of speech; we learn in schools that before 1989 we didn't have it, while now we do. But try publicly promoting Nazism or racism, or approving certain criminal acts; if you're consistent, they'll eventually pick you up and lock you up. So no, we definitely don't have freedom of speech, it's just that things that we're not allowed to say in public have changed; the truth is that we are now less constrained, but it is still not freedom. And it's not at all about whether we agree with such laws or not - I'm just pointing out that the declared freedom of speech is nothing but a lie; even if the laws prohibiting certain expressions were fine, that would not make it true that they are not prohibited, which is contrary to the declared freedom. Non-freedom of speech simply cannot be turned into freedom by stopping silencing educated and wise people, but instead silencing, for example, racists and neo-Nazis; freedom is when everyone can speak - including those whose opinions we find perverted, nonsensical, disgusting or stupid.

I consider the deification of the state and its symbols to be the most disgusting practices of the current educational system; why are our children taught, for example, to respect the flag, anthem and other national symbols as part of compulsory education? After all, it is nothing but idolatry! If a free man chooses, based on his life experience, to honor a flag or a song, that is of course his business, and I am the last person who would want to prevent him from doing so; however, this is diametrically different from forcing a small child to sit somewhere where they are being manipulated into doing something like that. How are people who have already gone through this educational system supposed to look at the state dispassionately and critically, if they have to worship it as an idol from an early age? Incidentally, this also applies to democracy, which is uncritically presented as a good in a similar way; note how often the word "undemocratic" is used as a synonym for "bad" (even in entirely democratic processes).

It is impossible that such powerful propaganda at the most sensitive age should not leave consequences on the people; everyone then "knows" that society cannot function without the state, without ever really thinking about it. When you first introduce the idea of a stateless society to someone, in the vast majority of cases, a negative reaction occurs within seconds. I can't help but wonder how anyone can take a stand on such a complex issue that takes tens or hundreds of hours to really think through in an instant; unfortunately the answer is that there is only one way - the person must have "known" it beforehand without any real submission to critical thinking and dealing with the arguments. Unfortunately, in moments when we "know" something without having arrived at that "knowing" by some reasonable path, we simply do not accept logical arguments; we hear them, but automatically consider them to be false and do not even admit that they could possibly be true.

Unfortunately, this does not only apply to discussions about the state, but also to many other topics; and none of us are spared from it. The only way to combat this is through a lifelong pursuit of awareness, where we accept all sorts of dogmas everywhere without critical evaluation. When I discovered several such cases myself, I was first pleased that I had "finally got rid of" them; however, years later, I realized that this pursuit probably has no end, and I will constantly discover new and new ones. How to do it? The first step is being honest with yourself; when I'm debating with someone, do I even consider as a real alternative that I could be wrong and the person in question could be right? Not in some hypothetical "we are all fallible" kind of way, but am I admitting that in the discussion? Another fairly clear sign of dogmatism is that we are more convinced of the conclusion than of the reasons leading to it; how often do we come across that someone defends his thesis with a certain argument, but after refuting it, there is no reflection and possible reconsideration, but an immediate frantic search for anything else to support that thesis?

On similar principles, compulsory schooling ensures a very effective blanket indoctrination by statism; children must by law be exposed to state propaganda for a long time and repeatedly. The state will send welfare to parents who defy it; and if they insist, their children can be taken away (and eventually indoctrinated anyway). If any other entity acted in this way, we would quite rightly find it absolutely unacceptable, however, precisely because of the indoctrination we have undergone, we even accept the state telling us how to educate our children and - if we don't - threatening to kidnap them; yes, by kidnapping - that's exactly what it's actually about (although of course the laws - the laws written by the kidnapper - say they're not).

I consider state education to be the most powerful tool for creating and consolidating the power of the state; while the military enforces it, the educational system plants in all of our minds all sorts of exceptions to the general moral rules we otherwise follow. Taking someone's resources under threat of violence is wrong; however, when the state does it, we somehow excuse it, because we have been told that there is no other way. Forcing someone to instill certain values in their children under the threat of abducting them is not only wrong, we find it highly reprehensible; but it is enough for the state to do exactly the same thing - and then we not only understand it, but even typically approve of it. Come on, when we've all been told since childhood that it's for our own good and it wouldn't be possible otherwise; what else can one think who does not want to think about this topic for long hours? Unfortunately, similar - perhaps even more popular - myths are also spread about the state welfare system; we will deal with their analysis and demolition in the next chapter.

name: 9. Social system
text:
Pensions, unemployment support, all kinds of social benefits and care for the poor in general are domains in which modern states are involved so significantly that many people already consider them to be one of the key roles of the state, and one can even often come across the opinion that if none of the above was addressed by the government and if solidarity were not forced by force, it would practically disappear. Because these views are already deeply rooted in society, people often forget the fact that governments controlling the welfare system are a relative novelty; however, previously these things also took place normally - only on a voluntary basis.

I definitely categorically reject variations on the theme that "it wouldn't work"; mainly because it has worked for hundreds of years, but also because if solidarity really is so important to people that they are willing to argue in favor of the government restricting their own freedom, I see no reason why it would need states and their laws to implement it.

The social system existed long before the state took on this task. It is even clear from the available sources that the voluntary social system at the time was probably relatively more effective than the current state system. Information on this topic is widely scattered in a number of historical sources, but an excellent compilation work dealing with charity, especially in the territory of the Czech Republic and Great Britain (also with references to corresponding historical writings), was written by Hynek Řihák, founder of the Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk Institute; those who are interested in the details can search on the Internet for example his texts "Education for the poor or let's not forget about charity", "Not so wild 'wild' capitalism", "Private education in Great Britain, child labor and the state in the 19th century", "Voluntary hospitals, medical care and the state in Victorian Great Britain", "Self-help societies", or "An outline of charity in Victorian Great Britain - old women for the poor".

Although the forms of the voluntary social system were numerous, they were mostly various charitable associations, of which two types were the most important. The first type were classic charitable organizations in which the wealthy joined together to support various groups of the poor. The other ones were like that

local "social insurance companies", which functioned in such a way that a large number of people joined them, regularly paid (relatively low) fees, and then when one of them had a problem, the association helped him. In the vast majority of cases, such associations did not generate any profit and were owned directly by their members. In addition to these mechanisms, there were many others (we can read about them in the files mentioned above).

In the past, people were in solidarity voluntarily, today they are forced to do so. How is it different? First of all, it is necessary to mention the most important thing: The state welfare system is implemented in such a way that it is first necessary to rob and beggar someone, only then can you help. After all, no one but the state has the audacity to first take most of the fruits of their labor from the people, and finally to say presumptuously to their faces: "You see, you don't have enough to feed your children or to buy bread in your old age. Be thankful that you will at least see a pittance from what the government stole from you."

The vast majority of the money that the government collects as part of the welfare system is paid out on old-age pensions. In connection with this, it is first of all necessary to realize that the state does not evaluate the selected funds in any way; on the contrary, it takes a significant part of them (even if we ignore corruption and waste, at least it has to pay for the army of officials who implement it all) and only redistributes the rest. It follows logically that if people saved the same money they pay for state pensions for themselves, they would be much better off. The most common counter-arguments are two. The first is that if someone saves in a bank, the bank can go bankrupt and deprive them of their deposit - sure, it can happen, but it can be prevented; for example, we can divide the money and deposit it in several banks, buy real estate, invest in shares, or maybe buy gold and hide it in a secret stash under the floor (none of this brings 100% certainty, but neither does the state; after all, we can observe how the retirement age keeps increasing). The second counterargument is that people are irresponsible and many would simply not save for retirement; and practically the entire fourth chapter of this book deals with its refutation.

Another essential difference between voluntary charity and a coercive state welfare system is that the government must essentially create a uniform system that applies to the whole country and all citizens, while the voluntary solidarity of free people works in a much more direct way. The advantage of a decentralized charity is that it can look different in each place according to what is needed where, and it is not bound by any universal rules that cannot in principle be good for everyone. As an example, the above-mentioned charitable associations can serve as substitutes for social insurance: Associations of those who performed riskier professions - for example, miners - typically collected more money, for example, to provide for families in the event of the death of a breadwinner, or to pay for health care, and so on; the central planning of a welfare system can never be so effective.

The addressability of charities and charitable associations also prevents the abuse of the welfare system much better. In the case of a local charity, abuse was overseen directly by those who contributed their own money to it; their motivation is therefore incomparably higher than the motivation of officials who are supposed to watch over parasitism on money that is not even theirs.

State officials, and generally those who implement and implement the social system, may not really care how long the recipients of support will be dependent on the state. On the contrary, it is in the enormous interest of charitable associations that the recipients of support stand on their own two feet as soon as possible! The functioning of the entire charity and the way of providing that support are mostly subordinated to this. Charitable associations, which actually functioned as insurance companies for their own members in case of job loss, typically actively monitored whether the recipient of any support found work, and often reimbursed him for related expenses (for example, travel expenses, retraining costs, and so on). Voluntary welfare systems - unlike state ones - are often guided by the fact that it is better to give a poor person a rod and teach him to fish than to just give him a fish.

An equally important problem with the state welfare system is that there is a "right" for someone to receive funds from it. It is not so difficult to imagine the difference in the approach to one's life situation between a person who realizes that he lives on handouts (and is therefore duly grateful for them) and a person who is convinced that he has a so-called "right" to the state money from which he lives (and instead of gratitude, there is often dissatisfaction with the fact that he does not receive more - after all, he has the "right" for others to provide him with a "dignified life"). In connection with this, it seems strange to me when I hear the opinions of some - especially right-wing - people who are already able to curse at "socks and nemakachenka who only live on support" and in the same breath add that "some kind of social system must be provided by the state", which also implies that there must be someone's "right" to support; how can someone claim to receive welfare benefits as a right and yet criticize the people who use this "right"?

A frequent argument in favor of maintaining the state welfare system is, among other things, that we are civilized people and as such we cannot let the poor die of hunger. Even if we leave aside that charity based on voluntariness can do the same thing (in addition, the help is better targeted), I would like to point out that in our geographical regions, realistically, no one is in such a financial situation that would force them to suffer from hunger. Even people on the street, the homeless, who sometimes don't even receive any support from the state (I personally know several of them and there are certainly not a few of them in general), do not starve, because it takes at most a few hours (and with a bit of luck, only a few minutes) to beg for food for the whole day in a busy place.

A very interesting question is why this is so. Some hundred years ago, the poor were starving (and often with the support of the state), five hundred years ago, the middle class was also often starving; but today in the "western world" even the homeless and beggars are not hungry. Of course, this is due to the fact that the entire company gets richer over time. What everyone else has today was only yesterday a matter for the rich. After all, for example, of people who live below the so-called "poverty line" in the United States, 76% have air conditioning, 66% more than two livable rooms per person, 97% at least one color TV, 62% satellite or cable TV, 75% a car, 30% two or more cars, 73% a microwave, 50% hi-fi equipment, 33% a dishwasher, 99% a refrigerator and 46% of them live in their own house. A hundred years ago, such conditions would have been considered absolutely luxurious. When we think about why the things we consider common today were once seen as luxuries, the answer is easy: Greedy and selfish businessmen in their pursuit of profit made all these goods available to the common people so that they could sell them and get rich; and for this they are so often condemned. Certainly this growth, which especially helped the poor so much, was not caused by robbing the rich; on the contrary, it effectively hinders it (one can only guess how many bankrupt companies could survive and make all the above achievements even more accessible to the poor, if they were not eliminated by the tax burden or state regulation).

And the indisputable fact is that the more the state takes care of the poor and declares it to be its role, the less the citizens care (why should they, if the state is already taking care of them; after all, for their money), which Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk understood as early as 1919: "Today we put social obligation in the place of humiliating grace." I ask the readers, when assessing the necessity of a state welfare system, to think not only about what is visible at first glance, but also about what does not work and does not exist because of it, and especially about what inevitable and unwanted consequences it brings with it, if you grant someone a "right" to other people's money just on the basis of being poor himself. It is not dissimilar to the "right" to medical treatment, which we will discuss in detail in the next chapter.

name: 10. Healthcare
text:
Health care is one of many areas that are so heavily regulated that they are de facto state-run and subject to central planning. The government accredits hospitals and individual doctors, thereby determining how many and which hospitals there will be where; at the same time, it also legislates practically everything that happens in those hospitals, thus - even if they do not directly own them - they actually manage them more than their potential owners. And as is the case with similar things, today almost no one can even imagine them without the state.

The most common argument against free market health care is that health services are so expensive that only the richest of the richest could afford them, and without the state it would not be possible to provide health care on the current scale. I honestly don't understand how anyone can come to such absurd conclusions. After all, the state doesn't do anything other than forcefully take the funds from the people, from which they then pay for their health care. It does not have any mysterious charms with which it somehow mysteriously evaluates the selected funds and pays from them something that people would otherwise not be able to afford. On the contrary, it has certain - considerably less magical - tricks to devalue a fairly significant part of the collected money. So the state definitely does not provide any greater scope of health care that people cannot pay for themselves (they pay for it themselves through the state, after all). On the contrary, unregulated waste, ubiquitous corruption, the impossibility of economic calculation (explained in detail in the second chapter) and the need to pay the army of officials who carry out the entire redistribution significantly reduce the scope and quality of available health care.

So how could the average person afford health care when surgeries cost tens to hundreds of thousands and there are even procedures and treatments costing millions? Should everyone have this money saved in a straw for Uncle Příhoda? Of course not. The insurance model (even health insurance) has been successfully operating here for hundreds of years even without the state. The principle is that if someone occasionally needs expensive treatment, it is not necessary for him to save the funds for it himself. It is richly sufficient for many people to pay a relatively small amount regularly, and then if something happens to one of them, the treatment is covered from the common fund. But the state is not needed for this at all.

And what about those who simply do not pay for insurance and do not have direct payment? Do we leave them to die in the streets? Well, charity is the last chance for such. In the past, such a charity typically assessed to what extent the disabled person was responsible for his situation, how much he could influence it, what his current options were and how expensive treatment the person in question needed. Help was therefore understandably provided mainly to children or the disabled; on the contrary, not idlers and irresponsible ignoramuses (but sometimes even such people got help, especially if it was not very expensive). More on the functioning of charity without the state can be found in the previous chapter. So the answer to the question is that we probably won't let the sick die on the streets if they are those who could not influence their situation much (children, the elderly, the infirm, the crippled), but maybe we won't be so lenient with irresponsible peccadilloes. Why this approach is desirable is explained in the fourth chapter of this book.

There is a certain humane idea that says something along the lines of: "Equal health care for all." I'm afraid that most of its supporters defend it only because they haven't seen it through. This is because "equal health care" can mean anything from a top-notch clinic full of the best experts to getting a vein in a dirty basement; the sentence does not say anything about a specific quality, but only that it must be the same for everyone. The misconception most people have is that in practice this means some average quality medical care for everyone; so their intuitive understanding of the idea is that the average person will have about as much medical care as they could pay for themselves, with the rich paying more to the poor to average it out.

However, almost nothing is further from the truth! The state spends part of the collected money on the salaries of officials who keep the whole juggernaut running, and also on corruption (which is an integral part of the state and bureaucracy; not something that can be "eradicated"). The rest, which is not stolen and paid out in official salaries, is then invested desperately inefficiently due to the impossibility of economic calculation (details can be found in the second chapter of this book). So the result is nothing like "average medical care for all", but very substandard to desperate care in proportion to the amount of money people are forced to pay; so even the "ordinary person" that politicians flaunt so much is beaten. If someone argues that this is the right thing to do, and that we should reduce ourselves so that everyone can be treated, even if they don't care about anything (and the "ordinary person" is not the case that should not be treated, as we explained above), then I ask them: "Do you really think it is morally right for your children to receive worse health care just so that a handful of irresponsible people can get the same treatment?"

Another - slightly less extreme - idea can be formulated as follows: "Okay, not everyone has to have the same health care, but some basic treatment should be provided to everyone." Something similar can be achieved through voluntary charity (a more detailed explanation can be found in the previous chapter). However, when the state does it, it is certainly not just about shifting resources from everyone to the poorest; an enormous amount is lost along the way and the rest is invested incorrectly (see above). So again, the state has no other option to achieve this goal than by worsening medical care for everyone else.

Another emotional argument that often comes after rebutting the above is that many ordinary people are already struggling to make ends meet, so there would be no way to pay for private health insurance. In addition to being refuted by the previous paragraphs, I would like to explicitly point out that these people have so little money precisely because they are so extremely taxed; the total tax burden of our state is so great that if we did not pay taxes, we would usually have several times more resources available than we have now.

The huge problem in health care is not just the payment system through the state; there are also a lot of laws and regulations that make it impossible for entrepreneurs to find effective ways to treat patients. A typical example is that any new drug must first go through a series of lengthy and expensive laboratory tests, and possibly even animal tests, before the government allows it to be tested on humans; and unfortunately even the consent of those people does not change anything, first it is necessary to ensure at least some security. Such regulation is correct, isn't it? We don't want evil pharmaceutical corporations testing on humans to increase their profits, do we? About 99% of people nod at this. And who is against it? Just a few crazy extremist libertarians advocating individual liberty at all costs, no one else... So everything is fine? Oh, I almost forgot, there is one more group: People who are currently being killed by a disease for which someone is developing a cure, but it still has to pass some tests, so they are out of luck. Are we really letting them die just so that some pharmaceutical company doesn't make money by testing drugs on people, even if they agree, it can help them and the person wants to live? And I am not talking about all those who are dying today from a disease that could have been successfully treated for many years if the state had not hindered the development of medicines. Let me add that I am categorically opposed to testing drugs on people who do not agree. Similar legislative obstacles can be encountered, for example, in connection with the ban on the sale of organs: It is said that it is not humane for someone to sell a kidney, so it is probably better if one dies rich of kidney failure and the other ends up on the street.

The existence of regulations is defended by saying that if there were none, every butcher could be a doctor and every lice-infested cellar a hospital. Sure, it can in principle. The question is who would go to such a doctor and which insurance company would conclude a contract with him. If there were no regulation, exactly those doctors and hospitals that people are interested in would make a living, unsuccessful ones would go bankrupt. A frequent question is how would it be possible to find out if the person standing in front of me has a medical degree at all, or if he derives his education from regularly watching Dr. House. Well, apart from the fact that something similar would probably already be provided by the insurance company (which wants to keep clients, so it is not in its interest to conclude contracts with doctors and hospitals about which it knows nothing at all), it will certainly not be difficult to open the website of the school (or some certification authority; it is described in more detail in chapter eight) at which the doctor allegedly studied, and perhaps find his benefit there. Today, such a service does not exist mainly because doctors and hospitals are accredited by the state; but if they didn't, a demand would be created and, of course, an offer.

Sometimes you can come across the objection that in some countries healthcare is "more market-based" after all, but the results are not very good; however, the catch lies in the misunderstanding of the greatest advantages of the free market, which include not only free competition, but above all the ability of people to try whatever they see fit, to fail if they fail, and to prosper if they succeed. The so-called "more market" does not mean only more private and less state entities, but above all freedom of business; even the number of regulations is not decisive, it depends on what and how it is regulated: Even health care, where all entities would be private, but the state would determine who and under what conditions is allowed to practice, can (depending on those conditions) fail more fatally than health care, which at first glance is much more regulated.

Many people think of key sectors - such as health care - that the state may mismanage them, but if we had more moral politicians, wiser advisers, more capable civil servants and more efficient government, it would be a good thing. If we leave aside that democracy does not lead to anything like that (which can be observed all around), then even if by some miracle it succeeds, something will improve, but in principle it will never be as effective as a market solution (see the second chapter). The same applies to the management of public spaces, which is covered in the next chapter.

name: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text:
All around us there are spaces that do not have a private owner, because the administrator of such territory is the state; it can be squares, parks, forests, meadows, fields, rivers and various buildings, but also roads and paths. In this chapter we will consider whether such lands could be better managed by free people. The only thing we will not focus on yet is transport and all transit functions of public spaces (especially roads and paths); the whole next chapter is devoted to this great subject.

I consider the most serious reason why the state (and by the state, I mean its municipalities) should not own any land, the same as for all other domains in which the state intervenes: Managing public space costs money; no government of any state is, and has never been productive in history, so that the means it spends must and always has had to rob its subjects. I see robbery as a strongly amoral act; and behind every state square, forest, building and road, of which we can see many around us, there is looted money. For this reason, I cannot agree to the state managing public spaces.

And as is often the case in a free market, morality goes hand in hand with efficiency, so there are also practical arguments. One of them was presented by the well-known scientist, Dr. Garrett James Hardin, in his famous essay "The Tragedy of the Common Pasture", where he compares the private person's access to his own pasture with the people's access to the state's pasture. The owner of the land grazes on his meadow only enough cattle so that he does not destroy it and that it can feed him. On the contrary, in sixteenth-century England there were pastures where anyone could drive his cattle; the result, of course, was that people allowed cattle to graze there too much, rendering the land no longer usable for that purpose.

Many other thinkers based their works on this idea. For example, my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, in his book "The Ethics of Liberty" describes the tragedy of the commons like this: "If the state owns the land and allows individuals to use it freely, this naturally leads to overuse of the resource and waste." In practice, this problem can be encountered, for example, in the state administration of unique natural monuments (there is no motivation to properly guard them), some protected animal species (if private individuals could make a profit from them, it would be in their own interest to protect them from poachers) or pollution of rivers or air (more on this in the thirteenth chapter).

However, I see a bigger problem (than overuse) in deciding how to use a space. If the state owns an empty lot, how does it decide whether it will be a park, shopping center, playground or parking lot? A group of officials will determine this somehow. Their motivations can be different - from someone bribing them, to the fact that they themselves live nearby and their children have nowhere to play, to the crystal clear belief that the park is exactly the best for the citizens of the neighborhood. In principle, the fairness of the motivations of such an official does not matter; he cannot know what is best for people, even if he happened to care. Even the results of a possible referendum will tell only about how many people voted for which option, but they cannot take into account the degree of how much someone wants this or that. Moreover, such a vote can show different results depending on how wide the neighborhood is included (commuters may be satisfied with a parking lot, or at home with a park, for example). When the work is finished, the state administers it from public money, and without an economic calculation (see the second chapter) there is no measure to determine whether it is beneficial or harmful.

However, when these lands are owned by entrepreneurs, what will be their goal? Generate profit, of course. And the biggest profit will come from building what people are willing to pay the most for, which is the very thing they want most. So entrepreneurs have an incentive to build exactly what people want (albeit for purely selfish reasons). Similar to officials, even entrepreneurs cannot know in advance which of the possibilities of using the given land is the best; so everyone will try something, many different projects will be created. The better they meet the wishes of consumers, the more they earn; bad projects are unprofitable, which leads quite naturally to being replaced by ones that people want.

A common objection is that if we leave the management of all land to private individuals, they will build shopping malls, parking lots and office buildings everywhere, but no parks and playgrounds. Similarly, after the Velvet Revolution, many people (including politicians and economists) argued that it was necessary to centrally plan grocery stores, because otherwise they would become scarce as entrepreneurs would run only boutiques instead. The reality, however, is that there is always an adequate supply for the demand; this goes for grocery stores as well as parks. If there is sufficient demand for parks, then they will certainly be created. If people aren't willing to pay for them, that means these parks shouldn't exist, because people are actually more demanding of something else (whatever they're willing to pay for). This idea (explained in more detail in the second chapter) is very important because it applies quite generally. It's good to remember that "demand for parks" doesn't just mean that people are willing to pay entrepreneurs to enter the park; it can also manifest itself in the way that enough people in the neighborhood get together, buy land and set up their own park there (unlike the state, however, it does not force anyone to do such an activity).

Private ownership of what are now called public spaces solves another significant problem. I imagine that many readers, after reading the title of the chapter, asked themselves what public spaces have to do with freedom of speech. Well, let's first examine the problems of trying to come up with some reasonable definition of freedom of speech. Virtually all states suppress freedom of speech: They typically prohibit either speech against the current regime, or promotion of other regimes, or both; often something more. The Czech Republic is no exception; for example, the promotion of fascism or racism is prohibited (I am definitely not a racist and as a libertarian I consider fascism to be pure evil; nevertheless, I will always defend freedom of speech even for those with whom I fundamentally disagree). Even so, they lie to us in schools that we have freedom of speech after the Velvet Revolution; this is simply not true - although the current regime persecutes fewer people, even today we can face brutal violence for some public statements and then sit down (the legitimacy of such actions can be debated, but freedom of speech is definitely not).

So should everyone be able to say what they want, otherwise it's oppression? At first glance, it might seem that way, but it is not. It also depends on where he will do so. It is obvious that if Jehovah's Witnesses ring your doorbell and you don't immediately let them into the living room and let them preach about the faith there, you are certainly not restricting their freedom of speech. However, if the law comes into force that prohibits Jehovah's Witnesses from evangelizing, it will be a clear violation of their freedoms. A fairly well-known example is the man who, for the sake of amusement, shouts "on fire" in a crowded theater and thereby causes panic; many philosophers and thinkers have dealt with this, but also the American judge Oliver Wendell Holmes, who came to the conclusion that the right to freedom of speech cannot be absolute and must be weakened and tempered with regard to "public policy". The weakness of this approach is that depending on changes in "public policy", freedom of speech can be completely suppressed (see totalitarian regimes).

So what is the moral and practical solution to this problem? Let everyone decide on their property what they can and cannot say there; there will be no state spaces. And just as everyone decides what they can and cannot say in their living room, they also decide what they can and cannot say in their park. This solution is completely natural and in accordance with property rights.

There is a feeling that if free speech was left purely to landowners, it could lead to a lot of pointless regulations and unnecessary restrictions on speech. However, this is extremely unlikely; if an entrepreneur provides his land (parking lot, cinema, park, swimming pool...) to people for the purpose of profit, it is not in his interest to issue senseless restrictions to discourage customers. Another concern may be that some views would remain prohibited - similar to now. However, this is completely unrealistic; while in a state it is sufficient for a ban to be approved by the government, in a free society all landowners would have to enforce it at the same time. And even if that happens by chance, the supporters of the suppressed opinion can buy their own land on which their rules will apply.

The argument from the opposite side, on the other hand, is that if only the owner decided what could and could not be said on a plot of land, there would be many places where people could say what they wanted. This is very likely. What could be wrong with it? Some might promote various ideas leading to violence, often lies. Sure, that would happen sometimes; on the other hand, their opponents have the opportunity to refute such delusions. Of course, this is no guarantee that a skilled manipulator will not win the crowds over; but - as history shows - not even the states, where there is also a danger that such a manipulator will appear directly in the government, from where he then has much more options to suppress his opponents with the help of legislation.

On further reflection, we find that with the same elegance with which freedom of speech can be defined in terms of property rights, we can do the same with freedom of religion, freedom of assembly, freedom to use one's own language, and so on. The rules in a space are always determined by the owner of the place. It is quite simple, clear, there is no need to define limits or generally applicable laws; above all, it is moral (everyone makes their own decisions) and consistent ("basic human rights" are thus defined using property rights, so they can never be in dispute). Although in this chapter we dealt with the effectiveness of the management of public spaces and the issue of freedom of speech, religion and assembly, the issue of freedom of free movement still remains open; however, the following chapter is devoted to just that and, of course, to the statist's favorite question: "If there was no state, who would build roads?"

name: 12. Road and traffic rules
text:
Perhaps the most frequent question of statists, which is heard after an anarcho-capitalist mentions a stateless society, is curiously not directed at the courts, the police or the army, but rather: "And who would build roads without the state?" Although this question is the basis of many a libertarian joke, which might indicate a very obvious answer, I personally do not find this topic particularly easy to explain; yet I will try to show why the correct answer is: "A free people, ruled by no one, will build roads; moreover, far more efficiently than the state."

First, let's focus on the problem of state highways and intercity roads, the construction and maintenance of which are extremely expensive today. The attentive reader can already guess that the causes of these problems are twofold: lack of motivation and the impossibility of economic calculation.

A manifestation of the lack of motivation is the omnipresent corruption, which practically eliminates all market prices and which makes it possible that the expenditure on highways - ranging in the order of hundreds of billions - sometimes varies from highway to highway by several times (and sometimes it is possible to build more cheaply in mountainous Austria than in the relatively flat Czech Republic, where, moreover, salaries are generally lower). The true market price of the highway is scarcely imaginable; but it could be significantly lower than now (just for comparison, a square meter of a Czech highway is more expensive than a square meter of an ordinary family house; building some space with family houses - without gardens, stuck on top of each other - is cheaper than running a highway there).

A manifestation of the impossibility of economic calculation is the fact that no one really knows from where to where it is worth building a highway for the given money; just as it is unclear how often it is beneficial to repair roads given their need and cost of repair. Not to mention that there is no way for the state to know whether we have too few (and which ones are missing) or too many (and which ones are over) roads overall. Any surveys of real road use cannot provide meaningful answers, because as long as the maintenance costs of each particular road are completely separated from its use, prices cannot express the scarcity of resources, so no one knows whether a driver currently using a road would do the same if he had to pay the market price for it (further explanation of this phenomenon can be found in the second chapter).

Private road ownership solves both of the above problems very elegantly. Corruption is minimized because entrepreneurs guard their money better than officials and politicians guard state money (and if they don't, then such entrepreneurs will soon have nothing to do business with). The problem of the impossibility of economic calculation completely disappears, since the profitable road is clearly beneficial; on the other hand, the road it passes through is not beneficial in its given form (people get less benefit from it than they would from the resources it consumes). In addition, from the above data it is possible to estimate how frequent and expensive repairs it makes sense to carry out on that road.

The most common objection to private highways is that when their owners (or owners of individual parts) raise the prices ad absurdum, people will have no choice but to accept and pay such prices. This could be partially true if there was no other transportation option. However, this condition is difficult to fulfill, because in reality there is an alternative to every road; both in the form of other roads (even if it is a detour) and other modes of transport (e.g. the railway competes with the overpriced highway). If someone sets their prices extremely high, they will lose customers. And even if by chance the owners of all transport routes between two points agree to raise prices, a new route can be created (cartels are generally unviable in the free market, details about this can be found, for example, in the chapter "Waste Producers" of the fantastic book "Defending the Indefensible" by the well-known libertarian thinker Walter Block).

The only "advantage" that the state has in the construction of highways over a free society lies in the possibility of expropriating the land through which the road was planned. I put the word advantage in quotation marks because it is a very confidential advantage; especially because the very act of expropriation is extremely immoral, since it is a robbery of land, the price of which is obviously higher for the owner than that offered by the state (if not, it would not be necessary to force him to sell it). So it might seem that buying up land for highways would be very expensive under anarcho-capitalism. However, the price without state intervention would be market, i.e. completely natural, and lower with state intervention; but at the expense of the owners of expropriated land! And if we remember the second chapter of this book, we find that if the cost of the freeway due to land acquisition would be so high that it would not be worth building (or would have to include detours), that means that the utility of the land that the freeway should run through is greater if the freeway is not there. If we think this statement through, we will find that the post-fidential advantage at the beginning of the paragraph actually represents a disadvantage.

Sometimes I come across the opinion that private highways could probably work, but they shouldn't be owned by too many different owners (and since the construction of a highway is not a cheap matter, it can be expected that more investors and entrepreneurs would join forces to finance it) so that it is not necessary to stop at a toll gate every few kilometers. The same argument is then usually used against the private ownership of city streets, because if tolls were collected at every corner, it would bring with it discomfort for drivers and traffic would not be very smooth. Of course, toll gates are not the only solution. Street owners can sell permanent tickets (something like highway signs) or GPS beacons, or – if someone wants a device in the car that will always record their location – chips that can be read by readers only on the relevant streets, or the cars could be equipped with something like a "taxameter" that would activate and deactivate external signals. All of these solutions (and the free market would surely come up with many more) can be used in parallel, and most importantly, multiple owners of streets and roads can use a common system; thereby reducing their transaction costs and providing greater convenience to customers (so no toll gates on motorways every few kilometres).

Although it can be assumed that highways and intercity roads would be mostly built by businessmen for profit, in the case of city streets and roads, on the contrary, it is possible to assume that many of them would be owned by the owners of adjacent houses (such a road can be created at the same time as those houses and there is no reason for it to be sold and residents have to pay for the passage). Relatedly, there is concern that cities could become congested because some owners would not allow foreign cars on their streets. Well, maybe some would. In any case, the bigger the problem, the more the prices would naturally rise, which always leads to an increase in supply (that is, for those for whom it was not worth it to let other people's cars drive through their street for a few bucks, it can already be worth reasonable money). Associations of street owners could also be formed with agreements on mutual access.

To the possible objection that the prices for using city roads owned by homeowners would be too high (which, of course, no one can say with certainty; but the opposite is also not the case), all that can be said is that they would cause precisely the kind of traffic situation that would ultimately bring the greatest benefit to society. It is hypothetically possible (although there is no evidence for this; but also for the opposite) that this would reduce traffic in the city - but only if the real benefit of city residents from quiet streets would exceed the benefit of drivers from traffic (this is a principle described in the second chapter).

It can also be assumed that the prices for using the roads would vary depending on the time of day; they would probably be higher at peak times (which would prevent road owners from overfilling them), and lower at off-peak times (thus attracting more customers). This would naturally incentivize drivers to plan their journeys (if they can) for non-congested times. Likewise, people's motivation to travel in groups (more people per car) would also increase - especially during peak hours, when prices are the highest. Many of the things that various transport experts are trying to do in vain, that we now pay for with taxes, would be solved by the free market quite naturally and spontaneously; moreover, these market goals are really set by the wishes of the public, as they are shaped by every driver and road owner every time they enter into a business transaction (as opposed to state management, where the ideas of various experts or officials about what people want can differ greatly from reality).

What about the rules of the road? This would always be determined by the owner of each road. In connection with this, one can encounter a very common objection that these rules would differ from road to road. Yes, it could be a little different, which - if it's about small things - is not a bad thing, because then the rules can be tailored to each specific road. However, the basic things (which side to drive on, where to give priority...) would be the same practically everywhere, because every road owner is interested in the fact that there are as few accidents as possible, traffic is smooth and his customers feel good (nonsensical - or too different - rules thus deprive him of profit). Examples of where the same principles already work today can be seen, for example, in the form of credit cards or barcodes. Despite the absence of state standards and regulations that would regulate the form of the barcode or the shape of credit cards at the time of their creation, credit cards from different companies are compatible with each other with readers, and millions of entities around the world use a few barcode standards. No one makes up any crazy or different rules because that would hurt themselves. There is no reason to believe that it would be any different with the rules of the road.

In conclusion, I would ask the esteemed reader to notice how many problems that various governments around the world have been unsuccessfully struggling with for many years could be solved by the free market without the need for some crazy social engineering, promotion of alternative means of transportation, traffic calming and other regulations at the taxpayers' expense. Something similar can be said about the environment, the management of which we will look at in the next chapter.

name: 13. Environment
text:
Environmental protection is one of the areas that is commonly cited as an example of a field where the so-called free market has failed, so that it is supposed to be regulated by the state. Unlike most state-regulated industries, around which much debate and emotion revolve, environmental protection is not so often shaken up in discussions of anarcho-capitalism; just as usual almost everyone "knows" that the state has to do it because otherwise "it wouldn't work". So let's think a little deeper about this topic.

Sometimes I ask myself how the state actually plays the role of environmental protector from a practical point of view; and unlike other industries, strangely, I can't answer at first glance around me that it does wrong. In the case of environmental protection, it is not very clear what it means that it is done well. It can be completely untouched nature and people living in trees, or "sustainable development" or whatever. So the only acceptable standard is probably that nature should look the way it suits people best; and the best way to achieve such a state is the free market. So here we could end with a reference to the eleventh chapter and a statement that the state should not exist, that is, should not own anything, and let the owner decide on the protection of nature on each plot; however, let's break it down in detail.

Environmental protection shows - perhaps better than anything else - the futility of the various methods of collecting data for central planning based on the government asking people something, letting them vote on it and so on. There are not a few people in our population who, on the one hand, claim that nature is suffering, evil industry is destroying it, people are tormenting animals, big cities are swallowing up forests, and when they are done, they go to their warm city apartment, where they enjoy genetically modified chickens, drink them artificial industrial soda, wash themselves in warm water and go to sleep in a wooden bed. It is precisely these people who often devalue the results of the vote by proudly advocating for the strictest possible protection of nature, without understanding that by doing so they are not only restricting some "bad businessmen", but especially their customers, i.e. themselves. For this reason, democratic decision-making on nature protection can go against the voters.

But why should private land owners care about nature? Wouldn't they prefer financial gain? Well, these two things very often go hand in hand. If someone owns a piece of nature that people appreciate, it is possible to make money from it; and the more they appreciate it, the higher the possible earnings. Many may also buy unspoilt places with no financial gain in mind, just for the nature itself; interested parties can also participate in such purchases within various associations and associations. Furthermore, the more "threatened" nature becomes and the rarer untouched places become, the higher their price will be and the lower the motivation to dispose of them (see the first chapter).

Sometimes one can come across the argument that if the various nature reserves had their own owners, no one could prevent them from building, for example, a production line in the middle of their pristine and beautiful forest. They could theoretically do that, but it is not very likely. Those who want a production hall are mostly looking for profit; and that is exactly why there is no reason to build it in the forest, for which some are willing to pay just to keep it untouched (which can be individuals, but also an association of people who agree to it, or an entrepreneur who wants to make some money from the nature reserve). Therefore, it is generally more advantageous for a manufacturer to buy land whose market price will be lower (or the location is better).

The same applies to the protection of endangered animals. Since the state typically does not allow such animals to be profited from (for example, ivory), the motivation to protect them is not very high, and poachers kill them no matter what (see the tragedy of the communal pasture in chapter eleven). One example for all: There were several million bison in America, on which the culture and society of the Indians, which the American government wanted to get rid of, were very dependent; therefore, in 1871, Congress passed a law that authorized the total extermination of bison (any hunter could shoot any bison regardless of who owned it), which almost led to their complete extermination (in 1889, there were a total of 542 left). When that law was repealed, the "Bison Rescue Society" and many private bison farms were formed. Today, bison are no longer an endangered species; their number is estimated at three hundred thousand pieces.

Pollution is a big problem for the environment. Who will prevent waste from chemical and industrial production from being discharged directly into rivers? The owners of those rivers, of course; in such a case, they can sue whoever pollutes their river (the possible course of such lawsuits in a stateless society is described in the next two chapters). Even if the polluter were to buy the piece of river into which he discharges his waste, it still doesn't solve anything, because he still damages all the downstream owners of that river who might sue him or try to assert their rights in some other way; in light of this, the construction of a treatment plant and the non-discharge of pollutants appear to be a reasonable investment. A similar principle can be applied to air pollution.

But what about waste? Without the existence of states, wouldn't we make the planet one big dump? In such considerations it is necessary to realize that without states there would be no "public lands"; each plot of land would have an owner who would be damaged by the dump. Waste disposal would therefore be operated by entrepreneurs who would be paid for this service by those who want to get rid of waste.

Many argue in relation to waste that the state supports and subsidizes recycling, so it is necessary. What is such recycling actually good for? On the one hand, it reduces the amount of waste and, on the other hand, saves new natural resources. On the other hand, the recycling process itself consumes some resources (both natural, but also human labor and the like). So how do you find the right measure of what to recycle and what not? Astute readers probably already guess that the answer to this question can be found in the first chapter of this book. When it is cheaper to make new products from waste than to process the waste on the one hand and extract other raw materials on the other, it means that recycling actually saves resources. If it is the other way around, it means that the resources consumed by the recycling process are more scarce than the resources needed to dispose of waste and extract new raw materials. In other words, recycling saves resources if and only if it is – without any subsidies – profitable. So government subsidies for recycling are harmful and lead to waste.

Another popular topic is sustainable development. This doctrine preaches that we should not consume so-called non-renewable resources (or only under the condition of complete recyclability). There is an assumption that a stateless society would not follow this thesis; after all, they don't do it even the current states, although it can be argued that some governments try to do so to a certain extent, at least occasionally. But what is the biggest flaw in this doctrine? It completely ignores development. It is not entirely dissimilar to the medieval theory of the maximum possible size of the city, which was based on the fact that such a city would be supplied by horses carrying grain from the surrounding fields, while due to the given minimum amount of land necessary for the sustenance of man and horses, the distance from a certain number of inhabitants would grow to such an extent that the horses overcoming these distances would consume all the grain that had to be transported for their own sustenance. The doctrine of sustainable development is equally short-sighted and naive when it assumes that humanity will continue to obtain energy in the same ways. For example, such oil: It is running out, thirty years ago it was supposed to run out in thirty years, today it is supposed to run out in thirty years, and in thirty years it will probably also run out in thirty years. All these forecasts take into account the current amount of known oil, but do not consider that the shortage increases the price, which motivates entrepreneurs to search for additional resources. And they don't take into account the possibility that over time oil may not be the basis of our fuels at all (coal used to be). In the words of Professor Julian Lincoln Simon: "Nor did the Stone Age end because we ran out of stone."

A similar problem is the cutting down of rainforests. This is not yet a threat to life on Earth; if it starts to happen, people will understandably be willing to devote their resources to finding a solution (planting new trees, buying up relevant land from opponents of felling, or whatever). Just because we can see a hypothetical crisis in the future doesn't mean the government has to regulate and tax us today; the closer we are to a threat, the more willing people are to donate funds voluntarily (which is already starting to happen - for example, billionaire Johan Eliasch bought a piece of the Amazon forest to prevent mining). Not to mention that the states "protect" us even from problems they don't even know how to solve yet; let's take global warming as an example, because of which we were forced to spend a huge amount of resources even on inefficient or even counterproductive solutions (for example fertilizing the oceans with iron, quotas for biofuels leading to deforestation, planting monocultures or electric cars in countries where energy comes from coal), just to "make something happen" - without sufficiently analyzing the impacts and consequences beforehand.

History shows that attempts to solve "global problems" tend to be either ineffective, or they solve something that isn't even a real problem, or both. Despite how many times someone has sounded the alarm in the name of "saving the planet" and how many times people have been forced to finance "solutions to the problem", only rarely has such an effort led to at least a somewhat meaningful result; however, it turned out more than once that we were just wasting resources unnecessarily. The free market, on the other hand, has already demonstrated its ability to solve problems (for example, by mechanizing agriculture or replacing coal - as a fuel for means of transport - with oil).

In conclusion, I would like to point out that even in the case of environmental care, we have - similarly to other fields of human activity - two options: Let free people decide for themselves what they actually want and express their preferences on the free market; or decisions about scarce resources can be placed in the hands of governments and their experts motivated to view problems only one-sidedly to meet (perhaps only an implicit) political agenda (see the "Climategate" affair).
