I will leave it to each reader to decide which is better. And already in the next chapter, we will finally get to one of the basic differences between anarcho-capitalism and minarchism (the theory supporting a minimal state), namely private and state justice.

name: 14. Judiciary
text:
Judiciary, security forces, defense against an external enemy. Finally we come to the most interesting and at the same time the most controversial topics of this book; in addition to the fact that most people do not even allow the hypothetical possibility of the existence of the above without states and their governments, they also make these areas stand out due to differences of opinion between anarcho-capitalists and minarchists (advocates of a minimal state). In this chapter we will focus on courts and the judicial system; however, we will leave aside for now the question of how to judge someone who refuses to cooperate, or how to subsequently force them to respect the court's decision - this is dealt with in chapter fifteen.

Why replace state courts with private ones? There are two basic reasons: the judiciary in the hands of the state is both immoral and inefficient. The immorality lies, as always, in governments funding the courts from taxes they have collected under threat of violence; everyone has to pay whether they want to or not, which is unethical and unacceptable. The inefficiency can be seen in the functioning of the courts themselves: Judges sometimes make completely absurd decisions, they often put the letter of the law above its spirit and practically always above the wishes of the litigating parties, no one is held responsible for court errors (unless it is demonstrably bad intent), and it is not an exception that court proceedings last for years (and almost nothing can be decided in less than a number of months).

At the very beginning of the defense of a free judiciary, I consider it important to mention that the ideas presented in this chapter certainly do not describe some unproven theory. There are many examples of well-functioning non-state courts. Leaving aside anarchist societies such as medieval Iceland or Ireland, where there were no state courts at all, one can also find many examples of private justice functioning in parallel with state courts. For example, mercantile law, which arose in England due to the inability of the state courts to resolve merchants' disputes, was not supported by state power in any way, and the decisions of the merchant courts were not enforced by force; yet – or perhaps because of that – it was so successful that it eventually became an internationally recognized law. Maritime law also underwent an almost identical development. In recent history, there has been a great boom in arbitration companies in the US, which have decided millions of disputes; although their decisions were not legally binding until 1920, their services were widely sought and used.

These examples clearly disprove the fairly widespread myth that the judicial system is useless without a repressive component enforcing its decisions by force; this is demonstrably not the case. Why? There are many reasons. First, there are other "punishments" than violent aggression (for example, merchant law was enforced by ostracization: With a merchant who disobeyed the court's decision, others stopped making contracts, thereby practically destroying his business; nowadays information spreads very efficiently, which makes ostracization probably much more effective than before, when the ostracized could solve his situation by moving far enough away). Second, violent dispute resolution is generally expensive; it may often be more beneficial for both parties to go to an arbitrator voluntarily – and respect his decision – than to enter into an open conflict (especially if the arbitrator finds a reasonable compromise). Thirdly, there may be disputes in which even the participants are not quite sure who is actually in the right and really care about finding the truth; there then a wise judge can help without using violence very easily. And fourth, the arbitrator can discover a solution to the problem that suits both parties, but for various reasons they did not come to it on their own. I am certainly not advocating the thesis that perhaps all conflicts could be resolved only by courts without force components enforcing their decisions; I am only pointing to the fact that even courts whose decisions are not enforced by force can solve problems on a mass scale to the satisfaction of their participants.

Who would appoint a judge in a stateless society? The answer is simple: Arbitrators would be "appointed" by the people themselves simply by requesting their services. The judge could be anyone agreed upon by both sides of the dispute, whether it be a totem pole-carving grandpa from Canada who decides a neighborhood dispute in a village, or a renowned corporation with many years of judicial experience who conducts a complicated arbitration between other huge corporations. The demand for such services would give rise to companies in the free market that would make a living precisely by deciding disputes.

So anyone can be a judge. But how do the disputing parties in a dispute agree on which arbitrator will resolve their dispute? Well, first of all, there is a huge group of cases in which this problem is likely to disappear completely. These are disagreements over some existing contract; in a free society without a centralized judiciary, it can be assumed that every contract will contain a clause about which arbitrator will resolve any disagreements related to the given contract - this way, problems can be avoided with minimal effort. The arbitration company can take care of more complicated contracts comprehensively, i.e. from their proposal to the resolution of possible issues. When there is no contract and the dispute arose spontaneously, two possibilities remain: Either both parties are interested in reaching an agreement (because fighting would be expensive and risky), so they agree on an arbitrator that is acceptable to both parties; or at least one of the parties is not interested in a peaceful solution, which we will deal with in the fifteenth chapter.

The most common—albeit very short-sighted—objection to such a system goes something like this: "And what's to stop private arbitrators from deciding the dispute in favor of whoever pays more?" The answer is very simple: The main thing private arbitrators live by is their reputation. Once they lose them and prove to be venal, people will stop seeking their services. The opinion of the disinterested environment determines the credibility of the court, which is critical for its survival. On the other hand, the tendency to bribery is much higher in the state sphere, where a corrupt judge can make one dubious decision after another, but until someone catches him practically with a bribe in his hand, he remains a judge and people simply have to entrust him with their cases. The fact that private arbitrators are much more difficult to bribe than state ones is best shown by the fact that for hundreds and thousands of years people have turned to them with confidence and paid for their services, even though they usually have the opportunity to use the so-called "free" services of the state.

The good reputation of a private court is, of course, not only based on impartiality and incorruptibility, but also on its efficiency, reliability, quick decision-making and customer friendliness. Unlike state courts, which have their income from taxes certain and cannot lose it, so they don't really care how their services are perceived by customers, private arbitrators have to work hard to keep their clients and attract others. There is no reason why there should not be a competitive struggle to lower the price and increase the quality of service precisely in the delivery of justice in the free market.

Despite all these indisputable advantages of independent arbitrators over state judges, one crucial question remains. Under what laws will private arbitrators adjudicate in the absence of uniform state legislation? Well, according to those that suit people the most; that's how it is in the free market. Each of the millions of entrepreneurs who decide to make a living as freelance judges will have their own vision of what the law should look like "correctly". Some of them declare in advance the laws according to which they intend to decide, others rely on common law, others choose a system of precedents combined with enlightened arbitrators, or anyone can come up with a combination of the above or with something completely new. Those whose ways will please the people will earn; others go bankrupt.

But won't there be total chaos in the judiciary if each arbitrator decides according to different laws? Here again, it should be remembered that the solutions that are successful in the free market are precisely those that suit people the most. In a society where legal confusion prevails, there will probably be a demand for unification, which will also give rise to a supply: Groups of judges will unify their laws and decision-making methods in an attempt to gain a competitive advantage over others and attract more clients, no longer wanting to study different rules or laws for every dispute (or contract they enter into). It can be assumed that in the end there will be a few less proven methods that will be changed only at least when needed by customers; after all, history shows that the problem of too many different ways of resolving legal disputes does not arise in a free market judiciary.

This way of making laws has one fascinating consequence: The rules are made just as the people they affect want them to be. There is no need to pay any (potentially corruptible) legislators to forcefully impose their idea of law on society; there is no need for a comedy called "democratic elections" in which we try to guess which of the political parties will fulfill at least a fraction of their promises. People can make decisions about laws simply by making them and supporting those whose laws suit them, directly by paying them to settle disputes.

One can often meet with the objection that the entire stateless judiciary will end up in such a way that the laws will be set only in favor of the rich and powerful, while the "ordinary person" will not have a chance to get the right. Little could be further from the truth. To enforce a harmful law in anarcho-capitalism requires a large number of independent judges to start enforcing it, and people would have to agree with it at least to the extent that it is not worth it for them to start using the arbitration services of other arbitrators en masse; however, when the rules of justice are determined by the state, the consent of a few (often paid) individuals is sufficient to enact such a malevolent law.

Although the idea of private provision of court services is not as absurd and crazy as it may seem at first glance, we have so far avoided analyzing cases in which at least one of the parties does not cooperate and is not inclined to settle the dispute amicably. What then? The answer to this interesting question can be found in the fifteenth chapter.

chapter: 14. Judiciary
name: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text:
The third chapter of this book discusses the principle of non-aggression (a system of law based only on property rights), which I assume to be "valid" in anarcho-capitalism (by validity here I do not mean its unconditional observance by everyone, always and under all circumstances, but only so much that most conflicts will be resolved approximately in accordance with it). Despite this, in Chapter Fourteen, where we dealt with courts and dispute resolution, the principle of non-aggression was not mentioned at all. For those who find it strange, this sub-chapter is intended, in which I will try to clarify the connection between property rights and a free judiciary; however, it is not a completely relaxing read, so whoever does not want to deal with this topic (which I am writing about only to maintain completeness and correct argumentation), should feel free to skip it.

From the previous chapter, private arbitrators in the free market decide disputes in the way that is most convenient for the people. At the same time, throughout the book, I am based on property rights. Aren't these thought constructs incorrect? Not if it turns out that free market arbitrators will typically rule in accordance with the non-aggression principle. That they do so judge is "coincidentally" shown by the whole history of private justice; almost all known human societies in which free stateless courts functioned (examples of which can be found in the previous chapter) were governed by natural (property) law roughly in the sense of the principle of non-aggression, or something very similar to it. This fact suggests to some extent that property rights may indeed be somehow "encoded" in our brains, as mentioned in chapter three (although there is probably no way to conclusively prove such a thing, this observation can be taken as some indication). Historical experience also gives rise to the assumption that since private judges have so often ruled approximately in accordance with the principle of non-aggression, they could continue to do so; yet it does not by itself explain why this is so, which I will attempt to do in this subsection.

Probably, each of us has already encountered the sentence: "The freedom of one ends where the freedom of another begins." Personally, I don't really like this vague phrase, because it's actually a tautology that applies under all conditions. After all, the freedom of the camp guards ended where the freedom of their prisoners began. In order for the claim to make sense, moreover, the unspoken assumption must hold that the limit of freedom lies "in the middle" between those affected. In that case, it is a very noble idea. Let's look at it now from two different points of view.

First, let's compare it with the principle of non-aggression. This is clearly not contradicted by the fact that a property-only system of law is completely non-arbitrary and does not grant anyone a priori more authority than anyone else, so that the limit of freedom between arbitrary individuals is always precisely "in the middle" in accordance with this principle. Of course, one can imagine other concepts of law that do not contradict the thesis that the freedom of one ends where the freedom of another begins (extended with the premise that the border must be "in the middle"), but such concepts are highly unsystematic and, moreover, contrary to property rights.

Second, let us compare this thesis with the decision-making of free judges. As stated in the previous chapter, the impartiality and impartiality of these courts form the cornerstone of their very existence. If a private arbitrator is not impartial, people will stop asking for his services. But what else is impartial decision-making other than trying to draw the line of freedom between the parties to the dispute as close as possible to the "mean"? That is exactly what private arbitrators will attempt.

These two perspectives on the same thing partly explain why free judges usually try to rule in accordance with property rights. Why is the explanation only partial? Because, as already stated above, there are still other concepts of law that do not contradict the search for the limit of freedom "in the middle" between conflicting individuals, but they contradict the principle of non-aggression. An example would be the imaginary legal system, which does contain the principle of non-aggression, but also its "extension", which imposes on everyone the duty to take care of their parents when they are old; such an idea may be noble, but contrary to property rights and requiring offensive violence - that is, aggression against those who reject this "law". However, opinions on similar modifications of the law based on the principle of non-aggression differ widely; each would prefer to apply others. If an arbitrator admits something like this, his decision-making process begins to differ from the others, putting him at a disadvantage against them and he may lose customers (see the previous chapter). The more he moves away from property rights, the more different his decisions will be compared to other judges, because the principle of non-aggression is a kind of smallest subset of rules that can be said to apply equally to everyone (and the judge therefore decides impartially according to them).

An objection to such considerations, which can sometimes be encountered, can be put something like this: "And where is the guarantee that the courts will actually recognize the principle of non-aggression? What if there is a market demand for mass trampling of property rights?" Of course, there is no such guarantee. Although history shows that this does not happen in free societies, it cannot be guaranteed that it will not be different in the future. But what guarantees does the state give us that it will not become a totalitarian state? Also none. However, there is one difference; all of history is full of examples of this actually happening. And the absence of such a guarantee in anarcho-capitalism also brings with it one more advantage: The principle of non-aggression is not an absolute given that people must follow no matter what (this is how states try to present their laws); a judge can - if he finds the strict application of property rights inappropriate in a specific case - simply decide otherwise (and if people think this decision is wise, the judge will gain customers, otherwise he will lose them; in this way, he bears - unlike state judges - full responsibility for his decisions).

I hope that after including all the above aspects, it is no longer a mystery to the reader why courts in free societies have mostly followed the principle of non-aggression, or some very similar concept. For the same reasons, property rights can be expected to be recognized in any civilized society that is not corrupted by the state. Today, however, it ensures the enforcement of court decisions in cases where at least one of the parties to the dispute refuses a peaceful solution; therefore, in the next chapter, we will focus on how this area could also function without state intervention.

name: 15. Law enforcement
text:
The preceding chapter deals with a free judiciary; shows why private arbitrators resolve disputes more morally and efficiently than state judges, but deals only with dispute resolution as such - completely ignores the enforceability of court decisions; this is especially crucial in cases where someone commits a crime and knows very well that any court would find him guilty, so he is not interested in any arbitration. The aim of this chapter is to explain how an anarcho-capitalist society could deal with such evils.

Most states use the police for these purposes. What's wrong with that? Apart from the two usual arguments, namely that it is not moral (the police are paid from forcibly collected money) and efficient (the free market can allocate resources for police protection better than the state - see the second chapter), there is one more fundamental reason why police power - the monopoly on violence - should not be entrusted to the state: History shows that whenever things go wrong and a despotic tyrant comes to power, this power is always used against its own citizens. Even so, most people argue against power components in private hands by saying that they could be misused against the population, although we know anarchist societies (medieval Iceland or Ireland) in which nothing similar happened on a mass scale not once in the many hundreds of years of their existence; on the other hand, history is full of cases of massive abuse of state forces, and it is actually impossible to find a populated area in the hands of the state where this has not happened repeatedly over such a long time horizon.

It can be assumed that not everyone will want to rely on their own abilities in the event of becoming a victim of crime; even the assumption that there will not be a majority of such people is not very bold. Demand for protection against criminals creates supply; entrepreneurs will be able to make money by offering people the services of their security agencies to help them in case they become victims of an aggressor. Payment for such services can be either one-time or flat-rate. These security agencies would likely employ both detectives to investigate crimes and mercenaries trained in the use of weapons to openly fight criminals.

So what will happen if, for example, someone robs a customer of such a security agency? The first problem is to find the perpetrator. The detectives begin to search and find evidence. If no one is found, the victim may – depending on the wording of the contract – receive compensation from the security agency because it failed to perform the task for which it is paid (this service is not unlike theft insurance). If the culprit is caught, it depends on how he reacts to the whole thing. When he capitulates and settles with the victim for compensation, everything is settled. However, if he protests (for example, he may plead not guilty, or plead guilty, but call the victim's demands for compensation absurdly high), the security agency will refer the matter to a private arbitrator (see Chapter Fourteen), who will decide on it; if the person submits to his verdict, all is well. If he does not comply, the security agency will force him to do so (in this case, however, it is not offensive violence, as it is committed against the person who first himself did not respect the victim's property rights).

I imagine most readers might have thought something along the lines of, "Why would an agency go to an arbitrator when it can force the alleged perpetrator to cooperate anyway and save court costs?" Well, such a reasoning supposes that the use of violence is cheaper than a settlement by arbitrators, which cannot be considered too probable; even if the salary of a private judge in the free market exceeded the salary of a mercenary, there are still a number of other factors that make violence more expensive: Even a trained mercenary can hypothetically be overpowered and killed by his target (especially if an attack is expected), someone else could be harmed as part of a violent solution (a potential or even a current client of a security agency), anyone can try to take revenge on the person in question (which potentially causes further losses) and last but not least, by extrajudicial killings, the security agency will make many enemies and will not enjoy a good name, which is important for such a company not only because people ask for its services, but also because it will often make its job easier if disinterested people cooperate with it in the search for criminals (if in the eyes of the public such a security agency is really a fair organization that pursues criminals, it can certainly be imagined that it will receive much more support for such an activity than if people perceived as a bloodthirsty mafia). Furthermore, security agency clients typically do not demand the death of the person who harmed them; much more often they want to be compensated, which murdering the criminal does not solve in itself.

It should also be noted that while all of the above arguments apply to those who are not clients of any security agency, there is an even stronger argument for everyone else (which may be the majority): If a given security agency were to try to eliminate a customer of another agency, an armed conflict could easily ensue, costing both sides money; war is expensive (especially for someone who pays for it out of their own money, not out of taxes) and waging it just to avoid a court service fee is absurd.

Thus, each security agency will likely have contracts with arbitrators. In the event of a conflict between two clients of the same agency - or a conflict between its client and someone who is not protected by any agency - one of the judges with whom the agency has a contract will decide. If there is a dispute between clients of two different security agencies, the decision will be made by one of the arbitrators with whom the two companies involved have a contract (if there is none, they can agree on something, which is still cheaper than war).

People often ask for assurances that the biggest security agencies won't band together and take over the entire company. Of course, this cannot be guaranteed. But what is the guarantee that any state will not become a dictatorship? Also none; and how many times has this happened! However, there are many arguments against a stateless society being controlled by its own security agencies. In addition to the fact that a corporation so large as to have the potential to enslave some larger territory is usually not decided by one person, but by many shareholders, it is not just about controlling "ordinary people", as there are many economically powerful entities in such a territory (of which there are - in all fields combined - probably more than security agencies); and they can defend themselves effectively - even if combat is not their primary focus, they can hire mercenaries. Not to mention that in an anarcho-capitalist society "ordinary people" will also be armed much more often, making it much more difficult to control them by force. In addition, even the remaining security agencies that do not join the "bad" ones will face the aggressors in the first place, because what is better advertising for a company doing business in the given field than to eliminate such a danger? And what if everything still failed and the company was taken over by a few powerful corporations? Well, then our fates would not be decided by a few deputies as now, but by a few shareholders; the most catastrophic result is the creation of a monopoly on violence, i.e. the state.

So far we have dealt with cases where the crime has already occurred; but how would it be possible to prevent the ones that are happening right now? Suppose that a robber has robbed an innocent person in the street, and there is a mercenary patrolman of a security agency standing nearby, who does not know whether the person in question is a customer of his employer; what now The victim can call that law enforcement officer for help, making a verbal contract with the security agency. But what if the attack is already in an advanced stage and the victim is unconscious? Will that private policeman intervene even without being asked? Most likely, his employer will give him such instructions. First, he cannot know whether his client is in danger; if that was really the case, the ranger would not have intervened and the case would have become known, people would probably have lost interest in the services of such a security agency. Secondly, with such help, the security agency can win a new customer, because the one whose property and maybe even his life were saved will be more amenable to concluding a contract. Third, it is possible that even if this robber's attack was not directed against a client of the given security agency and the mercenary let him escape, the next victim could be another customer of his employer, costing him additional resources. And fourth, there is a rational assumption that security agencies will enter into agreements to provide mutual aid to their clients in an emergency, since it is cheaper to prevent crime on the spot than to investigate it retrospectively.

It is often argued that if private security services are provided, the poor will not be able to afford them, so everyone will rob and kill them with impunity. This problem was solved with remarkable elegance by the free market of medieval anarchist Iceland: The aggrieved poor man – as the victim of a crime – was entitled to compensation from the perpetrator (in the case of murder, the heirs were compensated); he donated part of the claim in advance to someone rich who had the means to extort it. Such a gift was beneficial for the rich (he could demand compensation from the criminal without anything happening to him) and also for the poor (no one could harm him with impunity). It can be assumed that the poor could just as well enter into contracts with security agencies, which would take part of the compensation instead of a fee (the victim would receive less, but would gain a defense against the aggressor that they could not otherwise afford).

Much more could certainly be written about private security components, but the goal of this book is to provide the reader with a comprehensive idea of the possible forms of a free market society, which, in my opinion, could be harmed by too much detailed analysis. However, who would like to deal with this issue in more detail, I warmly recommend my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, who has devoted himself to stateless provision of security to a large extent in many of his works; or also the first comprehensive texts on this topic, written in the nineteenth century by the French free-market economist Gustave de Molinari. So much for protection against internal danger; in the sixteenth – the last regular – chapter we will deal with the defense against the external enemy.

chapter: 15. Law enforcement
name: Crime and Punishment
text:
Although the fifteenth chapter on the free market enforcement of law by security agencies mentioned the compensation that the criminal would have to pay to his victim after being caught, so far in the entire book we have not had the opportunity to read anything about punishing those who in some way violate someone else's property rights. I would like to remedy this in this chapter, in which I will offer several alternatives for how the free market in anarcho-capitalism could deal with the given problem.

Why several? Well, as we already learned in the very introduction, no one can predict with certainty a free market solution to any problem; if it were possible, there would be no need for a free market at all, as it would be enough to set everything exactly that way through central planning. However, the second chapter explains that such a thing is not possible, so we have to settle for uncertain assumptions, which can be variously accurate depending on the detail of the problem they relate to. Therefore, although most anarcho-capitalist thinkers agree on, for example, how free market education, healthcare, the judiciary or protective services could work, there are considerable disagreements in the area of punishing criminals, within which many theories arise, of which I am going to present three and add my fourth. I leave it to the reader to judge what seems most reasonable to him, or I shall be glad if he himself suggests another alternative and sends it to me; I'm certainly not averse to discussion, and I still haven't found a solution to the issue of punishing criminals that I find completely satisfactory, although I'm sure the free market would come up with one.

Before I start listing those theories, I would like to clarify the term "repair the damage", as I will use it in describing them. Damages repair means two things. First, an attempt to restore things to their original state: If it is theft, it is about returning the property to the owner; if damage occurs to non-unique tangible property (this can be a fence, for example), this means the purchase of a new such thing (or its repair, if the result is identical or if the owner agrees); if a unique material property (for example, the Mona Lisa) or someone's health is damaged, the solution is to pay all the expenses associated with trying to restore the thing to its original state (restoration of the painting, treatment of a fracture, etc.) and to pay compensation, the amount of which is determined by the judge based on an estimate of how much of the original value was lost (for the victim), or what the victim had to suffer (pain or permanent consequences). The distinction between unique and non-unique property in disputed cases is up to the judge. Second, reparation includes paying the costs of prosecuting the criminal and any courts, plus compensation for the time the owner was unable to use his property (for example, if someone breaks a programmer's arm and he can't program because of it, he - or his employer - should be reimbursed for lost profits).

The strictest of the theories says that if someone infringes someone else's property rights with proven intent, the victim is the only person who can judge how painful the aggressor caused him, so the punishment for him is determined by the victim to a completely arbitrary extent. In the event of an unintentional violation of property rights, the person who violated them must repair the damage. Personally, I find this theory the least acceptable, as it allows draconian punishments to be imposed for ridiculous misdemeanors.

According to another theory, the attacker, who disrespected the victim's property rights to a certain extent, must on the one hand repair the damage, and the victim also has the right to disrespect his property to the exact same extent that the person in question did it to the victim before. Therefore, if someone steals a million crowns, they must return the million (and pay all the expenses associated with obtaining it and any losses that the robbed person suffered because he could not dispose of the money) plus - as a punishment - pay the victim another million. If someone breaks another's arm, he must both repair the damage, and he can also break his arm (or agree with him not to do so if he pays him additional compensation beyond what he has already paid - as punishment).

The mildest theory, on the other hand, says that the aggressor should in any case only repair the damage and nothing more. His punishment should be additional expenses, as he would have to pay court costs, the costs of his prosecution, compensation for the time during which the victim could not dispose of his property, possible pain and so on. This solution seems to me the most natural of all; however, some may argue that perhaps it makes life too easy for criminals.

The above approaches can be combined in various ways; for example: In the event that someone intentionally violates another's property rights, the victim should be able to choose whether he wishes to have the damages remedied or whether he would prefer to violate the aggressor's property rights to the same extent. For damage caused to property, the differences will be minimal (someone took a million, so the robbed person either demands the million back from him or wants to take another of his millions; it probably differs only in that, as part of repairing the damage, the aggressor still has to pay court costs, other compensation, and so on). A more interesting situation occurs when someone damages another person's health. In such a case, he can either ask for standard compensation, or he can want to harm the aggressor out of a desire for revenge, but there is another possibility: The victim can choose to violate the aggressor's rights to the same extent that he did it to her, but the goal is not to maim him, but to ask him for money for not doing so, which can be more than what the victim would get in the standard way (or the attacker does not comply, he prefers to let himself be injured and the victim gets nothing). In case of unintentional infringement of property rights, the infringer would then have to repair the damage.

Implicit in all the above examples is the assumption that the victim of the violation of his property rights survived. But what if not? Well, in that case, her claim against the assailant passes to the heirs (which, of course, doesn't have to mean just family members; especially not if the murderer is among them), who sue the aggressor instead of the victim. For this reason too, I find the theory that the attacker should only try to repair the damage insufficient - if someone kills your child, the most they can do is pay you a lot of money. According to my theory, you can choose whether you want compensation or punishment (either you can kill the offender outright or come up with practically any other punishment for him, as he is very likely to accept it rather than death).

Are you wondering why the word "prison" has never been mentioned in this chapter yet? Well, that's because, although most states are so fond of using them as a universal means of punishing criminals, I consider this method to be probably one of the stupidest that can be invented. The victim of the criminal's stay in prison does not bring any financial benefit, at most a feeling of satisfaction from revenge, which can be achieved much easier (and cheaper; especially for taxpayers who have nothing to do with the crime in question). It is true that the criminal usually suffers in prison, which may deter him from further criminality, but this can also be achieved through other sufferings; incarcerating the person with other criminals and forcing him to live in this chosen society will give him enough space to adopt its moral values as his own, despite the fact that he can learn many new and interesting tricks from seasoned and experienced criminals that will allow him to improve in his "profession". And finally, there are "everyone else", who have absolutely nothing to do with the crime, but are nevertheless forced by the state to pay its punishment, which neither they nor the victim chose. It is easy to imagine that for a huge number of crimes, the victim would choose high financial compensation rather than revenge, the offender would also prefer payment to imprisonment, and citizens would welcome not having to pay for the criminal's stay behind bars; but why choose a solution that would suit all parties involved, when we have other, much worse, politicians and bureaucrats recognized as "proven"?

Regardless of the fact that even in a stateless society, the imprisonment of criminals as such is not completely excluded. For example, if someone inflicts an injury on you with serious permanent consequences, under most of the above theories you have the option of inflicting the same injury on them in return. But if you give him the choice of letting you lock him up for a few years instead in a prison you build for him on your property, pay him a guard and feed him there and provide him with the basic necessities of life, he will probably agree. An interesting question arises, how many people would probably voluntarily choose this solution (instead of, for example, getting compensation paid, or - if they wanted revenge - doing something to the perpetrator in return), which would mean only expenses and no profit for them except for a zoo with a prisoner in the yard. Something tells me that there probably wouldn't be many of them if it was their money, their land, their worry, their lost profit. But when "society" pays the bills, it's easier to squander it in the interest of the "higher good".

Although there are countless alternatives to how the free market in an anarcho-capitalist society could solve the problem of punishing criminals (and I hope to learn about some new possibility from one of the readers), I consider it almost certain that the result would not be as senseless as the state we can see around us. Indeed, if prisons were to function somehow in a stateless society, the prisoners would probably be forced to work in them and the fruits of their labor would be divided between the victims and the prison company; but something like that is just very hard to predict, because millions of entrepreneurs in a free market will practically always come up with a better solution.

name: 16. Army
text:
In this chapter we will deal with what is probably the most difficult subject - namely, the defense of a stateless territory against an external aggressor, which can almost certainly be assumed to be a state, for as the world stands, free people, ruled by no one, have never attempted to occupy a large territory and subjugate its population; From time immemorial, wars have been the affairs of governments and rulers, not of their subjects, who, however, always bear the consequences and suffer for the decisions of their rulers, who are able to convince them from time to time - for their money - with mass propaganda that they actually want war. As an answer to the question why an area should be managed by free individuals and not by the state, I have always presented two reasons throughout the book - morality and efficiency. Nothing changes on the side of morality; the levying of funds by a State for national defense from its subjects by threatening them with violence if they do not pay, cannot be called moral by any stretch of the imagination. But what's worse, this "national defense" very often degenerates into a "national attack" in the hands of politicians, even if it's not called that (probably every country has a ministry of defense and probably none has a ministry of attack; despite what such ministries of many countries do in practice). The number of victims of all wars in the last century amounts to roughly three hundred million; all these lives were ruined by states (the ones we have here so that people don't kill each other in anarchy) and their armies.

But what about efficiency? Although even in the running of the military the typically great anarcho-capitalist thinkers credit the free market with its usual efficiency, I cannot agree with them on this point. Indeed, if we think again about why free market solutions are so much more efficient than state ones, we will come to the fact that the reason is mainly a huge number of entrepreneurs, each of whom will try to satisfy customers in the way he considers best, with those who do it well making money while others lose (see the first and second chapters); a huge advantage of the market over the state is its self-cleansing ability, meaning that the authors of bad solutions lose their capital and go bankrupt. Although none of these laws lose their validity even in the field of running the army, a failed defense against an external enemy, who must necessarily be someone who does not respect the principle of non-aggression (otherwise he would not be an aggressor), logically means the end of the free market in the given territory; it is therefore not possible to try different solutions "with impunity" and distinguish good from bad using profits and losses, which is the alpha and omega of market efficiency. Of course, it does not follow that the state solution would be more effective; only in my opinion it cannot be said that it would automatically be inefficient compared to the market, which is typically assumed by the great anarcho-capitalist thinkers - even the brilliant Murray Newton Rothbard, who deals with national defense in some detail in his works, argued for the effectiveness of the market compared to the state in this area without first dealing with this objection in any way.

I see the greatest weakness of an anarcho-capitalist society in the very limited ability to prevent the movement of enemy troops on its territory. States usually have a large amount of heavy weapons and technology developed directly for the purpose of warfare and destruction. It may be supposed that free men, who are not compelled to acquire such instruments, will (assuming the same amount of wealth in society) have fewer of them; and even the limited amount they will have cannot be moved anywhere without the consent of the owners of the given lands (and if someone tries to do so by force, they risk resistance, which costs at least time to suppress). It is possible to expect considerable motivation to cooperate against a common enemy, but it will never be as easy as in a state that owns land communications and whose citizens are governed by government orders rather than the principle of non-aggression.

As for the total volume of funds that a country with a given number of inhabitants will be able to invest in possible armaments, I do not find an advantage on either side. An anarcho-capitalist society will certainly be far more economically efficient than a state (which is the central theme of the entire book), but people are unlikely to be willing en masse to voluntarily sacrifice everything they have, including their lives, to warfare; although - except in exceptional situations - they will not do this even for their government, however, it has the means to force them to do so if necessary.

The indisputable advantage of an anarcho-capitalist society, on the other hand, lies in the fact that, although it is probably not so difficult to penetrate the territory where it is located, its effective control appears to be an extremely difficult task. If the army of one state occupies the territory of another state, the defeated government capitulates and the existing power structures in the given territory begin to enforce the will of the conqueror, who suddenly gains effective power over the population, because it was already registered, controlled, paid taxes and generally obeyed the government's orders; so there will only be a change in who gives the orders - the already existing means of violently subjugating those who disagree will simply be used by someone else. There is no such thing in an anarcho-capitalist society. The conqueror faces not masses, but individuals, for whom no one can speak and negotiate, and who, moreover, often speak a language that the invader's soldiers typically do not speak. Not to mention that free people - without state regulations and prohibitions - will probably be much better armed. In order for an aggressor to take control of such a territory in a conventional way, he would have to build all the power structures on it from scratch, which includes registering the entire population and forcing them to submit to laws that contradict everything these people have ever known and are accustomed to; all this must be done despite the language barrier and the weapons in the hands of free individuals who - unlike citizens of states - are used to solving their problems on their own. An invading army may, of course, begin to use brutal methods of coercion, razing cities and killing the inhabitants of the conquered territory on the spot; however, when this becomes known and the attacked understands that they have nothing to lose by meeting a foreign soldier, they will be in the given territory practically like a shooting range (it must be remembered that for every soldier of the aggressor there will probably be several armed inhabitants of the attacked country; and they will most likely shoot at each other).

Great Britain has been convinced at least twice in history that the difficulty of controlling a stateless society is not just a theory. It took her several centuries to conquer the much smaller and weaker Ireland, as the Irish had no state and power structures that would transmit orders to the common population. The English could not understand that, without any form of state, the Irish warriors who made treaties with them could only speak for themselves; they could never bind any other group of the Irish population. The British encountered a similar problem when conquering Africa, when they tried to subjugate the territory of the Ibo tribe (with an area of between seventy and eighty thousand square kilometers, i.e. about the size of the Czech Republic); its inhabitants lived in real anarchy (and in accordance with some libertarian principles), so they had no chiefs or leaders to follow. Controlling (that is, not just conquering by army) such a small piece of land was more difficult for the British than subduing the whole of India, where they could rule for centuries without much trouble, because they only transferred their orders to the ruling Indian princes, who then enforced them on their subjects.

"Oh well," many readers may be saying to themselves now: "but in the end the British conquered the Ibo territory anyway and Ireland as well, so that anarchy won't be very viable after all." Well, although most of the historical anarchist societies really disappeared by being conquered by some state, it must be remembered that the same end awaited most states. Some bigger and stronger empire just appeared and crushed and occupied the smaller and weaker one. All of the above analyzes of the advantages and disadvantages of states and stateless societies in war are based on the assumption that it is a conflict between two comparable rivals. However, if we consider a fundamentally unequal conflict, it is probably irrelevant to its outcome what kind of social arrangements we can find on the individual sides. For example, if we assume a conflict between the USA and the Czech Republic, the USA will most likely win, regardless of whether anarcho-capitalism or the state will be on one side or the other.

But what is the actual reason why no one is attacking the Czech Republic at the moment? None of the governments of larger and stronger states is apparently interested in our territory. If such an interest were strong enough, a reason would always be found (and international agreements will not change that, as they have been violated to the world's cost). Would the establishment of anarcho-capitalism be such a reason? In my opinion, no one can answer this question in a sound manner. Either a stronger and larger country would mercilessly take such territory, or not. Anyway, even if the invasion were to happen and be successful, the anarcho-capitalist society will end up as a state again, nothing worse can happen. The absurdity of the argument that we need a state because anarcho-capitalism could end up having a state in the worst case scenario probably doesn't need to be discussed too much.

However, even if the indefensibility of an anarcho-capitalist society on some small territory were to prove practical, it is not necessary to discard this entire concept as unusable. It would only mean that it probably can't withstand overwhelming odds, which a state generally can't either. The inability of a small territorial unit to resist says nothing about the defense possibilities of a huge anarcho-capitalist country.

And finally, it is also possible that if anarcho-capitalism proved to be functional in some territory for a certain time, it would be a compelling reason for the citizens of all states to try to establish the same system; in the case of mass success of such efforts, our world could reach a state in which defense against an external enemy would not be necessary. A world without states also means a world without wars. To be sure, there would continue to be local conflicts in various places, but as long as these were paid for out of the pockets of those who lead them, they would probably not have the potential to grow to such gigantic proportions as state wars.

name: Myth busting
text:
In this bonus chapter, we will discuss some widespread misconceptions that are very often encountered in discussions of a stateless society, and which are typically characterized by the fact that they contain some kind of implicit assumption that is usually very well hidden in them and, moreover, appears to be true at first glance. The task of this chapter is to point out such assumptions and subsequently refute them.

I cannot begin otherwise than by mentioning a brilliant French thinker and economist who undertook this task absolutely brilliantly in the first half of the nineteenth century. He is none other than Claude Frédéric Bastiat. He dedicated his work "What is and what is not seen" precisely to the refutation of widespread errors; reading it, one can hardly help but be amazed at how many things that burned people two hundred years ago are still relevant today, as well as how many mistakes - disproved for two centuries - politicians are able to keep repeating and their voters believe. I strongly recommend everyone to read "What is and what is not seen" - it is a short reflection that is freely downloadable on the Internet; an hour or two will be enough to read it, during which you will gain more - and better - knowledge than by taking some economic - not to mention political science - course. However, within this chapter I will not deal with the fallacies that have been refuted for two centuries; anyway, the aforementioned French thinker did it much better than I could ever do.

A huge mistake, which in my opinion deserves a more detailed analysis, consists in the relatively widespread confusion of price and costs in fields that are practically completely controlled by the state. Just as the fact that Carl Menger - one of the founders of the Austrian school of economics - already in 1870 refuted Ricardo's cost theory of value (according to which the value of a good corresponds to the effort expended to create it) and replaced it with a subjective theory of value (the value of a good is equal to the highest price someone is willing to pay for it), did not prevent communists from following Marx's teachings in droves based on this disproved error, nor does it prevent today the general acceptance of the subjective theory of value (at least on an intuitive level) means that people often slip into the cost theory when judging the actions of the state. Then, for example, when the state pays price X to build a road, its value is assumed to be X (if there has been no embezzlement); however, this is obviously not true, because the value of the road is still equal to the amount that people would voluntarily be willing to pay for it, which could easily be less than X. In that case, the road should not have been built at all (or should have been built - perhaps worse - more cheaply). The same considerations can be encountered, for example, in the healthcare sector (people assume that the price of an intervention is fixed and equal to the current costs; they do not consider that it can be lower and the intervention should be performed cheaper - even if of a lower quality): Many people live in the idea that capitalist healthcare would look practically the same as the state one, only it would be financed differently; however, this idea (and all like it) contradicts the subjective theory of value and replaces it with the long-overdue cost theory.

Another mistake, which comes from the same roots, is often expressed by the objection: "If the state didn't pay for this or that, people wouldn't voluntarily give money for it." Even if we leave aside that such claims are typically based on the transfer of the current state to the anarcho-capitalist world (for example, the thesis that the state must provide people with pensions because they would not be able to do it themselves, since almost no one voluntarily saves for retirement now; however, the fact that people do not voluntarily save for pensions mainly because the state already does it for them is neglected), there remain some goods for which it is really true that if the state did not pay, people would not be willing to voluntarily finance them on the current scale. But what does that mean? Only so much that people prefer other things to these goods. Why? Because they'd rather buy something else with their money. So when the government forces people to pay something they would not voluntarily pay, they are worse off than they would have been without the coercion.

Very often, one can come across the following argument from the opponents of anarcho-capitalism: "What is the guarantee that one of the security agencies - or other powerful corporations - will not control the entire society and enslave everyone?" Well, of course there is no such guarantee. But not even in any state. Moreover - even if this were to happen - such a corporation would have a monopoly on violence and would effectively become a state. So this "brutal failure" of anarcho-capitalism means that it will turn into a state. "Sure," many argue, "but a state isn't like a state; a corporation that takes over an anarcho-capitalist society can be incredibly cruel and evil." It can, but why do so many people assume that the shareholders of large corporations will always do the worst, while politicians in government (however arbitrary) will not? Just look at the moral profiles of our current politicians! What is the probability that the shareholders of a corporation will be worse off?

Another popular argumentative nonsense is to compare anarcho-capitalism with a non-existent and unrealizable mythical ideal society that has no flaws, instead of comparing it with some concrete model (albeit a theoretical one). I have been a participant or witness countless times in discussions of anarcho-capitalism in which the proponent has been pushed by his opponents into a position where he has to defend a stateless society in completely absurd scenarios (the most extreme one I witnessed even involved a home-made black hole-creating device), while acknowledging that the result would be some kind of injustice, possibly someone's death, anarcho-capitalism is immediately ridiculed and considered bad. As if states did not cause anything like this, as if there were no wars in the modern world in which people die by the millions, as if there were no gulags and concentration camps, as if there were no evil. It must always be borne in mind that probably no anarcho-capitalist regards a stateless society as ideal and flawless; only for the best realistically possible. We do not claim that removing violent governments will solve all the world's problems; only that they will decrease.

When there is a general problem in a state-controlled society, people tend to call on the government to fix it. Is something wrong? Well, it will simply be banned, there is no easier solution. However, few people think about the side effects such a ban will have. And when someone rarely thinks about the direct consequences of a ban as such, they rarely include in their considerations the cost of enforcing it. If we are going to spend resources to enforce the ban, these must logically be missing elsewhere. Calling for state intervention should always be the last option (preferably so last that it doesn't happen at all).

Moreover, in our society we can see quite a few cases where the problem itself is caused by some law or regulation. A typical example is when states first force their citizens to accept unbacked currency and give banks the option to issue this currency, only to then have to create additional "regulations" to restrict banks in this activity, even though it would be sufficient to repeal the laws that cause this situation. By the way, who guessed why the word regulation is in quotes? Well, if something is regulated by one law, while a second law weakens the first, it makes sense to consider the second as deregulation, not regulation. From this, among other things, it follows that the so-called "deregulation" of banking, which is so often cited as the cause of the economic crisis, was in fact regulation (laws imposing the obligation to accept the national currency and enabling banks to issue it are regulatory; laws that weaken them are then deregulatory; ergo the weakening of these weakening laws constitutes regulation).

Considering that hundreds of such myths are planted in the minds of the general public, I could go on for a long time; and since new ones keep popping up, I've created a section on my website where I deal with refuting widespread falsehoods. You can view it at ankap.urza.cz; you can count on the fact that I will gradually expand it (at least I have done so so far).

However, I cannot close this chapter in any other way than with the words of the famous chef Zdenek Pohlreich, whose views are sometimes socialist, but he beautifully captured the principle why people are so prone to rejecting arbitrary changes (which of course also includes the transition from the state to anarcho-capitalism): "You know what most people consider the worst thing about every change? That then it's different." And indeed; how many arguments against anarcho-capitalism are de facto merely that something would be different?

name: Conclusion; and what next?
text:
With this conclusion I would like to close the main part of this book on anarcho-capitalism; my primary goal in writing it was to present this school of thought in a nutshell, to inspire the reader to think and to familiarize them not only with what anarcho-capitalism is, but also to explain what it definitely is not. I don't consider it very important whether you all agree with me; however, I try to ensure that your agreement or disagreement flows from deeper reflection and is not just the result of a first impression. And if, in addition, the world view of at least some of you is at least a little more liberal after reading this book, then the time spent writing has brought me double fruit; and you certainly don't need to immediately identify yourself as an anarcho-capitalist. I can very well imagine that many consider the state necessary in some industries and not in others, which is perfectly understandable; even if I haven't convinced you about the necessity of state courts, police and army, for example, there's no need to immediately reject, for example, the idea of free-market schools or money. And if you're not satisfied with anything I've written, please try to at least take this book as inspiration to come up with something better.

From time to time I am asked how I actually imagine the "introduction" or "establishment" of anarcho-capitalism in practice, but the answer to this question does not belong to the description of a stateless society, so you will not find it in any of the previous chapters; however, I will use this space for her. The only way to turn our society into an anarcho-capitalist one is to convince enough people of the beauty of freedom and the inviolability of property rights as the way to it. The more we are made to believe in this idea, the more will be its spreaders; at the same time, in democratic elections, people will give their votes to more liberal political parties, which can cancel both the laws that limit us the most, but also those due to which the state effectively spreads its propaganda, especially within the educational system.

Make no mistake, I am certainly not in favor of "change from above" (from politicians); very fundamentally I believe that the initial impulse must come "from below", however, for change, more forces coming from both "from below" and "from above" are needed. We need theorists, debaters, thinkers and think tanks, but also populists, charismatic faces, entertainers and catchy slogans, in addition to the desperate, the underground, civil disobedience and the gray economy, but also lobbyists, diplomats and unfortunately also politicians with their political parties; I don't claim that politics will save us, because I myself consider it to be dirt, but even the contents of a stinking cesspool must be manipulated from time to time, even if one gets dirty. I personally am very happy that others do it for me, because I don't want to sell my own soul; however, I will not condemn these people, although it seems likely that any successful political party will eventually be corrupted by its own power - but until then it can serve the ideas of freedom.

And when the state, as a result of this ants' work, is small enough to allow private entities to compete fully - without regulation - in all the areas in which it somehow interferes today, people will be able to convince themselves that it is not really needed; and if there is a sufficient number of such individuals with a non-negligible strength, the possibility of adequate defense against an aggressive state will arise for them. However, this one will by then be weak and - compared to the current one - relatively peaceful, so the opponents will probably not even try to take over by force, but will allow them to co-exist in parallel with it without interfering with their property rights, which I personally would consider an absolute victory; I don't need to destroy the state, I just want it to let me (and all those who wish the same) live in peace (even if such a "state" based on voluntariness will basically be a business).

I have just indicated how, in my opinion, anarcho-capitalism could be put into practice. However, I would like to explicitly write a few words about how this should definitely not be the case, or how it cannot even be done in any case. In principle, the path to anarcho-capitalism cannot be a revolution or a coup; if a revolutionary seizes power, he can establish almost any regime, but not one that in principle excludes the very fact that someone holds power. Anarcho-capitalism certainly cannot be enforced by force, for it is impossible to force people to value their freedom if they do not do so out of their own convictions; they can be forced to build a better tomorrow in communism, to occupy more space for a superior race in Nazism, to follow the results of elections in a democracy, to listen to the word of the ruler in a monarchy, but it is not possible to push them to freedom by force, because such means are in direct conflict with the goal. Even if someone took over the government by force, then abolished it and relinquished power, another government would soon be established, if the people did not wish to have no government; if the revolutionary in question forbade them, he would become the ruler and the state himself. Offensive violence is not only an inappropriate and morally unacceptable means, but also does not lead to the goal, as it is in sharp contrast to it. Revolution is certainly not the way (and especially not a bloody revolution a hundred times).

Although this conclusion is a full stop to the regular chapters in which we have always dealt with the free-market form of some whole industry now in the hands of the state, there are still other areas of state influence which I think deserve our attention; the following several - additional - chapters will be devoted to them, with which I will try to cover a few controversial topics that are often discussed in discussions about a stateless society.

Although I have a weakness for similes, I have tried to avoid them throughout the book, as they are often misleading and inaccurate; here, after all, I won't forgive myself one thing at the end under the line.

Let's imagine a country where people live unrestricted; they freely exchange their goods with each other, and no one interferes with their business. Then comes a group of "smart heads" who build a huge tunnel in the middle of the area. They will gather consumers on one side of this tunnel and producers on the other. "Smart heads" listen to the wishes of consumers, adjust them at their discretion, collect money from them and transport them through the tunnel to producers who produce on the basis of orders that also come to them from the tunnel. All exchange of certain types of goods outside the tunnel is prohibited. Producers and consumers thus become indifferent masses, individuality is lost. Consumer wishes are interpreted through an intermediary; the goods that come out of the tunnel are distributed among consumers regardless of payment, the key is the will of the "smart heads" and also how much someone shouts that they need. On the other side of the tunnel, producers do not try to provide their services tailored to consumers (they don't even know their preferences anyway), but only according to the wishes of the tunnel administrators.

It is sheer madness to look for the primary cause of people's dissatisfaction - as opposed to the situation where they can trade directly - in the fact that, for example, "smart heads" keep something for themselves here and there (embezzlement), that some money is sometimes lost in the tunnel (high bureaucracy costs), that sometimes one of the producers or consumers bribes the tunnel manager to gain an advantage for himself (corruption), or that the tunnel managers are incompetent and unwilling (normal state of civil service). These problems certainly exist; however, they are secondary. Even if they could be solved or removed, the resulting situation would not improve much. The primary problem is, of course, the very existence of that tunnel, in which individuals with individual preferences become gray masses, a lot of information is lost there, and in general it only brings ruin and destruction.

Above all, however – and I consider this much more important – it is not ethical for someone to dictate to another with whom and under what conditions they may and may not do business, or take their resources under the threat of violence; if he does so, he commits aggression towards him, which means only evil. The state is evil.

chapter: Other areas of state influence
name: Drugs
text:
It is not uncommon for people to believe that state regulation of narcotics—based on outlawing the sale and possession of many of them—protects society from drug addicts and related crime; I will now try to show why this reasoning is so incredibly misguided that even its opposite can be called a true statement.

Personally, I consider the main reason why the state should not interfere in who and how much destroys their body with what drugs, the simple fact that this body does not belong to the state, but to the individual in question; and therefore he, not the state, should have the right to decide on it. If the government and the police prevent him from doing so, it grossly violates his rights. Although I myself consider this argument so fundamental that I no longer need any more, I fully understand that many readers think more pragmatically and are primarily interested in the overall impact on society; this is exactly what I would like to address in this chapter.

When assessing the effects of prohibited narcotics on their users, one must first of all realize that addictive substances are not automatically bad for everyone, because only the person concerned can decide what benefits them and how much; if we try to impose our own assessment of life happiness on others, it will not work. There are people who will not even touch alcohol or even coffee (and if we were to adopt their standards, we should ban these drugs as well); then most have nothing against alcohol and coffee, but they do against many other drugs; some consider marijuana or LSD to be acceptable; and there are those who do cocaine from time to time but wouldn't touch heroin for anything in the world. There is no universally correct measure that we can prescribe for everyone. What gives us the right to judge which of the above approaches is the only correct one? Yes, some are riskier, but by that logic we might as well ban climbers from scaling mountains because many have miscalculated and paid with their lives.

Within the framework of the war on drugs, various anti-drug school events often do not differentiate between individual illegal narcotics, essentially describing the effects of heroin, whose properties are implicitly attributed to all prohibited substances; the dangers of legal drugs are typically glossed over in such lectures (we often hear the strange phrase "alcohol and drugs" - as if alcohol is not a drug at all). I am certainly not suggesting that taking drugs is safe, as the use of any addictive substance is always associated with risks; on the other hand, I don't think it's wise to lie to children about the effects of narcotics, because if they reveal this lie in the case of less risky drugs, they will probably lose respect even for the hellishly dangerous ones.

Although there are a number of ways to assess the danger of individual narcotics (for example, the degree of damage to the organism, the speed of addiction, the strength and type of addiction, withdrawal problems, withdrawal symptoms), for all decent people who would "never touch drugs, but like beer", I have bad news: Alcohol is one of the more dangerous narcotics (although there are even worse ones) and, for example, compared to LSD (which, by the way, is a non-toxic drug, so you can't overdose). it comes out disastrously wrong by almost every conceivable criterion. In fact, the differences between individual drugs are vast (I'm not talking about the hard and soft division now), and just as many people drink and smoke without getting drunk to death or dying of lung cancer (although it does happen), it's possible to use most narcotics for decades without serious consequences. Some can be habit-forming incredibly quickly (heroin), others are difficult to get used to (ecstasy), some cause physical addiction (nicotine), others psychological (cocaine), some damage health very fundamentally (barbiturates), others negligibly (LSD), and existing addictions to some drugs can be gotten rid of relatively easily (marijuana), with others it is extremely difficult (alcohol). Although many addictive substances can be considered a relatively reliable tool of slow suicide (crocodile), most drugs (LSD, alcohol, cocaine, caffeine, marijuana, ecstasy, tobacco and many others) can be used for a lifetime (of course with very different frequency depending on the user and the drug) and live a happy long life. Theoretical.

Why in theory? Because in practice, many drugs are absurdly overpriced, as the price is several orders of magnitude higher than the production costs due to their illegality. As a result, on the one hand, producers and sellers of narcotics, whose livelihood is anyway illegal and they are persecuted for it, regardless of the quality of the goods they supply, mix drugs with some kind of plaster, which makes them even more dangerous, but above all, drug addicts get into financial problems, before which they run back to the drug, so that their life is reduced to just looking for the next dose and addiction develops even faster; many then commit crimes in this state, thereby endangering others - but if it were not for the war on drugs, which increases the prices of narcotics by an order of magnitude, drug addicts would in most cases only destroy themselves, similar to what we can observe, for example, with homeless people drinking boxed wine. Please do not read this text as a defense of those who rob for the next paycheck; I don't excuse them, I just state that state repression worsens the whole situation (if the dose costs a unit of crowns, there is no need to rob or even kill for it - even for a drug addict there are easier ways to get change; however, if a drug addict needs to satisfy his needs - thanks to the state - many hundreds of crowns a day, he is much more likely to resort to violence).

I admit that in addition to the direct threat posed by predatory drug addicts, there is another problem - drug addicts are, on average, much sicker than other people (both because of the narcotics themselves, and also because of their illegality, which raises drug prices and thus brings their users misery, need, crazy living conditions, dirty needles, and the like). Others then pay for their health care; however, this is not an argument for drug prohibition (which makes the situation of drug addicts – and secondarily everyone else – even worse), but for free market health care, which solves this problem (see chapter ten).

A non-negligible objection of the supporters of drug prohibition is often the health of our children. If narcotics become legal, they can be sold around schools! Sure, but they are even now; if a schoolboy wants drugs, he will get them, let's not be under any illusions. We can take comfort in the fact that it is a "system failure" and "better policing" would solve everything, however, this is not true, but above all, it does not matter at the moment; the important thing is that it just happens. In the case of drug legalization, it would probably be a little easier, but the allure of forbidden fruit would disappear. Above all, the responsibility for children would be transferred back to them and their parents, who should protect and educate them, not rely on the state's illusion of safety (and recover from their mistakes by blaming the state). Do we want children not to fet just because no drug has accidentally gotten to them yet, or to understand why they should refuse?

Sometimes we can face the fear that if drugs were legal, the whole society would destroy itself and everyone would eat themselves to death; however, this can also be done with the use of legal narcotics. It is absurd to assume that the legalization of addictive substances would cause a drug apocalypse, since most people simply have no interest in destroying their lives (if they did, they still can today); moreover, increasing the amount of money spent on the war on drugs has not been proven to reduce the number of addicts in society, clearly showing that repression simply does not work. In Portugal, for example, drugs became a serious problem in the 1990s; huge numbers of people were dying of overdoses and the number of people infected with HIV continued to rise. In 2001, the local government legalized the use and possession of small amounts of all drugs (including heroin); the results? Within fifteen years, the number of overdoses dropped twenty-seven times (!) and the number of HIV-positive people stopped increasing.

The fact that Portuguese politicians - when they came under public pressure - decriminalized drugs shows that they were well aware of what the war on drugs was causing, they were just fine with it until they started losing political points (if they were serious about the effectiveness of repression, they would only tighten up then); it is no different in other countries, the politicians and officials who are already dealing with the issue know the data (not only from Portugal), but they are not interested in a real solution, because their career is based on drug problems. Which is also related to how the war on drugs actually started (I don't mean its main wave from 1971, but the very beginning in the 19th century in the USA); it was not about any protection of the population at all, but about lobbying (hemp competed with nylon in the production of fabrics and wood in the paper industry) and racism (Asians typically took opiates, South Americans and Africans took drugs from coca; by banning these substances it was possible to bully their users), which is not even a secret, because at that time it was not yet politically incorrect to announce it publicly (and politicians did so).

The war on drugs was not, is not, and never will be for the protection of society (it has been proven that it leads to the opposite), but only for reasons of power. Such a thing will never be admitted by those whose current careers depend on the fight against drugs, but the Global Commission on Drug Policy, a body composed of former powerful people who dedicated their lives to the war on drugs, but are no longer alive today (for example, ex-presidents of South American countries, ex-Secretary of State of the United States, former head of the United Nations, ex-Secretary of NATO, former high representative of the EU), openly declares: "The global war on drugs has failed with with devastating consequences for individuals and societies around the world.”
