Drug prohibition is exactly the same nonsense as alcohol prohibition in the twenties in the USA; the only difference is that it does not affect so many people, so its disastrous consequences are not seen at every turn. In a stateless society, however, one can imagine the sale of drugs in the same way as the sale of any other goods, which will undoubtedly have an impact not only on the purity of those substances; something like this would mean, among other things, the complete end of drug mafias, which are clearly created only and only by the war on drugs, because what is the point of smuggling or secretly storing and producing something that is normally available in stores?

chapter: Other areas of state influence
name: Arms
text:
It can be expected that in a stateless society everyone would arm themselves according to their discretion and financial possibilities; owners of private land could set arbitrary rules on their own land, i.e. restrict the carrying of weapons, but these would only be restrictions of a local nature. The idea that practically everyone can carry a firearm anywhere else is not doubly pleasant for many of us, because we are used to regulations whose creator - the state - instills in us from a young age the belief that without it and its laws, it would not be possible and we would all shoot each other here.

Empirical data from the past and the present clearly show that this is just a god-fearing scaremongering. So on one side are the strong emotions fueled by state propaganda that everyone "knows" that total gun deregulation would cause the apocalypse without ever really thinking about it, while on the other we have the facts; it's up to each of us what we lean towards. In the past, firearms were a common part of people's lives and their regulation was typically minimal or non-existent - for example, in the United States before 1934 anyone (regardless of age or any state permit) could buy any weapon (including heavy ones), and even in our territory restrictions were negligible until 1918; nevertheless, there were no disasters - not even massacres in schools, which were not "gun free" at the time - and people did not shoot each other (even children were used to guns, they were learning how to handle them, so accidents rarely happened).

Many will argue that without gun regulation we would have a "Wild West" here; we know it from westerns as a very bloody period and place. But there is a catch in the sources used - few people look up historical data when they think they know what it was like back then. However, the reality in this case is far from romantic ideas; the roughest of rough towns can serve as an example (to this day they are the inspiration for many westerns): Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Dodge City or Caldwell, where between 1870 and 1885 there were 19 murders per hundred thousand inhabitants annually - which is less than in contemporary Washington - not to mention that the statistics of the number of inhabitants at that time do not include various passing individuals (with their inclusion, the annual number of murders per hundred thousand inhabitants decreases from 19 to just over 1). Or let's look at the most famous gunfight of the Wild West, the shootout at the O.K. Corral (also a great subject for westerns), in which a total of nine (!) people participated, six of whom survived; and compare this famous battle with the gang wars of today.

When I talk about the Wild West, someone often comes up with the idea that there was a genocide of the Indians at that time; yes, that is indeed true. But who did it? They were not farmers and free people, already - although well armed - making (more or less non-violent and mutually respectful) agreements with the natives, but the state army, whose officers started the biggest and most terrible massacres to prove their indispensability in the territory. If you want to know more about this period, I recommend the book "The Not So Wild, Wild West" by Terry Lee Anderson and Peter Jensen Hill.

But back to the present. Proponents of regulation like to argue with statistics that the more affordable firearms are, the more people end up being shot; and they're right, this is indeed true, but... it's not relevant. Where rifles and pistols are hard to come by, people don't actually shoot themselves much, but stab, strangle, beat and hang themselves all the more (the anti-guns typically include suicides in those statistics). But why should we be interested only in the number of people shot? After all, what matters is how many people lose their lives (in any way), which firearms no longer have a demonstrably negative effect on; and as for the total number of murders, there their influence is even positive. If we look at all the countries of the world from which data can be obtained (as a source I can recommend the "Small Arms Survey"), we will find that statistically, there are fewer murders where the population is rather more armed (although you can also find such pairs of countries whose comparison indicates the opposite, there are many more that confirm this conclusion); the availability of firearms does not reduce the number of suicides, but it does not increase either (it only affects the way they are carried out).

One very important (and not very surprising) conclusion emerges from this observation: People typically don't start figuring out who to kill based on obtaining a firearm; rather, they first decide to kill and only then choose an effective means. If they have a firearm at their disposal, they will reach for it because it is effective, however, in the absence of one, they will not disdain a knife, an ax or a car. This brings us to the main reason why it makes no sense to regulate guns; we can kill a person with a stick or a stone (not to mention a hammer or a screwdriver), which are tools that no state can realistically enforce a blanket ban on, so whoever wants to murder will find a way.

On the contrary, regulation actually helps the killers. For weapons represent a means of equalizing the natural imbalance of power; some of us are physically weaker by nature (especially women and children), others are stronger. With the help of weapons (and especially fire ones, because with cold ones the strength of their user still depends significantly) even those who are not endowed with great physical strength can effectively defend themselves; thus, their bans will significantly disadvantage the weak versus the strong. And not only that! If I have the element of surprise on my side and the possibility of an ambush, the effectiveness of the weapon does not matter nearly as much to me as when there is a fight and I need to defend myself (in an unexpected attack from behind, it is not a problem to succeed even with a knife, while defending with it is very difficult); therefore, banning firearms hurts the defender more than the attackers.

And unfortunately that's still not all; gun regulations restrict law abiding citizens much more than criminals. Sure, banning firearms will make life a little more difficult for them, but given their disrespect for the law, it's far from disarming them all; however, it disarms all law-abiding citizens in one - precisely because of their respect for valid legislation. As a result, there will be another imbalance of power in favor of "the bad guys". When criminals know their victims have no defense, they can do whatever they want (because law enforcement simply can't be everywhere even if they tried), which is not the case where almost everyone carries a thunder stick; an armed society is a decent society.

Many people feel an aversion to firearms, usually only caused by the state demonizing these tools; however, this propaganda is nothing more than another (unfortunately quite successful) attempt to consolidate state power and instill in subjects that they cannot defend themselves and need to stand up for it. Not to mention that a disarmed populace has no way to resist government oppression (and it's no coincidence that dictators—Stalin, Adolf Hitler, Mao Zedong, Pol Pot, the rulers of the DPRK from the Kim dynasty, and others—have always confiscated people's guns); the founding fathers, for example, were well aware of this, as a result of which the US Constitution has the Second Amendment (which seeks to preserve the "anarchist freedom" of arms even for citizens subject to state power).

In the hands of an individual, the weapon has another fundamental meaning: thanks to it, the person in question has to take on more responsibility; the use - but also the non-use - of a weapon in a crisis situation is an act whose consequences often cannot be undone, one can only learn to live with it. Although this looks like a disadvantage at first glance, the one who voluntarily remains unarmed also makes that decision - in advance, without knowing the situation in which he might find himself; yes, most likely it will be easier for him to defend himself against his own conscience that "he couldn't do anything anyway", but in reality he could, only if he had thought about it earlier. In any case, the carrying of arms has the exact opposite effect of the suppression of responsibility, the consequences of which are addressed in the fourth chapter of this book.

Related to this is the fear of firearms in the hands of juveniles or various lunatics; sometimes even today they do enormous damage with them. However, this currently occurs precisely because there are unarmed people around the attacker who cannot effectively defend themselves, making them tempting targets. A man with a gun is the greatest threat where no one else has one; otherwise, a person who attempts a massacre with a knife or an ax will hardly do more harm than today - he kills one or two victims, then others stop him (in an armed society, shooters can be neutralized just as quickly, which puts murderous madmen at a disadvantage compared to today).

"But what about heavy weapons?" the reader may argue, "Why not regulate them?" Mainly because in order to do so, the state has to have even heavier weapons, which - considering the way it is financed - is immoral; not to mention the direct restriction of property rights. Moreover, such regulation does not make sense even from the point of view of "protecting society", because those who have enough funds to buy heavy weapons and want to do harm can already invest these resources much more effectively today; compared to the price of, for example, a modern tank, an attack using poisons or explosives (which can be produced from legally available raw materials) is a cheap matter. In addition, for example, in the USA, the sale of all weapons was completely free until 1934, and thanks to the second amendment, the weapons purchased at that time could not be taken from their owners, so even today some people there have (legally inherited) artillery - although it is outdated, but it is still possible to attack densely populated cities with it now; however, no one uses it to commit crime. And nuclear weapons? For those, state regulations lose their meaning completely, because whoever is rich and powerful enough to buy them, circumventing the law is no problem at all (and has a huge range of ways to do harm in other ways as well).

So even though governments try to tell us how much we need their regulation—it's in their best interest to trust them and not resist—let's never stop trying to see things as they really are. Let's not close our eyes to the facts (the statistics speak very clearly in the area of weapons), even though emotions can greatly distort our vision due to the omnipresent state propaganda. Consider, for example, the relationship between the number of guns and the number of people shot that I mentioned above; even if it is true information, it is far from enough to reveal the whole truth, on the contrary, it serves to distort it.

chapter: Other areas of state influence
name: Science
text:
Who would finance research without the state? Companies often make a direct profit from the applied one, they would certainly invest in it, but what about basic research, the results of which we typically only see after a long time? Who would invest their resources in something so uncertain? Well, inquisitive free people - that's my answer. But Jeff Vail once said, "The free market will ignore solutions that are not capable of generating profit." Wasn't he right?

Yes and no. It follows from the context of his work that by profit he meant only financial profit; and in such a case he is definitely not right, because the end customer (customer) in the free market typically pursues non-financial benefit. He who mines quartz sand is apparently doing so for monetary gain; the same reasons will surely be given to the factory worker who makes rods of pure silicon from that sand; the one who squeezes microchips out of those bars also wants to make money; and it will be no different in the case of whoever uses those chips to make a mobile phone... However, many buyers of this device do not get any financial benefit from it, they simply want to be in contact with their loved ones; this solution (buying a phone) is not profitable for them in terms of money (on the contrary, loss-making), but they still choose it because it will bring them a great non-financial benefit.

So, if we include in the term "profit" absolutely everything, i.e. not only money, but everything that a person acquires (even on the non-financial side), then Jeff Vail was absolutely right, but the above statement ceases to be a criticism of the market; on the contrary, it becomes his ultimate defense, because ignoring solutions that benefit no one is precisely what reduces waste in a world of limited resources. But how does this relate to science? Well, research doesn't have to be just a means of making money; it can also be a goal, an obsession, a passion. Humans have been very curious since time immemorial, and many scientific discoveries (even in the field of basic research) were made simply because someone wanted to know the answers to their questions; and this does not have to be only the scientists themselves, but also the rich sponsors of their research.

Many will argue that in today's society, although there are a lot of entities funding applied research, not so many are flocking to the basic one, so it "must" be done by the state; however, the catch lies in the fact that when the state first takes most of what they produce from people and then finances research, their motivation to do so on their own decreases rapidly, because on the one hand they have far fewer resources at their disposal, but above all they have no reason to finance from their own something that will anyway be paid for with "public" money.

After all, the Czech state subsidizes research and development at a stable rate of about two percent of the budget, which is probably nothing that people would not be willing to pay voluntarily, if they are not so massively robbed by the state; the poorer among us would probably contribute even less or nothing at all, on the other hand, many of the rich would undoubtedly contribute not only a larger amount, but also a higher percentage. Not to mention that everyone could contribute where they see fit, and there would be no need to fund all the twisted projects just because someone can skillfully apply for subsidies. In connection with this, there is understandably a concern that the importance of some research will not be appreciated by the general public, which is a very good reason to spread education, but certainly not to force coercion; if some research is really important, then it is certainly possible to explain why it is so - and if it is no longer possible to popularize it and get hundreds of crowns from the masses, a few rich people can be convinced to make larger contributions. Failing either, the question then arises as to whether (and for whom) the research in question is really that important when no one is willing to voluntarily bear the cost.

Of course, it can be argued that some discoveries will only be important in the distant future and people don't think that far ahead. The simple (and from my point of view, not very convincing) answer is that even the state is run only by people, and there is no reason why they should be more "enlightened" than others (especially when we look at them and see what they are). In my opinion, however, there is another problem with this argument; because it assumes that "thinking far ahead is good" and by extension that the more, the better. But what if I said I wanted to plan ten thousand years ahead? And that I need your money for that... Most people would probably disagree with that. But why?

Although it may seem that my example with the ten thousand years is an argument ad absurdum, I am going somewhat elsewhere. How far in advance does it make sense to plan development? Ten years? Certainly. Fifty years? Probably yes. A hundred years? Um, maybe, but that's enough. A thousand years? Definitely not anymore. But what answers would people living in the Middle Ages at a much lower technological level give to this question? Their time horizons would most likely be shorter. What about early humans who were just learning how to use tools? It made sense to them to plan maybe another day; and who knows if. However, I would not be surprised if, in a few hundred years, technology had advanced so much that development planning would begin to make sense even for the millennia. A superficial conclusion might be that early humans got it wrong and the further into the future we plan, the better off we are; but it is rather the opposite – the richer and more technologically advanced we are, the more we can afford to plan ahead. How would a primitive man have fared, who, instead of worrying about what he will eat now (or tomorrow), was interested in planning the future for his distant descendants? He would probably go hungry.

In general, the richer and more technologically advanced a society is, the further into the future it can afford to plan; also because it has more knowledge and information on the basis of which it can make reasonable predictions. But who is to decide what is the "right" level of planning for the future? Politicians? No. This is not objective, everyone has their priorities and needs, some are comfortable living from day to day, others building a family tradition; one cannot objectively say that the latter is "better", as time preferences are a purely individual matter. So let's let people fund whatever research they think is meaningful. Although development can be artificially accelerated, it is always at someone's expense - an extreme example is wars, which are generally claimed to accelerate research, which is often true, but at what cost? And if states also accelerate development through the violent plundering of resources, it is the same principle - only applied to a lesser extent.

Various educational institutions (much like universities today) would have another incentive to engage in basic research in the free market; why would they do that? Well, what better way to gain name and fame - as an entity focused on professional education - than by employing scientific capacities, publishing articles in the given field and bringing the latest discoveries? Of course, it is possible that only prestigious and top institutions could afford this "advertisement" on the free market, however, this is enough in the case of science and research, because it is here - more than anywhere else - that quality matters more than quantity.

It would probably be interesting to gradually analyze the individual scientific fields and estimate how they could probably be financed on the free market, but we do not have enough space for such a thing. I consider it more important to know that what is important to people, they will pay for it voluntarily; on the contrary, they obviously don't consider anything that they don't pay for to be that important (respectively they prioritize other things over it) - if they don't like it, they can try to change their opinion, but they shouldn't force them to do anything.

chapter: Other areas of state influence
name: Work
text:
In a free market without regulations and the state, there can of course be no labor code; therefore, everyone should enter into any contract that they agree with the other party. In such a society, without legislative restrictions, employers could refuse to employ anyone and would not be held accountable to anyone; even the termination of employment relationships would be limited only by who contracts with whom for the given work. Such an idea quite understandably creates uncertainty and perhaps even fear in some people; in most of them, state propaganda created the feeling that workers would be lost in a free market without regulations. This myth - along with several others - I will try to debunk in this chapter.

At the outset, I would like to state that the labor market is a market like any other! Some offer their time and skills on it, others buy them. Here, shoppers are in a similar position to sellers as customers are to stores; they too can simply not buy what they don't like or don't like. And there is nothing wrong with that at all. On the other hand, I find it completely reprehensible if someone should be threatened with violence to buy something they don't want, or at a price they don't agree with. After all, everyone understands that even desperation does not justify a bankrupt innkeeper to force anyone to become his guest, or to pay him more than he is willing; so why should the desperation of the unemployed be a reason to use force against a potential employer in order to negotiate better terms?

To be more concrete, I will give some examples: minimum wage, mandatory breaks, maximum number of hours worked, minimum number of vacation days and many others; the Labor Code is full of such regulations. And what exactly does this legislation mean in practice? Aggressive violence can be used against employers who already offer their employees different conditions (regardless of whether they agree or not), and in extreme cases the state will liquidate their business. I consider something like this to be highly unethical and fully comparable to the above-mentioned pub man forcing someone to go and have a beer with him instead of with a competitor.

Here too – perhaps more than anywhere else – morality goes hand in hand with efficiency. However, it is not obvious at first glance, because the most common objection against a free (unregulated by the state) labor market sounds something like this: "The labor market may be in theory a market like any other, but in practice the employers are in a much better position than the poor employees, who often have to accept terrible jobs just because they have no better option." I agree with this comment; however, it is necessary to look for the cause of that condition. As incredible as it may seem, state regulation is also to blame here; they put enormous obstacles in the way of anyone interested in becoming a tradesman or entrepreneur, which increases the number of those applying for work and, conversely, causes a decrease in the number of those offering work. We often forget that employees and employers are not fixed groups of people; one person can be an employee, a self-employed person or an employer - the decision is made based on, among other things, what conditions he has for what.

Without legislative obstacles, there would be nothing to prevent a newly fired saleswoman from getting up the next day, buying some ingredients, cooking some of them and selling them along with beer at the stand, whereas in today's over-regulated world she would have to set up a business, obtain a license to work with food, meet formal hygiene standards, keep accounts, electronically record her sales, deal with authorities and pay absurdly high taxes; if she were to succeed and want to hire someone to help, she would run into all the legislative obstacles that are meant to protect employees. Most people don't want to do something like that, so they go looking for a job; and because there are many of them (and employers for the same reason few), they do not have good bargaining conditions. In the end, therefore, any protection of the employee against the employer has one fundamental effect: It motivates people to be employees rather than employers, thereby, due to the market law of supply and demand, improving the position of employers and worsening the position of employees in the labor market; An interesting paradox, isn't it?

But that's not all. In order for an employer to make sense to hire someone, the person should be able to earn for themselves (that is, bring value to the employer that they value more than the money they pay them). But "employee protection" increases the costs associated with employing him or reduces the value he brings to his employer; as a result, this will have a negative impact on his salary, or on the willingness of potential employers to hire him. An example can be the reluctance to employ women, for whom employers must hold a place during maternity leave.

Another way the state tries to help workers is through the minimum wage; however, its consequences are also not as positive as it might seem. Those whose salary is high enough will not be affected at all (it won't hurt them, but it won't help them either); however, it will fatally harm those whose labor is worth less than the minimum wage on the market, as virtually no one will have the incentive to employ them. If the employee brings value to the employer through his work, which is worth ten thousand crowns to him, then the minimum wage of eleven thousand means only one thing - employing the person in question will be for the employer the same as flushing one thousand crowns down the toilet every month; but the person in question probably doesn't want to do that... And how will they solve it?

Having already bitten the cost of the employee's work, I can't help but mention taxes; because they massively increase the costs of his employment. If an employee is able to produce monthly values worth, for example, fifty thousand crowns, this limit is the maximum that the employer can pay him in order not to be at a loss. But how much money does an employee who costs his employer fifty thousand get? Currently in the Czech Republic a little over half, specifically about twenty-seven thousand; the rest is swallowed up by the uneaten state in various taxes (including those called "insurance", but in reality they are taxes), not to mention the fact that when spending this money, the state also takes VAT (thus robbing the person in question of much more than half of what he earned). And we have also dealt with a situation in which the employer does not earn a single crown.

Some laws, in turn, force companies to provide employees with certain workplace conditions; again, this may seem noble, but there is a catch. In principle, there are two possibilities: Either the employer would provide such conditions of his own free will, then the given legislation has no impact; or he would not provide them because the costs involved are simply not worth it and the state will force him to do so. However, these costs have to be borne by someone, so they are very likely to be reflected in the salaries of employees or in the final prices for customers; therefore, the state does not provide this improvement at its own expense - it does so out of the pockets of all of us, including those it is supposedly trying to protect.

The so-called protection of jobs - be it from cheap labor from poorer countries or machines that "take people's jobs" - indeed protects some employees, but harms the whole society and hinders its development. Work is a means on the way to well-being, not a goal; and if we can do it more cheaply (whether thanks to machines or cheaper workers), we will help each other, as it will be possible to invest the saved resources elsewhere. And what will the people who lose their jobs as a result do? They will go do something that is currently in demand. Although this may seem like mere theorizing, it is a time-tested practice: In the Middle Ages, almost everyone worked in agriculture; today, thanks to technological advances, it is enough for a small fraction of us to hold this job. Is it wrong? After all, practically the entire population "lost their jobs" during this process; and what happened These people went on to do other things, and society as a whole is much richer - despite the catastrophic predictions that began to spread as early as the Industrial Revolution and, with minor modifications, are still spread today.

In any case, we must also not forget that when someone accepts a job, even if it is extremely difficult and poorly paid, he demonstrates the following (if he is not forced to do anything by force): According to his own standards, his original situation (when he did not have the job) has improved after accepting this job offer; the person who made him that offer obviously helped him (and of course himself as well). If this were not the case, the employee in question would refuse the job; by accepting it, he shows that this is the best option he has in his situation. When someone then in connection with this curses evil corporations exploiting workers, then (provided that these workers were not forced to do the work by force) they are actually cursing the entity that has done at least something for them - as opposed to the one cursing.

We can see a similar animosity in our society among people who set themselves against corporations using cheap labor from poorer countries; at the same time, they forget that even the little they pay the workers there is obviously more for them than they can earn elsewhere (if it weren't for that, they don't work for a multinational corporation, but go do something else - people always choose the one they consider the best from the available options). It can be argued that these companies are taking advantage of the misery of others, but what would happen if they stopped doing this? The situation of the poor would get even worse! How do I know? Well, if they had a better alternative than working for that corporation, they would have taken it by now; since they didn't, it means it was the best option available to them, ergo its disappearance will force them to choose the second best option, which means deterioration.

An unregulated free labor market is nothing to fear; despite the fact that such a notion may fill some of us with an oppressive uncertainty, it is the best possible solution. On the one hand, it is more effective than state intervention and brings more benefits to people - customers, entrepreneurs, employees, tradesmen and employers - than violent regulation, but above all it does not require the use of offensive violence against those who want to run their businesses contrary to what politicians dictate to them. Giving people the freedom to make decisions about their lives is not only efficient, but also moral.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text:
The answer

The liquidation of the competition with the help of dumping prices may occur, but it must be remembered that the one who sells at dumping prices loses by doing so (and the customer can, on the other hand, buy at low prices); when (or rather if) subsequently the competition actually fails and the profit-seeking entrepreneur raises prices again, his profits will attract new competition into the industry and he can start over.

Not to mention the fact that, if the liquidated competition has at least some capital, it has the possibility to directly buy cheap competitive goods at dumped prices, which it can - after the prices return to the original level or above - later sell at a profit; it is necessary to realize that practically anyone rich has the opportunity to apply this strategy, not only competitors from the given field.

Despite all this, it is understandably possible that even in a free market, the strategy of dumping prices can be used to eliminate competition - under very specific conditions; however, it is a very risky strategy that may not lead to a goal, and the one who uses it does so at his own risk. However, the customer does not suffer in any case, because he buys at dumped prices for some time at most.

A well-known example of an entrepreneur who destroyed competition in this way was John Davison Rockefeller, owner of the Standard Oil company; however, the customer certainly did not suffer from these practices, on the contrary: During the period of operation of the Standard Oil company, the price of kerosene dropped significantly. There were also competitors who rebuilt their businesses over and over and made money by selling their infrastructure at a profit to Standard Oil.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: When the state will not protect us, businessmen can enter into cartel agreements; they will set prices while the customer suffers.
text:
The reason for the emergence of cartel agreements is, of course, primarily the desire for profit, which, however, is also what usually leads to the (sometimes secret) violation of these agreements; of course, each of the cartel members will still try to get as many customers as possible for themselves, which will very likely lead to the demise of the cartel.

Even if this were not the case, the possible large profits of the cartel members will begin to attract other entrepreneurs to the industry, for which it is most advantageous to set the price slightly lower than that set by the cartel agreement, whereby the new entrepreneur will begin to take over the cartel's customers; the only way the cartel can prevent something like this is by lowering prices, which then renders the whole agreement meaningless.

The only way a cartel can truly exist, function, and generate astronomical profits by ripping off customers is when the state prevents new entrepreneurs from entering the industry (usually through laws prohibiting business in the area without a state license). For the above reasons, free market cartels do not really arise, or they disappear very quickly.

The most commonly cited example of cartels is the South American drug mafias, which actually form cartels. However, this is because the drugs are officially illegal in that jurisdiction, which prevents new entrants from entering the industry (as discussed in the previous paragraph). Big and powerful mafias will defend their position against the state, but new (weak) competition will not.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does not protect us, monopolies will arise in the market; they will set the prices while the customer suffers.
text:
A true monopoly - one that can dictate its own prices - only arises when other entities are prevented from entering the industry, which is, of course, the result of state activities (specifically, laws that prohibit business in a given area without a license granted by the state), not the free market. If entry into the industry is not prevented, a monopoly - in the true sense of the word - cannot arise.

Even in a free market, a firm can win the majority of customers in an industry (what some call a monopoly), but only by providing better service than its competitors; if this "big player" tries to raise prices and make dizzying profits, those very profits will attract competition into the industry, which will take away its customers (unless it is a state that prohibits competition by law).

Perhaps the most famous example of a free-market "monopoly" was the petroleum company Standard Oil, which was outlawed by the United States government in 1911, although during its forty years of operation the price of kerosene fell almost constantly (and no competition could keep up with Standard Oil); prices began to rise only after the state—in the interest of “protecting consumers”—abolished Standard Oil.

An occasional objection is that these theories would cease to apply if one obtained a unique source of some natural raw material for which there is no substitute; everyone would then have to obtain the given raw material only from its sole owner. This objection is correct, but such a situation has never occurred before, and I cannot imagine any realistic situation in which it could occur.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals, they are no better than public ones!
text:
This very frequent objection certainly does not only apply to education and health care, it is often also directed at other areas that are controlled by the state, but under certain conditions allow private institutions to operate in the given area as well. The rules and regulations that bind such institutions are typically very strict, as the entire industry is firmly in the hands of the state.

To deal with this objection, it is first of all to realize that a "private institution" is not a charm of success; although the power of the free market also partly lies in the fact that companies are owned by private individuals, but above all it lies in the fact that millions of entrepreneurs around the world try their solutions, while those who do it well prosper and others fail (this is how the market "filters" the right solutions).

However, if these private institutions are heavily regulated by the state, the main advantage of the market is lost, as the owners of these institutions have almost no room to create non-standard solutions to problems, since these often contradict various regulations; the difference between a state institution and a private institution, which the state binds with strict rules and regulations, is therefore relatively small or negligible.

There are also many other (in my opinion, not so important) reasons why private institutions usually do not show very good results for customers in an environment overregulated by the state: Barriers to entering the industry prevent natural competition, artificial state competition providing its services "for free" does not allow to compete with a lower price, and so on (the list is far from complete).

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: The activities of speculators impoverish decent people; he had to rob someone else of the money the speculator made from his trades!
text:
Hatred of speculators stems from Ricardo's long-overdue cost theory of value, which was refuted by Carl Menger as early as 1870, when he came up with the subjective theory of value; however, many still mistakenly believe that the value of goods is fixed. In reality, however, it is attributed to them by people, ergo it is subjective and changes over time. Things can gain and lose value without changing in any way.

Speculators use this feature to enrich themselves; they buy cheap to sell at a higher price later. Does it harm others? To answer this question it is necessary to realize why the prices of goods fall and rise; a decrease means their excess, an increase, on the contrary, a shortage. Therefore, in order to make a profit, the speculator must buy surplus goods and sell shortages; what are the consequences of such action?

In times of surplus, speculators help producers not go bankrupt; in times of need, in turn, they supply shoppers with scarce goods, thereby reducing their price. In essence, they "smooth out" price fluctuations over time. That is what those of them who earn do; they help society and are rewarded for it. The losers, on the other hand, do harm (for which they themselves pay the most); and strangely so much anger is not borne on their heads.

The market is not a zero sum game! The gain of one does not mean the loss of another; this would be true if the prices of goods were objectively given. But this is not the case, because in a voluntary business transaction, each party values what it gains more than what it gives up (otherwise the trade would not take place); therefore, when one gains something, it does not follow that another has lost. Speculators do not make money at the expense of others.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Even if the market were to work in everything else, it cannot deal well with the problem of public goods; we absolutely need a (democratic) state in the matter of providing them and securing payments.
text:
Public goods are those that benefit everyone, whether they pay for them or not; Take public lighting as an example. The problem arises when the following way of thinking of individuals becomes widespread: Public lighting will benefit me, whether I pay for it or not; however, I will save money by not paying, and the chance that there will be no lighting in the end due to the absence of my contribution is minimal.

Financing goods, from the consumption of which it is difficult to exclude black passengers, can be difficult in the free market (although solvable, since everything is privately owned); the state is claimed to be able to "solve" this problem. On the one hand, this is not true (those who have nothing, do not pay taxes and are black passengers of the state), but above all, the state "solution" causes far greater difficulties; especially in a democracy.

The big problem with democratic elections is that in order for a citizen to make an informed decision about who to vote for, he would have to spend an enormous amount of time studying electoral programs, both in terms of practical implications and credibility; and even if the voter spends that time, the chances of his vote making a difference are slim to none, ergo a smart strategy is to not care about the election if he doesn't enjoy it.

Does this remind you of anything? A relatively high price must be paid for the slim chance that a person can make an impact; this, of course, makes many individuals prefer not to pay the price (whether it is dozens of hours of studying political party programs or a contribution to public lighting). So democracy offers only the transformation of a relatively small problem (public goods) into a huge one (the whole government), but not its solution.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: All those anarcho-capitalist theories are nice, but show me a single real working anarchist society; such can never exist.
text:
Anarchy has already proven itself in history. Take Iceland as an example, which has been an anarchy for almost a thousand years since its settlement; although it was formally annexed by Norway and Denmark after a few centuries, the population there actually lived in anarchy. Although the Icelandic National Assembly Althing is sometimes referred to as the first European parliament, it was more of a "council of elders" that did not issue laws applicable to all residents.

Another example of functioning anarcho-capitalism was the United States during the period of colonization. Despite what westerns show, crime at that time was significantly lower than it is today; not only in absolute numbers, but also in per capita terms. The colonizers got along well with the natives (they bought land from them and made treaties that were respected) until the European states sent an army there.

Another example is medieval Ireland, although there is some debate as to whether this society can be described as anarchist. On the one hand, there was no Irish central government, but on the other, many different territories were ruled by local warlords at different times, with the degree of freedom of the people in these areas varying greatly - sometimes really high, sometimes not.

Until recently, the most famous anarchy was Somalia; the truth is that compared to modern and developed states, Somalia has no chance to succeed. On the other hand, no judgmental anarchist claims that arbitrary anarchy is better than arbitrary state; it's just that in every time and place anarchy is better than the state, which is also confirmed by Somalia: The situation on its territory without a government was significantly better than with it (though worse than here, for example).

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: All historically known anarchies functioned only under specific conditions; but that does not mean that anarcho-capitalism could be functional today, in the contemporary world.
text:
This objection is no doubt quite valid; it is just an objection to an argument that does not defend anarcho-capitalism. The assumption of the functioning of anarcho-capitalism in today's world results from elaborate and still unproven theories, which are based on several axioms (resulting from economics - praxeology - and ethics), from which they are derived using pure logic.

Examples of functioning anarchies in the past certainly support these theories, but they do not form their basis; nor does anyone try to construct those historical anarchies as proof that anarcho-capitalism could be feasible even today. The theories of anarcho-capitalism are certainly not based on the fact that sometimes anarchy worked well somewhere.

It is also true that all functioning anarchies of the past had certain common features, which include low population density (however, this is also due to the fact that in the past the overall population density was practically everywhere much lower than today), or a relatively "remote" geographical location; however, it does not follow that anarcho-capitalism could not function in other conditions.

Furthermore, it must be realized that things cannot be declared impossible just on the basis that they are not currently realized anywhere; if so, nothing new could ever arise, because we would dismiss everything as pointless, since there is no real example on which the functionality of that idea can be demonstrated (and this very argument prevents the creation of such an example).

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Entrepreneurs only pursue short-term goals and only make investments with a short payback period; for really long term projects we need government.
text:
First of all, it should be mentioned that with politicians it is not exactly a win in the long term, as they are typically elected for four years and their interests usually do not extend beyond that; if they invest for the long term, then mainly because the money they invest is not theirs - so the decision about what to invest in does not depend so much on the necessity of this step, but rather on how many votes it will get the politician.

The problem with long-term investments lies mainly in the fact that it is very difficult to know which ones are "right" and which ones are not; and since it's possible to invest in a plethora of different things, it's probably the most sensible thing to leave it to free people to decide what they want to finance with their money and what not - after all, it's their money that they've been able to earn, so they can hopefully spend it.

People sometimes think that the more "long-term" an investment is, the better; this may not always be true. In general, the higher the current wealth, the more it "pays off" to invest in the long term, which applies both to individuals and to society (when we "don't have anything to do", we usually save less for retirement than when we live in abundance); however, there is no need to "manage" it in any way, people behave this way completely naturally.

An example of such a failed "long-term investment" is the decades-long massive subsidy support for biofuels in the fight against global warming, which led to deforestation (which its authors could have foreseen if they had not been incentivized to the contrary); such a waste of resources is typical when the funds are "public", so the one who decides about them is not the one to whom they belong.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: If the state did not finance some projects, they would never have been created, because people would not voluntarily contribute to them; so the state must subsidize these projects!
text:
The first possible response to this objection is that the statist in question who raises it is simply wrong; many projects that are generally considered to simply have to be financed by the state in order not to disappear, have already existed in history without state intervention. It is, of course, in the interest of the state to claim that this is not the case, as it is a very good way to maintain a corresponding monopoly without anyone objecting.

The second possibility is that the statist who raises the above objection is right; that project would really disappear without state support. What does this mean? Well, only so much that people are simply not interested in the project in question, or rather they want to invest their money in something else that they consider more important, and no one other than the person concerned can properly judge this importance.

Therefore, if the state implements a project that would not have been created without it, it actually does the people a disservice, because it takes their savings and invests them in something, instead of which the people in question would rather buy something else that is more important to them (if this were not the case, the project would have been created even without state intervention); therefore, it is a simple waste of resources on less important things at the expense of the more important ones.

A common counterargument is this: "People want the project, but they're struggling with poverty, so they just can't afford it." On closer reflection, however, we come to the fact that this is all the more in line with what was described above: The people in question are poor, so they prefer to buy food and other basic things with their money, and so then they cannot afford the given project; by the state forcing them to buy it anyway, it certainly won't help them.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: The state must provide people with things that they themselves do not want to pay voluntarily (to a given extent); these are, for example, subsidies for mass transport, firefighters and rescuers, certain types of art, and the like.
text:
First of all, it must be said that statist scaremongering on the topic of what would not exist without the state is indeed a very popular pastime of some people, but it is rarely based on any real basis; if we look into historical anarchies, we will find that many services that the general public thinks cannot function without the state have already been provided without the state in the past.

This is due to the fact that if there is a demand for a service in society and people are really willing to pay for such a service, an opportunity arises for entrepreneurs who can provide that service and make money from it; thus, an offer is created for each demand, and the more urgent the demand, the more people are willing to pay, which correspondingly increases the motivation of the bidders.

It is important to realize that in the event that a service provided by the state does not actually arise on the free market, it means only one thing: There is no interest in such a service, because its operation and provision costs more resources than how much benefit it brings to people, which means that if these resources were invested in another (earning) way, the benefit of society would increase without providing such a service.

This, by the way, refutes a favorite argument that statists like to use to defend various social experiments (often in transportation, but not only): "Even if it saves just one single human life, it's worth it." Not necessarily; resources are limited and another investment could save more lives or benefit people in some other way.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Just look at the "ordinary people", they just need the state to take care of them; they make a lot of stupid decisions and if it wasn't for the state, they would starve to death in the streets.
text:
The fact is that some people behave irresponsibly and often do not think much about their actions. But the reason why they are so is mainly because they can afford it, because they rely on the protection of an all-powerful state; and the more the state convinces them that it provides them with "safety" and "certainties", the less will be the need for these people to take care of themselves and bear responsibility.

The state inculcates in its citizens from a very young age, from school age, that one of the tasks of a proper state is to take care of the weak, the old, the helpless and all those who "were not lucky in life"; in this way, the state practically confirms to its citizens that if they have a problem, it will take care of them and provide for them, thereby actually taking over their responsibility for their own lives, and thus making them individuals without autonomy.

The sad truth is that if the state in any way mitigates the consequences of any type of irresponsible behavior, it also motivates people to this behavior; being irresponsible and not worrying about anything is of course very convenient (compared to building savings and providing for bad times), so people will not happily do it if someone promises to do it for them (obviously with other people's money).

People are not incapable of taking care of themselves. With a strong state behind them, they just don't have much reason to even attempt such a thing; until the state took responsibility for the people, they took care of themselves, even in conditions far worse than the ones we live in now. People aren't self-righteous idiots, they're just naturally comfortable and most don't want to take responsibility when they don't have to.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Banks must be regulated by the state to hold any fractional reserves; if they were not regulated in this way, they would issue an unlimited amount of money (after all, without state laws, anyone could print money).
text:
The reason why this fallacy is relatively widespread is extremely sad. It consists in the fact that the state has already distorted most people's idea of the essence and meaning of money to such an extent that almost no one can even imagine free market and non-state money; this confusion then results in ideas that private money could not work because everyone could print it.

The catch, of course, is that the state has established some currency as official and forces people to accept it, so if anyone were to be able to issue this money without any restrictions, it would be a disaster. However, in a free market there is no forced currency, the acceptance of which is enforced by force, ergo untrustworthy money that is created by someone simply will not be accepted in the market.

Another reason why banks in the free market cannot afford to keep fractional reserves too low is so-called hostile clearing, which is a form of competition between banks that buy as many of their competitor's banknotes as possible, then ask them to exchange these notes for gold - it is actually an artificially induced run on the rival bank; when the latter does not have enough gold, it goes bankrupt.

Even in history, free market banks functioned well, private money did not cause problems; as long as the currency was hedged, there were no business cycles. An example is the "Bank of Scotland" and the "Royal Bank of Scotland", which in the eighteenth century kept gold reserves very high without any regulation (due to hostile clearing), thereby preventing economic crises that affected neighboring England.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Banks must be heavily regulated because their deregulation caused the economic crisis; this crisis is also an example of the failure of the free market.
text:
If there is any law that restricts the free market and individual freedom, it is a regulation. If another law then comes into being that limits the first law in some way, this law can be described as deregulation. And if the government then introduces a third law that limits the validity of the second law, this law is again regulation, not deregulation.

With the first law, the state forced the people to adopt a single national currency, a completely illegitimate act of violence that governments mostly justified as the need to finance war activities (which are typically nothing more than another needless violence); selected banks were granted the privilege by the state to print and create this currency (based on some rules). So it was about regulation.

With another law, the state set stricter rules for banks to issue new money and make loans; although some label this law as regulatory and so-called "pro-market", however, considering that it is a limitation of the power of the banks given to them by the state despite the free market, this label is completely misleading. This law is therefore deregulatory.

Finally came a law that loosened the rules for banks to issue more money and make more loans; however, if the free market currency is typically 100% bullion-backed, while the state currency is only a fraction, a further reduction in the level of this backing is certainly no deregulation, no step toward the free market. Ergo, the laws that caused the economic recession were regulations, not deregulations.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Libertarians so often defend the outmoded and old-fashioned gold standard; if we went back to it, should we start carrying pouches and paying in gold again?
text:
A gold or silver backed currency is certainly not something that "has long since been outgrown and discarded as a bad concept"; the hedged currency was not actually abandoned by free people, but was forcibly abolished by states that needed to print unhedged money to finance their war appetites (often with politicians promising to return to the gold standard after the war).

Even if we leave aside the fact that by issuing money the state through banks is robbing its subjects (and thus doing practically the same thing as illegal counterfeiters), so that it is actually another form of taxation (from which this time the banks also profit), nothing changes the fact that a fiat currency is the cause of economic cycles and depressions (they only started to occur with a fiat currency; for the justification, look for the word "ABCT" on the Internet).

There is in principle no reasonable reason why the state should hold the currency; unlike other sectors of the market, where there are various pseudo-reasons centered on "protecting ordinary people", there is no such thing in the case of money (apart from the popular labeling of a hedged currency as a "long outdated concept"). A currency backed by precious metals (even a private one) worked for hundreds of years without problems around the world.

After the (re)introduction of the gold standard, it would of course not be necessary for all payments to be made by counting gold grains (although coins, especially silver ones, would probably find their place); in today's age of modern technology, of course, it would be possible to store gold in banks that would manage our accounts, allow card payments and the like, only the units would not be crowns, but grams of gold.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: In anarcho-capitalism, situations can arise in which injustice, inefficiency, injustice and all kinds of evils occur; so it won't be such a great social arrangement.
text:
Similar phenomena will naturally occur in anarcho-capitalism; similarly as in any social arrangement. Nobody offers a recipe for a perfect and ideal world, and anarcho-capitalists are no exception. It does not make sense to look for hypothetical situations in which some social arrangement can fail, but rather to look for an arrangement in which these situations occur least often.

No judgmental anarchist sees anarcho-capitalism as a panacea for all the world's problems; they claim only that anarcho-capitalism is a better social order than an arbitrary state. It is therefore of little use to merely point out the potential faults of anarcho-capitalism without mentioning another system (either the current one or some hypothetical one) that would be able to deal with these faults better.

There may even be anarcho-capitalist societies whose overall condition is worse than that of some state-controlled societies; if poor and uneducated barbarians live in anarchy, their standard of living will be lower than that of educated and wealthy people who live in a state, but both societies can be assumed to function better without a state than with it.

Simply pointing out the faults of anarcho-capitalism without mentioning any social order that can solve this problem better (and at the same time not cause other and worse problems) is practically equivalent to comparing anarcho-capitalism with an ideal - non-existent - society that solves all the world's problems that can potentially arise.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Anarcho-capitalism is nothing but social engineering; and this must be unequivocally rejected, because it is a nice piece of crap.
text:
If anarcho-capitalism is social engineering, then social engineering must be the design of an arbitrary social order. To build a state is to manipulate people through social engineering into submission to the state; if people are manipulated by the theories of anarcho-capitalism for anything, then only to be free and responsible for themselves.

Social engineering is typically used to manipulate people in order to benefit someone in particular by making the manipulated masses do what that person wants, which is most often to submit, let themselves be ruled by them, pay money for something they would not want to pay for without this manipulation, or change their behavior for the supposed "benefit of the whole" or "the welfare of society".

Anarcho-capitalism is the exact opposite; people will not be ruled by anyone, they will be free and take responsibility for themselves. The so-called "benefit of society" is the sum of the benefits of all its members, which, however, is best ensured by each individual, because only he knows best what he actually wants. There is no need for anyone to rule such a society and whom the supposed social engineering should serve.

The term "social engineering" can have many different meanings, and it cannot be ruled out that for some, anarcho-capitalist theories also fall under this term; however, if this is the case, it must consistently include practically any proposal to change our social order, so in principle it probably cannot be anything bad.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Anarcho-capitalism is a beautiful theory, but so was communism; in reality neither would work.
text:
First of all, it must be said that communism is definitely not a good theory, because it is entirely based on the teachings of Karl Marx, who was based on Ricardo's cost theory of value, which was refuted by Carl Menger as early as 1870, when he came up with the subjective theory of value; that this fact was ignored by those who were still trying to build bright tomorrows a hundred years later does not make communism a good theory.

Communism is no example of a system that works well in theory but is unworkable in practice; the theory of Communism was debunked long before a group of ignoramuses tried to put it into practice. Anarcho-capitalism has not yet been refuted on a theoretical level; yes, it can happen, however, until it does, we should treat it as an unproven theory and not compare it to communism.

Although anarchist societies have existed throughout history, they have been stable and successful; an example can be medieval Iceland, but also the USA at the time of colonization or medieval Ireland (in the latter case, there are doubts as to whether it was really anarchy; some call the given state anarchy, others claim that it was a large number of mini-states in a small area).

One can understandably object that it was a long time ago and today there is no modern functioning anarchy; this is true, but it does not invalidate the anarcho-capitalist theory in any way and does not put it on the level of the refuted communist theory (communism has always failed in practice, anarchy does not exist in modern society, but we do not know of any case of its failure; historically, on the contrary, it worked).

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: The tradition of states goes back thousands of years; if anarcho-capitalism were a better order of society, it would already exist somewhere; however, evolution clearly shows the superiority of the state over anarchy.
text:
It is only a few hundred years since the same could be said of slavery; slave societies had a tradition at least as long as states, they existed absolutely everywhere, slavery was quite common and nobody questioned it. And not only that! No one could even imagine a society in which there were no masters and slaves; slavery seemed to be a completely natural and unchangeable part of the world.

Everyone knew that "a negro can't take care of himself without a master"; just like today, it is clear that "man cannot take care of himself without the state". It was also (or is) obvious that we also need slavery (or the state) from an economic point of view, because otherwise it wouldn't work. Also, if slavery was so bad, how could it be so widespread? After all, there would be societies without slaves.

And when someone then compared the violence of a master to a slave to the same violence to a free man, it was completely absurd, and everyone knew at once that it could not be compared, since it was something completely different; just as everyone knows today that comparing taxes to protection money does not make sense, because they are completely different. Just read some texts from that time; similar arguments seriously failed.

What came next? It only took a few hundred years for the institution of slavery, with a tradition dating back thousands of years, to fall in almost all countries of the world. In the beginning, however, someone had to stand up, start talking about it, be ridiculed and considered a dreamer building castles in the air that have no connection with reality; yet he persevered, spread the idea, didn't give up and inspired others... Until finally freedom won.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Anarcho-capitalist theories assume that people will treat each other nicely, or at least always logically; but people aren't like that, you're missing out on real human qualities.
text:
I have encountered the objection that anarcho-capitalist theories attribute to people different qualities than they actually have countless times; but no one has ever been able to list for me which specific properties they are, and to show in any of my texts (or the texts of anarcho-capitalist authors to which I refer) where I assume some unrealistic properties or neglect real ones.

Sometimes someone objects that I do not account for human selfishness, but he is unable to show me exactly where; no wonder, as few things are further from the truth. After all, the free market and its functioning are largely based on the selfishness and greed of entrepreneurs who try to make money by providing people with services they are interested in.

Sometimes one can also meet with the objection that people do not always behave so logically that it fits into the usual economic theories about perfect competition and the like. Of course they don't breed! After all, this was one of the great objections of Ludwig von Mises and the entire Austrian school of economics, on which anarcho-capitalism is built, against mainstream economics, which rejects anarcho-capitalism.

So before you condemn anarcho-capitalist theories on the basis that they "do not take into account real people", please try to answer for yourself the question of whether such a thing actually happens, or which specific theses are based on such assumptions; if you really find such a specific place in anarcho-capitalist theories, I would be very happy if you let me know.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: People sometimes murder, rob, disrespect property, and initiate violence; as long as the principle of non-aggression is violated, anarcho-capitalism can never work.
text:
It is true that anarcho-capitalism is based on respect for property rights, but it does not require their 100% observance always and everywhere; it is understandable that there will always be people who do not respect the property of others, but if there are not too many such people, anarcho-capitalism will not significantly disrupt this (and if there are so many, then no state will save them either).

Although, for example, democracy is based on the fact that every citizen meeting certain criteria (typically age) has the right to participate in elections, even if someone accidentally denies someone this right (for example, locks them in a cellar and does not let them out), the elections will not be repeated because of this, and this system will still be called a democracy; nor will anarcho-capitalism disappear through a single violation of the principle of non-aggression.

Anarcho-capitalists do not assume that people will turn into saints out of nowhere and will observe the principle of non-aggression out of love for their neighbor, but rather that the function of protection against criminal elements will not be performed by the state, but by private companies (and as you know, private companies typically provide their services better than the state) and by the people themselves (whom the state will no longer prevent from arming).

A society in which property rights are respected is, on the whole, a better place for most of its members to live than a society in which the principle of non-aggression is not respected, which is related to the fact that, in the long run, trade is typically more beneficial to most people than war, which is expensive; countries go to war so much, among other things, because those who declare and conduct wars do not pay for them from their own money.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Anarchists are violent and want a bloody revolution!
text:
Some do; however, there are many anarchist schools. Some of them indeed preach violent revolution, but by no means all; anarcho-pacifists, for example, reject any violence (including defensive violence). Anarcho-capitalists allow violence only to remedy a situation where someone's property rights are being violated. So, from their point of view, is it legitimate to use violence against the state and plan a revolution?

Although defense against an aggressor is undoubtedly permissible, and states represent the greatest aggressors of today, it is certainly not legitimate to take an action that will make the situation worse as a result and in addition harm a lot of innocent people; and I claim that violent revolution is exactly such an action. Even if I were to ignore the ethical side of the matter, I will not support a violent revolution; for it cannot lead to success.

People can be forced to do anything; however, freedom cannot be imposed on them by force. Let us imagine that I should succeed in taking power and abolishing the state against the will of the people; what then? Either I will give them liberty, which they will immediately dispose of by forming a new state; or I will forbid it to them, which will make me a state myself (because I will limit their freedom by force). Either way, the result will be the state, not anarcho-capitalism.

What is the solution to this situation? The only way is to convince people that they don't need the state. When that happens, there will be no need for a violent revolution, because they can then peacefully vote democratically to abolish the state; however, as long as the states will, the revolution is completely meaningless for the reasons described above. So don't worry about anarcho-capitalists, we are not thugs; we fight with words, not with Molotov cocktails.

chapter: AMEN: analysis of many statist objections
name: Anarcho-capitalists completely ignore human rights, and nothing but property is sacred to them; this approach is completely unacceptable and inhumane.
text:
Although it is true that anarcho-capitalism is built on private property and the principle of non-aggression, it is not quite true that anarcho-capitalists ignore human rights, they only derive them from property rights; the huge advantage of human rights defined in this way is that they do not contradict each other, they do not go against each other and there is no dispute about what is still a human right and what is not.

So how are human rights described by property rights? So, for example, the right to life follows from the fact that when someone kills someone, they violate the victim's property rights to their body; freedom of speech is ensured in such a way that everyone can say what they want on their land (or with the consent of the owner of another's land); it is the same with freedom of religion, education and the like.

Property rights do not ensure human rights exactly in the form in which they are written, for example, in the inconsistent Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms, because all rights that can be derived from property rights are negative rights, not positive; one can assert negative rights even without initiating violence against someone else (positive rights cannot; therefore LZPS is inconsistent).

Examples of negative and positive rights: the negative right to education means that no one can stop me from getting an education; a positive right to education means that someone will be forced to provide me with an education; the negative right to housing means that no one can forbid me to have a home; a positive right to housing means that someone must provide housing for me. Only negative rights result from property rights.
